title: Groebner-fan bi-weight order for the bilinear Semaev S3 subspace system
handbook_section: 17.1.4.2 Parameter estimation using the Groebner fan of an ideal
mechanism: Binary curve, x3 = x(R) fixed, x1 = sum a_i v_i and x2 = sum b_j w_j with v_i, w_j in F_2-subspaces V, W of GF(2^n). S3 = x1^2 x2^2 + x1^2 x3^2 + x2^2 x3^2 + x1 x2 x3 + b (up to curve constants). Squaring is F_2-linear, so S3 has no a_i a_j or b_i b_j monomials, and its n bit equations are affine-bilinear in (a,b). Use the Groebner fan of (equations + a_i^2 - a_i) to choose the weight vector. Candidates are the bi-weights (1^m,0^m), (0^m,1^m) and sums, which keep F4 Macaulay matrices bi-homogeneous, instead of defaulting to grevlex.
claim: On the bilinear S3 system with |V|=|W|=2^m, m in 8..12, the best fan-selected bi-weight order lowers the largest F4 matrix (rows x cols) by at least 2x against grevlex. F4 total cost still stays above the direct baseline of 2^m quadratic root-solves plus linear membership checks.
prediction: Matrix-size ratio (best bi-weight / grevlex) in 0.3 to 0.7, with the gain shrinking as m grows. F4 time stays at least 10x above the 2^m lookup baseline for m >= 10. The gain is real for the solver but gives no route past enumeration.
cheapest_test: Toy n=2m=20 over GF(2^20), random b, random target x3. Build the 20 bit equations over F_2[a_1..a_10,b_1..b_10]. Run msolve or Sage F4 under grevlex, under weights (1^10,0^10) refined by grevlex, and under 5 random fan weights. Record max matrix dimensions, degree of regularity and wall time over 50 targets. Compare with brute force over a (2^10) with Gaussian elimination in b.
falsifier: Best bi-weight matrix size is at least 0.8x grevlex over 50 targets, or the bi-weight order loses a paired sign test (p<0.05). If F4 under any order beats the 2^m lookup, that is a surprise and counts as a win.
lean_sketch: Definitions: Bits k := Fin k -> Bool; structure Sys (m n) := (c : Bits m -> Bits m -> Bits n) with hypotheses bilinear_a : c (a+a') b = c a b + c a' b, and likewise bilinear_b. smoothCount V := #{(a,b) | S3 a b = 0}. Provable in core Lean: (1) S3 is affine-bilinear given sq_add : sq (u+v) = sq u + sq v; (2) smoothCount = sum over a of (if consistent then 2^(dim ker) else 0), by linear algebra over Fin 2 with decide-checked toy n. Not provable: any bound on F4 matrix size; that stays an empirical Cost.descent entry compared numerically with the baseline Cost (factorBase = 0, relations = 2^m * c1).
novelty_note: Generic F4/F5 on Weil-restricted Semaev is integrated; the bilinear-in-F_2-bits structure of S3 and fan-selected multi-weight orders for it are not. Likely modest gain; main value is closing the question.

title: Kloosterman/Walsh-spectrum ranking of affine cosets for a non-invariant factor base
handbook_section: 17.2.1 Mutually unbiased bases (Gauss/character-sum flatness over F_{2^n})
mechanism: MUB constructions rest on flat character-sum spectra over a family of bases. Take the factor base as an affine coset V+t. S3's quadratic in x2 is solvable exactly when T(x1) = T(x3), where T(x) = Tr(x + sqrt(b)/x), i.e. point validity. The count of valid points in V+t is 2^(m-1) plus half a Kloosterman-type sum over V^perp. Rank cosets t (and normal-basis windows V) by that dual-sum spectrum instead of drawing t at random.
claim: Among the 2^(n-m) cosets of a fixed V, the number of valid x-coordinates, and hence relations per target per factor-base element, has spread above binomial noise. The Walsh/Kloosterman prediction ranks cosets with Spearman rho >= 0.6 against measured relation yield, so best-of-K coset gives at least 1.05x more relations per unit factor-base size than a median coset.
prediction: Spread of valid-count across cosets is about 1.0 to 1.5x the binomial standard deviation. Predictor correlates at rho about 0.6 to 0.9. Best-of-64 gain is 1.03 to 1.10x in relation yield, weakening as n grows because the sum is O(2^(n/2)) against 2^m.
cheapest_test: n=17, m=8, all 512 cosets of one V. For each, count valid points, then measure actual S3 relations over 2000 random targets by full pair enumeration. Compute the predicted valid count by the Walsh transform of x -> (-1)^T(x) over V^perp and correlate. Repeat for 5 random b.
falsifier: Spearman rho < 0.3 between predicted and measured yield, or best-of-64 yield gain < 1.02x with a bootstrap 95% CI containing 1.
lean_sketch: Definitions: Coset V t := fun x => x in V + t; validCount via smoothCount; hypothesis hpart: cosets partition the group, so sum_t smoothCount (V t) = total. Provable without Mathlib: the average over cosets equals total / 2^(n-m) (finite-sum partition lemma over Fin), so any gain is a pure variance effect and cannot raise the mean. A deviation bound by 2^(n/2) needs Weil's bound, carried as a named hypothesis kloosterman_bound, not provable here. Cost.relations scales by 1/(yield ratio) only under the measured ratio.
novelty_note: Subspace FBs are integrated; selecting the affine shift and window by a character-sum spectrum is not. Expected effect is small and may be pure noise.

title: Frobenius-invariant subspaces are cyclic codes: structural audit and window-factor-base merge factor
handbook_section: 17.1.6.3 Linear polynomial dynamical systems
mechanism: In a normal basis Frobenius on GF(2^n) is the cyclic shift of F_2^n, a linear PDS. Its invariant subspaces are the cyclic codes of length n, i.e. divisors of x^n - 1 over F_2 (n odd). If n is prime and 2 is a primitive root mod n, x^n - 1 = (x-1)*Phi_n with Phi_n irreducible, so the only invariant subspaces have dim 0, 1, n-1, n. This holds for n = 53, 83, 131 (ord_n(2) = n-1; checked by hand for 131: 2^65 = -1, 2^26 = 53, 2^10 = 107 mod 131). For n = 109, ord = 36 gives invariant dims 36, 72, 108 only; for n = 113, ord = 28. So a Frobenius-invariant factor base of dim about n/2 does not exist for most Koblitz sizes. Proposed replacement: the window V = span{x, x^2, ..., x^(2^(m-1))} (a cyclic-shift window), whose Frobenius merge factor is set by window overlap, about 2, not n.
claim: (i) For n in {53, 83, 131} no Frobenius-invariant F_2-subspace of dimension strictly between 1 and n-1 exists. (ii) For the window V of dim m about n/2 the number of Frobenius classes of V is |V|/c with c in [1.8, 3] independent of n, so the orbit quotient of this factor base shrinks columns by about 2, not by n.
prediction: (i) Exactly the 4 trivial invariant subspaces (certain by the factorisation). (ii) Mean class size about 3.0 (+- 0.1), classes/|V| about 0.5 (range 0.33 to 0.56). Linear-algebra B^2 term falls about 4x at best, with an extra per-entry lambda^j twist factor.
cheapest_test: Part (i): factor x^n - 1 over F_2 for n = 53, 83, 109, 113, 131 (one polynomial factorisation each). Part (ii): n = 19 and 29; enumerate all 2^(n/2) window elements, compute classes by repeated squaring, report class-size distribution and classes/|V|. Repeat for n = 11, 13, 37.
falsifier: (i) any factor of degree between 2 and n-2 for n in {53, 83, 131}. (ii) column reduction >= 4 for window V at n = 29 or 37.
lean_sketch: Definitions: rot : Bits n -> Bits n (cyclic shift); Invariant S := forall v, S v -> S (rot v), plus xor-closure. orbitRepresentatives N k = N / k is the accounting lemma; the idea shows it is the right count only when every orbit has full size k and lies inside the factor base. Provable by decide for n = 5, 11, 13 (2 primitive): the only xor-closed rot-invariant sets are the 4 trivial ones. Generally, with hypothesis hprim : orderOf2 n = n-1, any invariant subspace containing a vector with both a 0 and a 1 coordinate is the full non-constant space (needs hand-built gcd over Bool). Window class count: the number of window elements whose k-shift stays in the window is 2^(m-k), by bit counting.
novelty_note: Frobenius-invariant FBs are listed as integrated; the existence obstruction by ord_n(2) and the window-merge replacement are not. Part (i) is a pure fact check, part (ii) quantifies the loss.

title: Overlap-bounded, degree-balanced relation selection (Hamming-correlation design) before filtering
handbook_section: 17.3.5 Sequences with small Hamming correlation
mechanism: Frequency-hopping sequences from Reed-Solomon codewords (i, c_i) have pairwise Hamming correlation at most k-1, and every symbol (i, c) occurs equally often. Treat each collected relation as a support set over the B factor-base columns. Choose a subset greedily so that column coverage is balanced and pairwise support overlap is capped (the low-correlation property), using the RS design as the target degree-and-overlap profile. Singleton/clique filtering acts after the matrix is built; this acts before, aiming at duplicate or near-duplicate rows and starved columns.
claim: At fixed B with weight-3 relations from a toy Semaev decomposition, the number of selected relations needed for full column rank mod r is at least 5% lower under RS-profile greedy selection than under uniform subsampling of the same pool, with final matrix weight not higher.
prediction: Relations to full rank are 3 to 12% fewer (central 6%). Gain shrinks with larger pool size since random pools are already near-balanced; zero gain when pool size equals the needed count.
cheapest_test: Toy n=23 binary curve, subspace FB of dim 11 (B about 2000), pool of 6000 weight-3 relations. For 200 seeds find the smallest N such that the first N relations (uniform order vs greedy-balanced order) give rank B-1 mod a 31-bit prime. Compare paired N differences with a bootstrap CI. A/A control: shuffled arm labels.
falsifier: Paired mean reduction of N below 2%, or a bootstrap 95% CI for the reduction including 0 while the A/A arm is centred at 0.
lean_sketch: Definitions: Relation B := Fin B -> Int; support r := {i | r i != 0}; Overlap r s := card (support r inter support s); Coverage c := number of relations touching column c. Hypothesis hcover : forall c, Coverage c >= 1. Provable in core: (1) uncovered_column_undetermined: a column with coverage 0 forces rank <= B-1 (explicit kernel vector e_c); (2) for an RS design over Fin q (small prime q by decide) each symbol is covered exactly q^(k-1) times and overlap <= k-1. The rank-at-N claim is empirical; Cost.relations is read from measured N, and 'selected <= uniform' is a measured inequality, not provable.
novelty_note: Filtering after the fact is integrated; pre-selection to a bounded-correlation profile is not. Honest prior is a small gain.

title: Coded sparse matrix-vector product (fountain-type code) for block Wiedemann on Spot
handbook_section: 17.3.8 Coding over networks
mechanism: Network-coding style erasure codes reconstruct from any sufficiently large subset of coded packets. Split the relation matrix A (mod r, sparse, weight w per row) into k row blocks and add n-k parity blocks, each the sum of a small random subset (degree about ln k, LT/fountain style). Coded SpMV results from any about k(1+eps) of n workers recover A v, so a preempted Spot node does not force restart or checkpoint replay. Dense MDS rows would multiply row weight by k and lose; the sparse code keeps weight inflation near ln k.
claim: With per-worker preemption probability q per iteration, sparse-coded SpMV with redundancy n/k = 1.25 has expected time per iteration at most 1.15x the no-failure time, and at q = 0.1 beats both 2x replication and checkpoint-restart (restart cost 20 iterations) in total core-seconds.
prediction: Added flops per iteration are 1.3 to 1.6x. Break-even preemption rate above which coding wins is q about 0.03 to 0.08; below that plain checkpointing wins. Gain at most about 1.4x in the linear-algebra Cost at q=0.1, zero or negative at q<0.03.
cheapest_test: Simulation on a toy matrix B=20000, w=6, k=16 row blocks mod a 61-bit prime, n=20 workers; Monte-Carlo preemption q in {0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3}; count total multiply-adds including decoding and restarts for four policies (restart, 2x replication, dense RS, sparse fountain). Verify decode against uncoded A v.
falsifier: Sparse-coded total cost >= min(replication, restart) at q = 0.1, or decode failure rate above 1e-3 at 1.25 redundancy.
lean_sketch: Definitions: Cost with linearAlgebra := total mult-adds; relation matrix as Fin R -> Fin B -> Int; code as Fin n -> (Fin k -> Bool) (parity selection). Hypothesis hdec: the selection matrix restricted to any received index set has full column rank k (decide for small k,n). Provable: given hdec, A v is a linear function of received coded results (elimination over a field, modulus prime as hypothesis). The cost inequality is arithmetic on explicit parameters, provable; the preemption model is a probabilistic hypothesis only.
novelty_note: Block Wiedemann/Lanczos are integrated; erasure-coded straggler tolerance for sparse SpMV is a hardware/orchestration change measured in total cost, and is not a mathematical speedup. Report only against matched restart policies.

title: Online rank tracking with early stop at target determination
handbook_section: 17.3.8 Coding over networks (online decoding), with 17.1.6.4 conjunctive-network propagation
mechanism: Network-coding decoders keep an echelon basis updated as each packet arrives and report the moment a symbol becomes decodable. Keep an incremental reduced echelon form of the (B+1)-column system mod r (FB logs plus target column) and stop when e_target lies in the row space, not at full rank or a fixed excess. A conjunctive-network propagation rule (a column is determined when it is the only unknown in a relation whose other entries are determined) gives cheap early partial determination of low-weight parts.
claim: On toy weight-3 systems the median number of relations at which the target log becomes determined is at most 0.97x the number needed for full column rank (B-1), and a fixed margin B+20 overshoots the online stopping time by at least 3%.
prediction: Online stopping time / full-rank time about 0.93 to 0.99 (central 0.96). Fixed margin overshoots by 2 to 6%. Gain is at most a few percent of the relations phase, since random sparse systems become determined only near full rank.
cheapest_test: n=21 toy curve, B about 700, weight-3 relations mod a 31-bit prime. For 300 seeds record N_det (first N where the target log is determined, by rank check on the augmented system) and N_full (rank B-1), and compare with the fixed rule N = B+20. A/A arm: same policy, different seed streams.
falsifier: Median N_det / N_full >= 0.99 with a CI above 0.98, so no gain beyond the fixed margin.
lean_sketch: Definitions: Relation B := Fin B -> Int; Determined M j := e_j in row space of M over ZMod r (hypothesis hprime); DLPInstance with log : G equiv Fin n; FactorBase B := Fin B -> G. Provable: monotonicity (adding a relation never un-determines a column) by induction on list append, hence N_det <= N_full per instance; and the solve lemma (determined implies the log of F_j is a fixed linear function of relation constants). Not provable: the distribution of N_det. Cost.relations := N_det.
novelty_note: Over-collection margins and 2-core filtering are standard; stopping on determination of the actual target is a collection-phase stopping rule. Expected gain is small.

title: Canalyzing-depth and minimal-determining-set pre-sieve for the post-trace decomposition predicate
handbook_section: 17.1.4.1 The minimal-sets algorithm (with 17.1.6.1 Nested canalyzing functions)
mechanism: The minimal-sets algorithm finds smallest sets of input variables determining an output from data. Apply it to P(a) = [x2(a) in W] over the bit vector a of x1 in V, after the trace test T(x1) = T(x3) (point validity) has been applied. A nested canalyzing function has a variable whose single value forces the output. If the n bit components of the Weil-restricted S3, or P, had canalyzing depth above 0, a few bits of a would fix the outcome, giving a cheap pre-sieve before the half-trace and membership test. Otherwise there is no pre-sieve beyond the trace test.
claim: P and the n components of the bilinear S3 have canalyzing depth 0 for at least 99% of targets, and the minimal determining set of P has size at least 0.9 m, so no pre-sieve using at most m/4 bits discards more than 5% of post-trace candidates.
prediction: Depth 0 in over 99% of component functions; minimal determining set about m (0.9 to 1.0 m); best pre-sieve discards 0 to 3% beyond the trace test. Expected outcome is negative; the point is to close this route cheaply.
cheapest_test: n=18, m=9, 500 targets. Enumerate all 512 values of a per target, compute P(a), run minimal-sets (or brute force over subsets up to size 3) and test every (variable, value) for canalyzing. Also test all n component bit functions of S3. Negative control: random Boolean functions with the same bias.
falsifier: A determining set of size <= m/4 for more than 5% of targets, or a pre-sieve discarding at least 10% of post-trace candidates with zero lost relations, or canalyzing depth >= 1 in more than 5% of component functions (random control about 2^-(m-1)).
lean_sketch: Definitions: Pred m := Bits m -> Bool; Canalyzing f := exists i v out, forall a, a i = v -> f a = out; DetSet f S := forall a a', (forall i in S, a i = a' i) -> f a = f a'. Provable by decide for explicit toy m (<=5) that a given f has no canalyzing variable. Provable lemma: pre-sieve soundness (no relation lost) follows from DetSet; smoothCount = sum over a of P a. The probabilistic depth claim is empirical.
novelty_note: Trace pre-sieve (halving) is standard; a learned bit-subset pre-sieve is untested. Prior is negative.

title: Early termination of block Wiedemann by confirmed linear-complexity profile
handbook_section: 17.2.4 Period finding (applied to the linear-recurring Krylov sequence; with 17.3.1 sequences)
mechanism: The Wiedemann sequence u^T A^i v is a linear recurring sequence over F_r, and its minimal polynomial is the order of a recurrence, found by Berlekamp-Massey. The standard schedule runs a fixed N/m + N/n + O(1) iterations. Instead run BM online, record the linear-complexity profile L(t), and stop when L has been stable for a certificate window of delta extra terms. The chance the window misses a later jump is about r^(-delta). Use this probabilistic verification, as in order checking in period finding, to stop at about 2 L* terms. After relation filtering, kernel and repeated-eigenvalue structure may make L* smaller than N/m.
claim: For filtered relation matrices from toy Semaev decompositions, the stable linear complexity L* of the block sequence is at least 3% below the worst-case bound N/m + N/n, so confirmed early termination saves at least 3% of SpMV iterations with failure probability below 1e-6.
prediction: Savings about 0 to 4% (central 1%). Generic random sparse matrices have L* equal to the bound; the saving comes only from kernel dimension, about (kernel dim)/N of the iterations. Null result is the most likely outcome.
cheapest_test: B=3000 weight-3 toy matrix mod a 31-bit prime after clique filtering; run scalar and block (m=n=4) Wiedemann with online BM; log L(t) and first stable time; compare with the fixed schedule over 100 matrices and check the recovered kernel vector.
falsifier: Median saving below 2%, or any early-terminated run returning a wrong kernel vector (failure rate above the stated 1e-6 bound over 1e4 runs).
lean_sketch: Definitions: Seq := Nat -> ZMod r (hypothesis hprime); LinComp s t := least L such that a recurrence of length L fits s_0..s_t. Provable in core: monotonicity of LinComp in t, and LinComp <= N for s_i = u^T A^i v given hypothesis hcayley : minpoly A has degree <= N (Cayley-Hamilton not available). With hcayley the stopping rule at 2*LinComp + delta is sound whenever the recurrence is verified on the window. The failure probability r^(-delta) needs a counting argument over random u, v: hypothesis only. Cost.linearAlgebra := 2 * L* * nonzeros.
novelty_note: Block Wiedemann is integrated and early termination is partly folklore; the claim is only that filtered IC matrices have measurable slack. Likely null.

title: Frobenius-linear decision test for 2-point decomposition over interval factor bases
handbook_section: 16.7.2 Arithmetic using polynomial operations (with 16.3.3.12 linearization)
mechanism: Binary Semaev S3 = pi^2 + x3*pi + x3^2*s^2 + b with pi=x1*x2, s=x1+x2. Squaring is F2-linear, so for fixed target x3 this is an F2-linear equation in the bits of (pi,s). Take V = span{1,t,..,t^(d-1)} with 2d-1 <= n. Then pi = x1*x2 is a plain polynomial product with no reduction, so pi lies in W = polys of degree < 2d-1 (dim 2d-1). The set {s in V : x3^2 s^2 + b in Phi(W)}, with Phi(pi)=pi^2+x3*pi, is an affine subspace of V of dimension >= 3d-1-n, found by one n x (3d-1) Gaussian elimination. Only the candidates in that subspace need the root test (half-trace, then check the roots lie in V). This replaces the usual enumeration of all 2^d values of x1.
claim: For interval V (or any u*V, or t-Frobenius images) with 3d-1 <= n, deciding whether x(R) is a sum of two factor-base x-coordinates costs poly(n) (about n^3/64 word ops), not 2^d. The returned decompositions are exactly those found by enumeration over V.
prediction: Per-relation cost drops from 2^(n-d) to about 2^(n-2d)*n^3/64 for d <= n/3. Total IC cost, relations plus linear algebra, is about 2^(n-d)+2^(2d), optimised at d=n/3 with total about 2^(2n/3) against 2^n for the enumeration m=2 baseline. At n=31, d=9 the per-target speedup is at least 100x and the decomposition sets are identical. Extra gap to rho at n=131 is about 2^22 (2^87 vs 2^65.5). The same oracle serves descent steps.
cheapest_test: Toy Koblitz a=1, b=1, n=31 (also 23 and 37), d=9, polynomial basis. For 2^16 random targets x3, run the enumeration decomposer and the linear decider. Compare the decomposition sets for equality and time both. Fit log2(cost per relation) against n at d=floor(n/3).
falsifier: Any target where the linear candidate set misses a genuine decomposition. Or speedup under 10x at n=31, d=9. Or slope of log2(cost per relation) vs n at d=n/3 not within 20% of 1/3.
lean_sketch: Hypotheses: a type X with addition and Frobenius sq that is additive, sq (a+b)=sq a+sq b (stated as a hypothesis, no Mathlib), and hS3 : decomposes x1 x2 x3 -> sq (x1*x2) + x3*(x1*x2) + sq (x3*(x1+x2)) + b = 0. Define cand x3 : List X from the V-basis, and relCostPerHit n d := 2^(n-2*d). Provable: soundness (decomposes -> mem cand), by unfolding hS3 and additivity of Phi. Provable: relCostPerHit n d <= 2^(n-d) for d >= 0, via Nat.pow_le_pow_right. Not provable without linear algebra: the candidate-dimension bound 3d-1-n (state rank-nullity as a hypothesis). The Cost record would carry relations := 2^(n-2d)*polyN.

title: Kneser/Freiman-extremal factor-base subspaces (small V*V)
handbook_section: 16.7.2-16.7.3 (polynomial and matrix multiplication structure)
mechanism: The linearised test of idea 1 costs 2^(3d-1-n) candidates, driven by dim(V*V), where V*V is the span of products. Linear Kneser (Hou-Leung-Xiang) gives dim(V*V) >= 2 dim V - dim H, with equality for V in an arithmetic progression of basis monomials (geometric progression of powers t^(g*i)) and H the stabiliser. A random d-subspace has dim(V*V)=min(n,d(d+1)/2). Classify and count the extremal subspaces (u * span{t^(g i)}) and pick one that also makes the factor base Frobenius-compatible.
claim: Among d-dim subspaces of GF(2^n), n prime, those with dim(V*V)=2d-1 are exactly the u*span{1,w,..,w^(d-1)} for w generating the field, and only these give the 3d-1-n candidate dimension. Random subspaces give dim(V*V)=min(n,d(d+1)/2).
prediction: For n=23, d=7, random V gives dim(V*V)=23 (all of F) and zero speedup. Interval V gives 13. Of 1000 sampled subspaces with a planted extra relation, none other than the interval family drops below 2d-1. The number of extremal subspaces is about 2^n * n / n, i.e. about 2^n/(dimension-preserving symmetries).
cheapest_test: n=17..23, d=5..8: enumerate or sample subspaces, compute dim(V*V) by Gaussian elimination of pairwise products, histogram the values. Check the minimum equals 2d-1 only on the AP family.
falsifier: A non-AP subspace with dim(V*V) < 2d-1 (n prime), contradicting the Kneser prediction. Or random subspaces with dim(V*V)<min(n,d(d+1)/2) at rate above 1%.

The converse Kneser direction needs a hypothesis (state the Kneser bound as an axiom-parameter). Cost record: relations := 2^(n - (2d-1)) scaling with prodSpan.

title: Hankel rank spectrum of the trace-component pencil and yield overdispersion
handbook_section: 16.3.3.8-16.3.3.9 Rank attacks / MinRank
mechanism: Component gamma of the Weil-restricted S3 has quadratic part Tr(delta*x1*x2) with delta=gamma^(1/2)+gamma*x3. On V=interval the d x d bilinear matrix is Hankel H_delta(i,j)=Tr(delta t^(i+j)), whose rank is the linear complexity of the trace sequence prefix. For 2d-1 <= n, delta -> (s_0..s_{2d-2}) is onto, so the Daykin count gives #delta of rank r (1<=r<d) = 3*2^(n-2d+2r-1), up to a factor 2 from the 1-dim kernel of gamma -> delta. The number of decompositions of a target is 2^-n * sum_gamma +/- 2^(2d - rank/2) (Walsh spectrum of quadratic forms), dominated by low-rank gamma.
claim: The distribution of decomposition counts over random targets is overdispersed relative to Poisson(2^(2d-n)), with variance inflation set by the low-rank Hankel spectrum. Low-rank combinations of the n equations (rank r) become linear after branching on r bit-forms.
prediction: n=19,d=8: number of delta of Hankel rank 1 is 48 and rank 2 is 192, exactly matching 3*2^(n-2d+2r-1). Variance/mean of decomposition counts over all targets exceeds 1 by a computable amount (about 1+ small), measurable at n=17..21.
cheapest_test: n=19,d=8: loop over all 2^19 delta, compute Hankel rank, histogram versus formula. Then for all 2^19 targets count decompositions by brute force and compare Var/Mean against the Walsh-sum prediction.
falsifier: Histogram deviates from 3*2^(n-2d+2r-1) (beyond the 2x kernel factor), or Var/Mean equals 1 within sampling error across n=17..21, meaning no exploitable overdispersion.
lean_sketch: Definitions: hankelRank : (Fin (2*d-1) -> Bool) -> Nat, count : Nat -> Nat for sequences of rank r. Hypothesis: Daykin counting formula as a lemma statement (provable for small d by decide, e.g. d=2,3, with Fin enumeration). Statement: sum_r count r = 2^(2d-1) (provable) and count 0 = 1. title: Automorphism-orbit quotient (order 3/6) for j=0 curves over F_q^n with q = 1 mod 3
handbook_section: 16.6.5 Endomorphisms (with 16.6.4 Restriction of scalars)
mechanism: For y^2=x^3+b every S_m is weighted-homogeneous: all monomials have degree = 1 mod 3, so S_m(w x)=w S_m(x) for a cube root w of unity, which lies in F_q when q=1 mod 3. Any F_q-subspace factor base V is then closed under x->w x and under negation, so the symmetry group has order 6. Quotienting columns by this action gives B/6 orbit representatives. A relation for target R gives the relation for w R = lambda R mod l, and in the quotient they are the same row. Solve the symmetrised system in the invariants x_i^3.
claim: With the order-6 orbit quotient the number of relations needed is B/6 instead of B/2 (negation only). Per-trial decomposition probability is unchanged, so relation-collection cost falls by 3x on top of negation, and the linear algebra size by 3x.
prediction: Toy q=97, n=3 (q^n about 2^19.8), j=0, prime-order subgroup with l = 1 mod 3: relations to reach full rank ratio (negation-only)/(order-6) = 3.0 +/- 10%. Degree of regularity of the invariant system does not increase.
cheapest_test: Run the existing Diem-style IC on a j=0 toy twice (negation-only orbit reps vs order-6 reps) with the same V, counting relations to full rank and trials; compare ratio to 3.
falsifier: Ratio of relations-to-full-rank below 2.5, or the quotient having rank deficiency from lambda-twisted signs (log relation not consistent mod l).
lean_sketch: Hypotheses: act : Fin 6 -> G -> G with log(act j g) = lam^j * log g mod ell, lam^2+lam+1 = 0 mod ell. Provable: relation count needed = orbitRepresentatives B 6 + overhead <= orbitRepresentatives B 2 + overhead (Nat.div_le_div_left), and a Cost record with relations := B/6 * trialsPerRelation. title: Optimal normal basis canonical orbit representative and trace as parity
handbook_section: 16.7.4-16.7.5 Normal bases / optimal normal bases
mechanism: GF(2^131) has a type-II ONB: 2n+1=263 is prime and 2 has order 131 mod 263 (2^131=1 since (2/263)=1). Likewise n=53 (107 prime, 2 primitive). In an ONB, Frobenius is a cyclic bit shift, Tr(x) is the parity of the coordinates, and multiplication has complexity 2n-1 (261 AND gates). Frobenius-orbit canonicalisation is the lexicographic least rotation of the n-bit string (Booth, O(n) bit ops), with no field squarings. Compare to polynomial basis, which needs up to n-1 squarings.
claim: With the Frobenius-orbit factor base, canonicalising each candidate x-coordinate costs about n bit-ops in ONB against about (n-1) squarings (about 0.1-1 GAE each at the section 5a band) in polynomial basis, a cost-model change measured in counted unit. Basis change cost is paid once per curve.
prediction: At n=131 the orbit-canonicalisation share of relation-collection cost is 5-20% in polynomial basis and below 1% in ONB; end-to-end relation-collection speedup is 1.05-1.25x. Below 5% share at n=53 means no gain.

falsifier: Canonicalisation under 3% of per-relation cost at all three prices in polynomial basis (no headroom), or ONB multiplication overhead outweighing the saving (end-to-end ratio < 1.0 at 1 GAE).

title: Koblitz twin-curve amortisation: S3 is independent of a
handbook_section: 16.4.1.3 Special curves / 16.4.2.2 Pairings and twists
mechanism: For y^2+xy=x^3+a x^2+b the polynomial S3 does not contain a. Solutions of the x-only system over F_q are therefore relations on E_a or on its quadratic twist E_{a+1} (Koblitz a=0 and a=1 are twists). A mixed pair (P1 in E_0, P2 in E_1) has conjugate sum with x(P1+P2) != x(P1-P2), so x3 lies in F_q only for degenerate cases. So each F_q-solution is pure E_0 or pure E_1.
claim: A single decomposition run over V yields relations for both curves: about 50% of solutions are E_0-relations and 50% E_1-relations, mixed under 1%. One solve serves DLP instances on both curves, 2x amortisation. For a single curve, half the solved solutions are discarded unless filtered by the type Tr(x+sqrt(b)/x)=Tr(a).
prediction: Toy n=23, a=1, b=1: among all F_q solutions of S3=0 with x1,x2 in V, 50% +/- 2% are E_0-pure, 50% E_1-pure, mixed < 1%. Throughput per solved system for a two-instance workload is 2.0x.
cheapest_test: n=23, d=8: enumerate all (x1,x2) in V^2, compute all x3 roots of S3, classify types of the three x's by the trace test, tabulate counts.
falsifier: Mixed solutions above 1%, or pure split differing from 50/50 by more than 5%, or no two-instance workload exists in the lab protocol (then no measured improvement).
lean_sketch: Definitions: type : X -> Bool (trace condition), S3 a-free. Hypothesis hmix : type x1 != type x2 -> not (exists x3 in F_q, S3 x1 x2 x3 = 0 and nondegenerate). Provable: S3 a-independence (the definition ignores a); with hmix, solutions partition into pure0 and pure1, so smoothCount_total = smoothCount_E0 + smoothCount_E1 (Nat arithmetic). Cost: relations amortised := total / 2 for two instances, provable from the partition. hmix itself needs curve arithmetic, so state it as hypothesis.
novelty_note: Solving a-independent S3 for two twin instances is a throughput trick for paired workloads; for the single ECC2K-130 target it gives only filter hygiene. Report honestly as an amortisation, not a single-instance improvement.

title: Density-evolution threshold for relation filtering overhead
handbook_section: 16.3.3.12 Direct attacks using polynomial solvers (sparse linear solving); coding-theory cross-over
mechanism: Relation rows have weight m over B orbit-representative columns, so the matrix is the parity-check of an irregular LDPC-like code. Singleton/clique filtering is peeling decoding. Density evolution predicts the surviving 2-core as a function of the relation/column ratio c=r/B: for uniform 3-uniform hypergraphs the 2-core appears at c*=0.818 (m=4: 0.772, m=2: 0.5). Column popularity is not uniform for orbit/Frobenius bases, giving a degree-distribution-dependent threshold.
claim: Choosing c just above the full-rank requirement c=1+epsilon yields a filtered core whose size is predicted by the density-evolution fixed point within 5%. The cost-optimal overhead is where marginal relation-collection cost equals marginal core-size cost, predictable without running linear algebra.
prediction: For m=3 with a uniform factor base the core fraction at c=1.02 is 0.45-0.60 of B; at c=1.2 it is within 3% of the fixed-point prediction. With the measured column degree distribution from toy Frobenius-orbit runs, the predicted core size matches within 5% and the optimal c differs from the current default.
cheapest_test: On archived toy relation sets (n=23..29), sweep c from 0.8 to 1.3 by subsampling, measure core size after peeling, compare with the density-evolution recursion x = 1-exp(-c m x^(m-1))-type fixed point using measured degrees.
falsifier: Core size deviates more than 15% from prediction, or the lab's existing filtering already operates within 2% of the optimal c (no headroom).
lean_sketch: Definitions: Relation rows as Fin B -> Int with weight m; peel : List Relation -> List Relation removing a row with a column of count 1; Cost record linearAlgebra := coreSize^2. Provable: peel preserves the solution set of the DLP system on remaining columns (singleton column elimination lemma) and terminates (list length decreases, Nat.lt_wfRel). The threshold fixed point is not provable without analysis; state as a numeric hypothesis checked by decide on a rational grid.

title: Trace dead-target filter for 2-decompositions in a trace-zero subspace
handbook_section: 16.3.3.1-16.3.3.2 linearization equations / critical bilinear relations (big-field Frobenius-additive structure, 16.3.2.4)
mechanism: Binary curve y^2+xy=x^3+ax^2+b: S3(x1,x2,z)=(x1x2+z(x1+x2))^2+z*x1x2+b. With s=x1+x2, p=x1x2 this is A(p)=z^2 s^2+b where A(p)=p^2+zp is F2-additive with image {w: Tr(w/z^2)=0}. Solvability therefore forces the linear condition Tr(s)=Tr(b/z^2). If the factor-base subspace V lies in ker Tr then s in V gives Tr(s)=0, so a target x(R)=z has NO decomposition P1+-P2=+-R with x1,x2 in V unless Tr(b/z^2)=0. One bit test on the target discards half of all targets before any enumeration; live targets carry double the expected relation yield.
claim: For V a subspace of ker Tr, every z with Tr(b/z^2)=1 has zero pairs (x1,x2) in V^2 with S3=0; every z with Tr(b/z^2)=0 has on average twice the unconditional mean count. Point additions per relation in the m=2 loop (descent step or m=2 collection) fall from 2^(n-k) to 2^(n-k-1).
prediction: Exactly 50% (+-2%) of targets are dead; zero counterexamples; mean count on live targets = 2.0x (+-10%) the all-target mean; measured additions per relation ratio 0.50 (+-0.03) versus baseline that loops x1 over V for every target.
cheapest_test: n=17 and n=19 binary curves, b=1 and random b, random k=8 subspaces inside ker Tr and random k=8 subspaces not inside; for all x(R) enumerate x1 in V, test whether x(R+P1) is in V; tabulate counts against Tr(b/z^2). Seconds of CPU.
falsifier: Any target with Tr(b/z^2)=1 having a V-decomposition when V is in ker Tr, or dead fraction outside 0.48-0.52, or live-target mean not near 2x.
lean_sketch: Abstract the algebra: structure with Target, Cand, predicate Dec : Target -> Cand -> Prop, and a decidable bit tr : Target -> Bool with hypothesis h_dead : forall R c, Dec R c -> tr R = false (that is the field-theoretic fact, taken as hypothesis; its proof needs GF(2^n) trace and is out of core-Lean scope). Cost record with relations := number of enumerated candidates. Provable: filtering targets by tr preserves the set of relations found (List.filter lemma) and relations-cost <= cost_baseline; with hypothesis that exactly half of a Finset-like list of N targets pass, cost = baseline/2 (Nat division). smoothCount over a DLPInstance's Fin n log bijection is unchanged.

title: Lifted (s,p) enumeration: separate target and factor-base variables bilinearly
handbook_section: 16.3.2.5 Oil and vinegar (vinegar fixed, remaining system linear) with 16.3.3.2 critical bilinear relations
mechanism: For fixed z the S3 equation is affine over F2 in (s,p). Enumerate s in V (2^k values, not pairs): p=z(s+H(s)+H(b/z^2)+eps), eps in {0,1}, H half-trace (n odd), all F2-linear in s with z-dependent constants. Existence of x1 needs Tr(p/s^2)=0; since p/s^2 = z*(s+H(s))*t(s) + z(h0+eps)*t(s) with t(s)=s^-2 precomputed once per s, the test is two F2 dot products against precomputed vectors W(s), t(s) (a bit-GEMM over targets x s-values, no field multiplication). Survivors (about 1/2) need one multiplication to form x1=s*u and a linear membership test x1 in V. For m=3, loop x1 in V computing z=x(R-P1) once, then the lifted inner loop shares the tables across all (R,x1).
claim: Per candidate pair the lifted loop uses <=0.6 field multiplications and no inversion, versus >=4 for point-addition enumeration with Montgomery batch inversion, and returns the identical relation set.
prediction: Same relation multiset as baseline on toy curves (exact); multiplication count per candidate 0.5 +-0.1 vs 4-5; wall-clock speedup 3-6x on n=45,k=15 (m=3, tables 2^15 x 2n bits in cache), shrinking to <2x once tables exceed L2 (k>=22).
cheapest_test: C/Python harness on n=33 (m=2, k=16) and n=45 (m=3, k=15): count mults and time both loops over 1000 random targets, compare relation sets.
falsifier: Relation sets differ, or wall-clock gain <1.5x at k<=18, or table memory traffic erases the multiplication saving.

Hypothesis h_bij: Dec R (x1,x2) <-> exists s p, Lift z s p /\ roots s p x1 x2 (the algebra; assumed). Provable: lifted.filter Dec = naive.filter Dec up to swap (orbitRepresentatives 2 style quotient N/2), and Cost.relations lifted = |V|*c <= |V|^2 = Cost.relations naive when c <= |V|. title: Factor-base subspace selection by Fano-factor of solution counts (stream-cipher correlation view)
handbook_section: 16.2.1 Basic concepts of stream ciphers (nonlinear filter functions, correlation/Walsh bias)
mechanism: The number of S3-solutions N(V)=#{(x1,x2,x3) in V^3: S3=0} equals 2^-n sum over nonzero characters psi_a of sum_V^3 psi_a(S3). Bias of the Boolean functions Tr(a*S3) restricted to V^3 (computable for all a by fast Walsh/Moebius butterflies, the same butterfly as the polar transform of 15.6.2) makes N(V) over-dispersed relative to random. Pick V with large N(V) among sampled subspaces, at identical |V|, so the same factor-base size and linear-algebra size yields more relations.
claim: N(V) over random k-dim subspaces of GF(2^n) is over-dispersed relative to a matched null (random function with the same S3 symmetry group of order 6 and density), so best-of-M subspace selection gives >=1.2x mean relations per enumerated candidate at fixed |V|.

cheapest_test: n=19, k=7, m=3: 300 random V, count N(V) by brute force (2^21 triples each); compare dispersion with null and positive control.
falsifier: Dispersion within 0.9-1.1 of the symmetric null, or best-of-M gain <1.05 after multiple-comparison correction.

title: Closed-form 2-core prediction of the relation matrix after peeling (fountain-code density evolution)
handbook_section: 15.5.2 LT and fountain codes, 15.5.3 Raptor codes (peeling and inactivation decoding)
mechanism: Rows of weight m over B columns form a random m-uniform hypergraph; peeling (degree-1 column elimination) leaves the 2-core, whose size follows q=1-exp(-m c q^(m-1)), c=rows/B, core columns = 1-e^(-l)(1+l), l=m c q^(m-1). For m=3 this is 0.607B at c=0.9, 0.723B at c=1.0, 0.76B at c=1.05, 0.85B at c=1.2 (checked by simulation, B=2e5: 0.607, 0.723, 0.763, 0.847). So over-collection beyond c~1 buys almost no filtering and sparse-LA nonzeros after peeling stay ~0.79*3B.
claim: On real toy-curve m=3 relation matrices the post-peeling core fraction equals the density-evolution value within 3 points at c in [1.0,1.2]; any systematic deficit measures structure (orbit, symmetrisation, large-prime sharing) that can be engineered, any excess measures hidden bias.
prediction: Core column fraction 0.72+-0.03 at c=1.0 and 0.85+-0.03 at c=1.2 for pure weight-3 rows; with Frobenius-orbit columns merged the core is >=5 points smaller than the unmerged prediction.
cheapest_test: Generate relations on an n=31 Koblitz curve with m=3 subspace FB (B~2000), run existing singleton filter, compare core size with the formula; repeat 20 seeds.
falsifier: Measured core within +-1 point of the formula (then nothing to engineer), or measurements >5 points off in both directions without a structural cause.
lean_sketch: Relation := List (Fin B x Int). Define peel step as removing a row that is the unique row containing a column. Provable without Mathlib: peeling terminates (row count decreases), preserves solvability of the kernel on remaining columns (if column j occurs in one relation, any assignment of the rest extends), and Cost.linearAlgebra after peeling <= before. The density-evolution constant is real analysis, not provable in core; state it as hypothesis h_core : coreCols <= coreFrac * B and derive the Cost bound.
novelty_note: Singleton/clique filtering is integrated; the new content is the quantitative closed-form baseline and using it as a falsifier/diagnostic for hidden structure, plus the observation that stopping at c~1+epsilon loses nothing. Cost-model, not itself a speed-up.

title: Functional-only Wiedemann: read kernel coordinates from the BM sequence, skip the N-matvec assembly pass
handbook_section: 16.2.1 Basic concepts of stream ciphers (LFSR synthesis, linear complexity, Berlekamp-Massey)
mechanism: Wiedemann for A x = b normally costs 2N matvecs for the scalar sequence s_j=u^T A^j b plus N more to assemble x = sum c_j A^j b. The final DLP needs only a few coordinates of the kernel vector (logs of the m factor-base points in Q's decomposition and one normaliser). The scalar u^T x = -(1/c_0) sum_{j>=1} c_j s_{j-1} comes from the same sequence, so with u = e_i (and e_i', the normaliser, computed as extra dot products per iteration, O(N) each) the assembly pass is dropped. Applied to the preconditioned square system with a random right-hand side A y, the kernel vector is y - x.
claim: Recovering log(Q) via coordinate functionals uses 2N+O(1) sparse matvecs instead of 3N, a 33% cut of the linear-algebra phase for single-instance DLP, with identical output.
prediction: Matvec count ratio 0.67 +-0.02; log(Q) identical to the full-kernel answer in 100% of 200 toy runs (failure only when random u gives a short BM, probability ~1/ell).
cheapest_test: Toy matrix 3000x3000 weight-3 mod a 40-bit prime from an n=31 curve's relations; run standard Wiedemann kernel and the functional variant; compare matvecs and log(Q).
falsifier: BM on the single scalar sequence fails to produce the minimal polynomial of A wrt b in >5% of runs (then two-sequence/block fallback erases the saving), or measured ratio >0.8.
lean_sketch: Cost record with linearAlgebra := matvec count. Model a linear recurrence over Int mod ell as List Int; hypothesis h_min : c annihilates s (from BM). Provable in core: if c annihilates the sequence s_j=u(A^j b) then u(x)=sum formula for x defined by c (linearity of u, written for a abstract linear map u and iterate function), and the cost identity 3N-N=2N as Nat arithmetic. DLPInstance log bijection used to state that the recovered ratio log Q / log P pins a unique Fin n element.
novelty_note: Wiedemann and block Wiedemann are integrated; scalar-functional extraction of a few solution coordinates (rather than the whole vector) is a known trick in computational algebra but not recorded as used in the lab's IC baseline; modest, exact, checkable gain.

title: Optimal-normal-basis (T-F-S) coordinates minimising monomial count of the Weil-restricted S3 system
handbook_section: 16.3.1.1 standard (bipolar) construction P=T o F o S, 16.3.1.3 isomorphism of polynomials
mechanism: The bipolar view says the same central map F gives different public systems under input/output affine changes S,T; solver cost (Macaulay matrix density, F4 row weights) depends on S,T though the solution set does not. Choose S on V as a block of consecutive elements of an optimal normal basis (type I/II, fields n=52,58,60,66,... with n+1 or 2n+1 prime) and T as the same ONB: multiplication tensor has about 2n-1 nonzeros so each output bit of x1*x2 has ~2 bilinear terms, Frobenius is a cyclic shift (S3 is Frobenius-stable for b=1), and the squared bilinear term (x1x2)^2 stays 2-sparse.
claim: Versus a random basis pair the Weil-restricted S3 system has >=10x fewer monomials and the F4/XL Macaulay matrix at equal degree is >=3x sparser, lowering decomposition solve time at equal degree of regularity.
prediction: Monomial count ratio random/ONB about n/2 (10-30x for n~30-60); F4 time ratio 2-5x; degree of regularity unchanged (isomorphic systems).
cheapest_test: n=29 (ONB type II, 2n+1=59 prime) and n=28 (type I, 29 prime): build S3 on k=9 subspace in random vs ONB basis, count ANF monomials, run existing F4 with fixed hybrid guesses, record time and max degree.
falsifier: Monomial ratio <2 after restricting to V (non-consecutive V loses sparsity), or F4 time not improved although density is.
lean_sketch: Model basis change as a bijection S : Fin k -> Fin k and a cost proxy monomials : System -> Nat. Provable: if two systems are related by an invertible linear substitution their solution sets are in bijection (relation lists map under S, smoothCount equal) so Cost.relations is unchanged while a density hypothesis h_dens : monomials sys' <= monomials sys / c gives a proportional bound on the Cost.relations proxy. The sparsity value is empirical.
novelty_note: Weil restriction is integrated; deliberate basis/IP choice for sparsity (including ONB-supported n) is not listed. Likely small, and F4 behaviour may be dominated by degree of regularity rather than density.

title: GF2P8AFFINEQB bit-matrix applies for the lifted enumeration's linear maps
handbook_section: 16.2.6 AES (Rijndael) RIJNDAEL: S-box as GF(2^8) inverse plus affine map; wide-trail linear layer
mechanism: The inner loop of the lifted enumeration (see lifted (s,p) idea) is F2-linear maps on n-bit vectors (p from s, membership functional, half-trace) and F2 dot products. AES hardware-derived GFNI instructions apply an 8x8 bit matrix to 8 bytes per 64-bit lane (8 lanes per zmm). An n x n bit matrix is (n/8)^2 such blocks applied across 8 independent candidates per instruction in transposed (byte-sliced) layout; with lookup tables replaced by register-resident constants there is no cache traffic.
claim: On GFNI+AVX-512 hardware the linear-map part of the lifted loop reaches >=2x the candidates per cycle of the 8-bit table-lookup implementation at n=64..131, because it is throughput- not load-bound.
prediction: cycles/candidate: table version ~ n/8*2 loads (about 20 cycles at n=131); GFNI version about 0.5*(n/8)^2/8 instructions amortised per candidate, ratio 1.5-3x at n=64, falling below 1x at n>=131 (quadratic block count).
cheapest_test: Microbenchmark of one n=64 and one n=131 F2-linear map over 2^20 random vectors, table vs VGF2P8AFFINEQB, with perf stat cycles on a GFNI host (isolab-eks); report crossover n.
falsifier: Table lookup is faster at n=64 or crossover below n=48; or the host lacks GFNI/AVX-512 (then the test is void, not a refutation).
lean_sketch: Cost record fields as cycle proxies; no hardware semantics in core Lean. Provable only the counting lemma: blocks(n)=(ceil(n/8))^2 and instructions = blocks * ceil(T/8) for T candidates, with hypothesis that each instruction applies one 8x8 bit matrix; and that the composite equals the F2-linear map defined by the matrix (Fin n -> Bool functions, XOR-linearity by induction).
novelty_note: Hardware phase; GFNI use for binary-field multiplication exists elsewhere, but as the linear-algebra engine of a lifted ECDLP decomposition loop it is new. Pure constant factor, only meaningful after the lifted idea is measured.

title: Fountain-style stopping: peel online and stop at the first decodable moment, restricting to the core actually needed
handbook_section: 15.5.2 LT codes, 15.5.3 Raptor codes (rateless decoding overhead)
mechanism: LT/Raptor decoders are rateless: collect symbols until decoding succeeds, overhead epsilon small. IC collects a fixed (1+eps)B relation budget. Maintain the peeling state incrementally (degree counters per column, union-find over the core) and stop at the first time the descent set (the m columns in Q's decomposition plus the normaliser) is determined, i.e. lies in the span after peeling and a rank check on the core component containing them, instead of the whole B-column matrix.
claim: Collection can stop at c_stop significantly below the fixed budget: the coordinates needed lie in the giant component, which is determined earlier than the whole matrix (isolated columns of degree 0 are never needed).
prediction: c_stop = 0.55-0.75 of the fixed 1.1B budget on n=31 toy runs, because the needed columns become determined when the giant component has density just above the rank threshold; relation-collection cost down 25-45%.
cheapest_test: n=31 Koblitz toy, m=3 subspace FB: record per-relation online state and the first c at which the target log becomes derivable (full solve at each checkpoint, c in steps of 0.05); compare with 1.1B.
falsifier: The target's log is not derivable until c>=0.95 of the fixed budget (coupon-collector bound of ln B/3 dominates), or the extra rank checks cost more than the saved relations.
lean_sketch: Relation list as List (Fin B x Int); define Determined (j : Fin B) (rels) : Prop := every kernel assignment agrees on j up to scale. Provable: Determined is monotone under appending relations (kernel shrinks); a stopping rule 'stop at first prefix where Determined holds' yields Cost.relations = prefix length <= budget; correctness holds for the DLPInstance log bijection if the logs satisfy all relations. The c_stop value is empirical.

title: Stop relation collection at the orientability (ML) threshold, extract t from the first left-kernel vector
handbook_section: 15.3 LDPC and Gallager codes over finite fields; 15.5.1 Tornado codes (BP threshold vs ML/MAP threshold of sparse parity-check systems)
mechanism: Write relation k as sum_i c_ki L_i = a_k + b_k t (mod ell), with t = log_P Q. Only t is wanted, not all B factor-base logs. t is determined as soon as the factor-base part M_L (N x B) has a left-kernel vector y with sum y_k b_k nonzero, and then t = -(y.a)/(y.b). With generic coefficients mod a large prime, the rows of M_L are independent iff the relation hypergraph is orientable (Hall matching). The first dependency therefore appears at the orientability threshold: N/B = 0.9179 for 3-uniform relations and 0.5 for graphs (m=2), not at B+1 or at the coupon-collector count B ln B / m that full-log solving needs. Use Wiedemann on M_L^T for a left-kernel vector, or solve the bordered system, instead of requiring full column rank. This is the LDPC fact that ML decoding (Gaussian elimination) works beyond the BP/peeling threshold (0.818 for m=3), applied to the stopping rule.
claim: For m-fold decompositions with Frobenius-orbit coefficients that look random mod ell, the first dependency that determines t appears at N = c_m B (1+o(1)) with c_2 = 0.5, c_3 = 0.918, c_4 = 0.977, independent of B. This is below the B+1 requirement of full-rank solving, and far below B ln B / m.
prediction: A scratch simulation I ran (random m-uniform hypergraph, coefficients uniform mod 2^31-1, incremental sparse elimination, 6 seeds) gave first-dependency N/B = 0.919, 0.907, 0.923 for m=3 at B = 200, 400, 800, and 0.52, 0.52, 0.56 for m=2. On a real toy curve, expect N_dep/B = 0.92 +/- 0.03 for m=3, and relations saved of about 8% versus B+1, rising to about 4x versus the coupon count at B ~ 1e5. The relation phase is the dominant phase, so the saving is about 8% of it for m=3. Only the m=2 saving (about 2x) is large.
cheapest_test: Binary Koblitz toy, n = 23..29, m=3 Semaev decomposition with subspace factor base l ~ n/3 and Frobenius-orbit columns. Log real relations (columns, a, b) in collection order. For each prefix N, compute the rank of M_L mod ell and record the first N with rank < N and y.b != 0. Check that the recovered t equals the known log. Compare N_dep with B+1 and with the random-hypergraph prediction. Repeat on 20 curves/seeds.
falsifier: Median N_dep/B on real toy relations outside [0.88, 0.96] for m=3 (so the uniform-hypergraph model fails), or t recovered wrongly, or the left-kernel solve on M_L^T costs more modmuls than the relations saved. Also falsified if a pure-simulation threshold depends on B, i.e. is not a constant.
lean_sketch: Definitions: DLPInstance (n : Nat) with G, op, log : G -> Fin n bijective (exp its inverse); FactorBase B := Fin B -> G; Relation B := {coeff : Fin B -> Int, a : Int, b : Int}, meaning sum coeff_i * L_i = a + b*t mod n. Cost record {factorBase relations linearAlgebra descent : Nat}. Provable without Mathlib: soundness lemma. Hypotheses: relations hold mod n for the true logs, y : List Int is a dependency (for each column i, sum_k y_k*coeff_ki = 0), and (sum y_k b_k) is a unit mod n. Then t = -(sum y_k a_k) * (sum y_k b_k)^(-1) mod n. This follows by Int.emod algebra over List sums. Monotonicity lemma: if N_dep <= N_full and the other phases are equal, then Cost.total (stop at the dependency) <= Cost.total (full rank). Not provable in core: the threshold 0.9179 itself (probabilistic, needs random hypergraphs and rank over a field). State it as an explicit hypothesis HasDependency rels, or as an empirical constant c_m.
novelty_note: Singleton/clique filtering and block Wiedemann are integrated, but the stopping rule and target-only left-kernel extraction are not. The B+1 requirement is the textbook habit when solving for all logs. The claim is a relation-count reduction, not an accounting change, but its size for m>=3 is small (8%), so it is a measured-improvement candidate rather than a breakthrough.

title: Closed-form peeling core size to price the linear-algebra phase, with max-degree inactivation ordering
handbook_section: 15.5 Raptor codes (inactivation decoding); 15.5.1 Tornado codes; 15.3 LDPC density evolution
mechanism: Peeling (remove a column of degree 1 with its relation) on an m-uniform relation hypergraph has a density-evolution fixed point q = 1 - exp(-m c q^(m-1)). The core has a fraction P(Poisson(m c q^(m-1)) >= 2) of the columns and q^m c B relations. Raptor inactivation continues peeling past the stall by marking one column (the highest-degree column in a minimum-degree relation) as inactive, i.e. symbolic, until a small dense core remains. Run Wiedemann (or a dense solve) only on that core and back-substitute. The fixed point gives the post-filter dimension and weight before any run, so the cost record linearAlgebra can be priced and the stop point chosen.
claim: For m=3 uniform relations the surviving core is 0.635 B columns at N = 0.918 B and 0.723 B columns at N = B (edges minus vertices of the core = 0 at 0.918, about 0.06 B at 1.0). Peel plus inactivation then Wiedemann on the core costs at least 1.5x fewer modmuls than Wiedemann on the unfiltered matrix.
prediction: Measured core fraction within 3% of 0.635 and 0.723 on random hypergraphs at B = 2^14. On real toy relations, within 8% (non-uniform column popularity). Core-only Wiedemann modmuls (dimension 0.64 B, weight after elimination about 2x) about 0.4-0.7 of the unfiltered count.
cheapest_test: Python/C++ peeler on the saved relations of the toy-curve run (n ~ 27, B ~ 2^12..2^14). Log the core size after plain peeling and after inactivation ordering. Count modmuls of block Wiedemann on the core versus the full matrix at equal block width. Compare with the existing structured Gaussian elimination at equal final weight.
falsifier: Core fraction off the fixed-point value by more than 8% on real data, or the core-only Wiedemann modmul count is not below 0.9 of structured-GE + Wiedemann at equal weight. Either one means the idea is a relabelling of existing structured elimination.
lean_sketch: Definitions: Relation with support as List (Fin B), the degree function, and a peel step (relation, pivot column) removing a degree-1 column. Provable without Mathlib: (1) peel-step invariance, meaning a solution of the reduced system extends uniquely to the original by back-substitution (needs the coefficient to be a unit mod n); (2) the Cost accounting identity, where core dimension d gives linearAlgebra cost <= d*d*w by hypothesis. Not provable: the fixed-point value (real analysis, probabilistic).
novelty_note: Singleton removal and structured elimination are integrated. What is new is the predicted core (the fixed point) used as a cost-model input and the Raptor ordering rule. Marginal over structured GE, so the first falsifier decides it.

title: Walsh/trace-code bias criterion for choosing the shape of the factor-base subspace V
handbook_section: 15.1.2.4 Subfield and trace codes (Delsarte); 15.1.2.3 Reed-Muller codes; 15.1.6.1
mechanism: On binary curves S_3 = e2^2 + e3 + b (I checked it numerically on y^2+xy=x^3+a2 x^2+b over GF(2^9), a2 in {0,1}, 6000 random point pairs, 0 violations). With x3 fixed, S_3 is an F_2-quadratic map V x V -> GF(2)^n (the squared terms are Frobenius-linear). The number of decompositions of a point with x-coordinate r is N0(r) = 2^-n sum_gamma sum_{x in V^2} (-1)^Tr(gamma S(x)). Each inner sum is a Walsh coefficient of a quadratic form, equal to +/- 2^(2l - rank(B_gamma)/2) when it is nonzero (Dickson). The mean of N0 over r is |V|^2/2^n/2 for every V. The variance across r depends on the rank profile of {B_gamma restricted to V x V}, which is the weight structure of a trace code (Delsarte). So V can be chosen (prefix of a polynomial basis, trace-0 hyperplane inside, random, cyclic code) by the rank profile.
claim: At fixed dimension l, the dispersion index Var(N0)/E(N0) over targets r differs across subspace shapes of V (polynomial-basis prefix, containing 1, trace-zero, random). The Poisson heuristic (index 1 after accounting for the x1<->x2 pairing) does not hold for structured V. A criterion based on the low-rank mass of B_gamma picks the V with the largest P(N0 >= 1).
prediction: At n = 17, 19, 21, 23 with l = n/2: dispersion index within 5% of 1.0 for random V, but 1.15-1.6 for the prefix subspace and for V containing the F_2 line {0,1}. P(N0>=1) differs by at least 0.03 absolute between best and worst shape. Direction of the difference is not preregistered.
cheapest_test: Exact count of N0(r) for all r in GF(2^n)* and each V shape, by the per-s Artifact-Schreier enumeration (s in V, Tr(s) = Tr(b/r^2); 2^l steps per r). n <= 21 means 2^21 targets x 2^10 steps, which is fine. Tabulate mean, variance and P(N0>=1) per shape with a 95% bootstrap interval, using 20 random V per shape as the negative control and a deliberately degenerate V (subfield-like, n=21 with GF(8)) as the positive control.
falsifier: All shapes within +/-5% in dispersion index and 0.01 in P(N0>=1) at every n tested, meaning the subspace shape has no first-order effect on yield, or the rank-profile predictor fails to rank shapes correctly (Spearman < 0.5).

title: Frobenius-invariant subspaces are cyclic codes: availability table by n, and the ECC2K-130 consequence
handbook_section: 15.1.3 Cyclic codes (15.1.3.1 Algebraic preliminaries, 15.1.3.2 Properties); 15.1.4 spectral approach
mechanism: Via a normal basis GF(2^n) is a free F_2[x]/(x^n-1)-module of rank 1, with Frobenius acting as multiplication by x. F_2-subspaces closed under Frobenius are exactly the ideals, i.e. the cyclic codes of length n, with dimension n - deg g for g | x^n - 1. For prime n, x^n - 1 = (x-1) times (n-1)/d irreducibles of degree d = ord_n(2). So the invariant dimensions are {a d, a d + 1}, and the number of distinct invariant subspaces of a given dimension is a binomial coefficient in the number of degree-d factors.
claim: A Frobenius-invariant subspace factor base of dimension near n/2 or n/3 exists only for n with small ord_n(2), and for n in {53, 59, 61, 67, 83, 101, 107, 131} (2 a primitive root) the only invariant subspaces are 0, F_2, the trace-0 hyperplane and the whole field. In particular none exists for the ECC2K-130 field GF(2^131).
prediction: I computed ord_n(2) for the primes in 53..131: 53:52, 59:58, 61:60, 67:66, 71:35, 73:9, 79:39, 83:82, 89:11, 97:48, 101:100, 103:51, 107:106, 109:36, 113:28, 127:7, 131:130. Invariant dimensions within 1 of n/2: n = 71 (35, 36), 73 (36, 37), 79 (39, 40), 89 (44, 45), 97 (48, 49), 103 (51, 52), 113 (56, 57), 127 (63, 64; C(18,9) = 48620 distinct subspaces). Near n/3: 109 (36, 37) and 127 (42, 43). So the Frobenius-invariant-subspace orbit speedup (factor n on relations) is structurally unavailable at the eight primitive-root n including 131. At 131 the only n-fold gain has to come from a non-subspace, union-of-orbits factor base.
cheapest_test: Pure computation, already done for ord_n(2). Next step: for toy n = 31 (ord 5, six factors of degree 5), n = 23 (ord 11) and n = 41 (ord 20), build invariant V and random V of equal dimension, run the same m=3 decomposition, and compare yield per attempt after the orbit multiplier. Predict equal yield per attempt (within 5%), with the orbit factor n applying only to the invariant V.
falsifier: Any Frobenius-stable F_2-subspace of dimension in [2, n-2] found in GF(2^131) (impossible if the factorization argument holds, so a computation of the factorization of x^131-1 over F_2 would refute it), or a toy run in which invariant V loses more than 10% yield per attempt versus random V.

Provable in core: `decide` that ord 131 = 130 and ord 127 = 7 via a bounded search; the dimension set {a*d, a*d+1} follows from the factorization degrees if stated as a hypothesis (irreducible degree-d factors of x^n-1), which needs polynomial arithmetic over F_2 that core does not have beyond a toy implementation. title: Artifact-Schreier / Gray-code enumeration of the m=2 decomposition over the affine hyperplane Tr(s) = Tr(b/r^2)
handbook_section: 15.1.2.4 Subfield and trace codes; 15.1.2.1 Standard array decoding (syndrome-first filtering); 15.1.2.3 Reed-Muller codes (affine-hyperplane restriction)
mechanism: From S_3 = e2^2 + e3 + b with x3 = r, put s = x1+x2 in V and w = x1 x2. Then w^2 + r w + r^2 s^2 + b = 0. Writing w = r rho gives rho^2 + rho = s^2 + b/r^2, solvable iff Tr(s) = Tr(b/r^2). This is an affine F_2-hyperplane condition on s, applied before any multiplication, as a syndrome would be. rho is then an F_2-affine function of s (half-trace matrix, precomputed). The roots x1, x2 of z^2 + s z + w exist iff Tr(w/s^2) = 0, and then x1 = s sigma with sigma^2 + sigma = w/s^2. Enumerate s over V intersected with the hyperplane by a Gray code, updating rho and w by XORs, with a precomputed table of 1/s^2 (size B, shared with the factor base). Per candidate this costs one field multiplication (w * (1/s^2)) plus a parity, against about 6 multiplications for 'x(R-P) with batched inversion plus hash lookup'. The same inner loop gives the x-coordinates of all pair sums x(P1+P2) for m=4 two-list collisions.
claim: Gray-code enumeration over the Tr-hyperplane finds all m=2 decompositions of a target over V with at least 5x fewer GF(2^n) multiplications per found relation than hash-lookup of x(R-P) over the factor base, and finds the same relation set.
prediction: Candidates halve (hyperplane), multiplications per candidate drop from about 6 to 1 plus a parity, so multiplication-count ratio is 8-12x and wall-clock ratio 3-6x (memory-bound table of 1/s^2 limits it). Both methods return identical relation sets.
cheapest_test: C or Python with GF(2^n) bit-matrix arithmetic, n = 31, l = 15, 10^4 random targets. Count field multiplications and cache-missing table reads in both implementations. Check set equality of the relations (x1,x2). Then repeat for n = 41, l = 20.
falsifier: Relation sets differ (derivation wrong), or the multiplication-count ratio is below 2, or wall-clock is not better because of the 1/s^2 table's memory traffic (ratio < 1).
lean_sketch: Definitions: toy field as Fin n -> Bool or Nat with carryless multiply mod an irreducible polynomial, tr, V as a list of Nats, DLPInstance not needed for the algebra. Provable by `decide` at n = 5, 7 with explicit b: for all r, s with Tr(s) = Tr(b/r^2), the pair (x1, x2) built from rho and sigma satisfies e2^2 + e3 + b = 0 (finite check). General lemma: S_3(x1,x2,r) = 0 iff w^2 + r w + r^2 s^2 + b = 0 (ring identity in char 2, provable with a commutative-ring typeclass written by hand, or `decide` on the toy). Cost: multiplication count per candidate as a field of a Cost-like record; the theorem is an inequality of counts. The cost claim itself is empirical.
novelty_note: S_3 and Weil-restricted solving are integrated, so the point is not the system but the explicit m=2 closed form with a syndrome-first trace filter and Gray-code reuse. m=2 is BSGS-equivalent, so the gain is a constant factor in an inner loop (m=4 collision lists), not an exponent.

title: Cyclic-code census of Frobenius-stable subspaces closes the stable-subspace factor base for ECC2K-130
handbook_section: 14.9.2 Weights of multiples of polynomials (cyclic codes C_n^f; factorization of X^n-1 over F_2)
mechanism: In a normal basis, Frobenius on GF(2^n) is the cyclic shift, so Frobenius-stable F_2-subspaces are exactly the ideals of F_2[X]/(X^n-1), that is, cyclic codes of length n. Their dimensions are sums of sizes of the cyclotomic cosets of 2 mod n, plus the all-ones coset of size 1. When 2 is a primitive root mod a prime n, X^n-1 = (X-1)*Phi_n with Phi_n irreducible, so only dimensions 0, 1, n-1, n occur. The n-fold column reduction from a Frobenius-stable subspace factor base is therefore unavailable at those n. Partially stable coordinate subspaces keep almost no quotient gain, because the fraction of elements sharing an orbit with another element is tiny.
claim: For n in {53,59,61,67,83,101,107,131} the only Frobenius-stable F_2-subspaces of GF(2^n) have dimension 0, 1, n-1 or n. A stable subspace of dimension within [n/4, n/2] exists only for n with small ord_n(2). Confident examples: 127 (ord 7), 73 (ord 9), 89 (ord 11), 71 (ord 35), 79 (ord 39), 103 (ord 51). For a coordinate-support subspace V_I (dim about n/2) the number of orbits meeting V_I is at least 0.97*|V_I|, so partial stability gives under 3% column reduction.

title: Normal-basis Hamming-ball factor base: Frobenius-stable, table-free membership, exact orbit count
handbook_section: 14.9.2 Weights of multiples of polynomials (weight in the cyclic F_2[X]/(X^n-1) model)
mechanism: For n with an optimal normal basis (type II: n=53, 83, 89, 131 since 2n+1 is prime with 2 of suitable order), Frobenius is a cyclic rotation of coordinates. Hamming weight is rotation-invariant, so F_w = {x : wt_ONB(x) <= w} is Frobenius-stable for any n, including those closed by idea 1. Membership is one popcount. Orbit representatives are necklaces, counted exactly by sum_{i<=w} C(n,i)/n for prime n (minus fixed points 0 and all-ones). For m=2, solve-and-check works for any set: fix x1 in F_w, solve the F_2-linearized quadratic a*x2^2 + c*x2 = e for x2 by half-trace, then test membership. The ECC2K-130 rho attacks already use ONB Hamming weight to make their walk Frobenius-invariant. This transfers that invariant to IC factor-base definition.
claim: At equal |F|, a Hamming-ball factor base gives the same number of m=2 relations per target as a random Frobenius-stable orbit union, within 10%. Its column count is |F|/n, and its membership test needs no table.
prediction: Relation yield ratio ball/random in [0.9,1.1] (null). Column count = (sum_{i<=w} C(n,i) - 2)/n + 2 exactly. In a micro-benchmark with synthetic |F| = 2^28, popcount membership is at least 1.3x faster per candidate than a hash lookup. End-to-end gain is at most 1.1x because the half-trace solve dominates.

title: Cayley-graph walk candidate generation: one point addition per relation candidate
handbook_section: 14.10.3 Expander graphs and 14.10.4 Cayley graphs
mechanism: Instead of forming R = aP + bQ by a fresh double scalar multiplication per candidate (about 1.75 log2 N additions), walk R_{i+1} = R_i + s_{j_i} on Cay(Z_N, S), where S = {alpha_j P + beta_j Q}, j_i is drawn from an external PRNG, and (a,b) is tracked by integer addition. By Alon-Roichman, an abelian Cayley graph needs about log N generators for constant spectral gap, but only decorrelation of the decomposition indicator along the walk is needed. The mixing time of the walk is about r*N^(2/r), exactly computable from the characters sum_j cos(2 pi k s_j / N). Choose S to minimise lambda_2, with r = 8 to 16 for hardware.
claim: For toy curves with N about 2^24 and r in {8,16}, the walk yields the same relations per candidate as i.i.d. (a,b) within 3%, with the same relation-matrix rank growth per relation, at at least 5x fewer group-operation equivalents per relation for m=2.
prediction: Yield ratio walk/iid in [0.97,1.03]. Lag-1 autocorrelation of the success indicator |rho| < 0.01. Duplicate-point rate < 0.1% over 10^7 steps. Group ops per candidate drop from about 42 to 1, and per relation (including a half-trace solve of about 5 op-equivalents) by 5x to 9x. Ratio grows with log N. For r=4 inflated duplicates appear (mixing about 2^12 steps).
cheapest_test: Prime-field curve of prime order N about 2^24. Arms: iid scalars (control), walk r=4, 8, 16 with random S, walk r=16 with lambda_2-minimised S. Count relations, distinct relations, rank of the relation matrix at R = B+20, and ops. Compute lambda_2 by FFT of the indicator of the log set in Z_N.
falsifier: Yield ratio < 0.9, or rank at R = B+20 deficient in more than 1% of runs where iid is not, or success autocorrelation above 0.05 at r>=8. If the lab baseline already walks, this is accounting and not an improvement.
lean_sketch: Definitions: inst : DLPInstance with log : G -> Fin N a bijection; Relation with Int coefficients (a, b, coefficient vector over Fin B); steps s : Fin r -> G with known (alpha_j, beta_j); walk : Nat -> G x Int x Int defined recursively. Provable by induction: for every i, log (walk i).1 = (walk i).2 * 1 + (walk i).3 * logQ mod N, so every emitted relation is sound, and Cost.relations (walk) = steps*1 + test cost. Provable via the character-sum formula for return probabilities: P_k(0) = (1/N) sum_chi (sum_j chi(s_j))^k. Mixing and yield are statistical and would be hypotheses only.
novelty_note: Walk candidates are standard in rho and in some IC practice; the proposal is the explicit lambda_2-based generator selection plus per-relation accounting against the lab's current candidate generation. If the baseline already walks, this reduces to no improvement; check the repository first.

title: Maximal-point function fields as decomposition covers
handbook_section: 14.8.3 Constructions of (t,m,s)-nets (Niederreiter-Xing function fields with many rational points)
mechanism: Digital nets of low t come from algebraic curves with many rational places (Niederreiter-Xing), tabulated as N_q(g). For Weil-descent or GHS covers of an elliptic curve (genus g cover over F_q, q=2^l) the number of degree-g divisors that split into rational points is about N^g/g!, against #J about q^g. So the relation probability is about (N/q)^g/g!. Among the covers available (twists, choice of Artin-Schreier parameters, isogenous GHS candidates) pick the one with the largest N, not a random one. For small q and g, N can be 2 to 3 times q.
claim: Relation probability per random divisor class scales as N^g/(g! #J(F_q)) across genus-g curves over a small field, and the top-decile-N curves yield at least 3x the bottom decile.
prediction: Over 2000 random genus-3 curves over F_8: Pearson r > 0.95 between measured fraction of J(F_q) expressible as a sum of g rational points and N^g/(g! #J). Top N decile / bottom N decile yield ratio in [3,10]. At q=16, g=4, the ceiling N=49 vs average 17 gives a factor (49/17)^4, about 69, upper bound on the effect.
cheapest_test: Magma-free: enumerate hyperelliptic y^2 + h y = f over F_8 (g=3), compute N from point counts and #J from the L-polynomial over F_8, F_64, F_512. Compute the sumset {P_1+...+P_g} in the Jacobian by Cantor arithmetic (lab tool hyperelliptic-cover and Mumford arithmetic exist). Compare the covered fraction with N^g/(g!#J).
falsifier: r < 0.8, or top/bottom decile ratio < 1.5. If the actual GHS cover offers no choice of N for the target curve family, the idea does not apply to ECC2K-130.
lean_sketch: Definitions: g N J : Nat with J > 0; smoothCount g N := choose N g (own def, since core lacks Nat.choose). Provable: N <= N' -> smoothCount g N <= smoothCount g N' (monotone). Provable: if the sum map Fin g -> places is surjective onto a group of size J, then smoothCount g N >= J, giving a lower bound on N. The Cost record gets factorBase := N and relations := ceil(J / smoothCount * g!) as arithmetic, with the statement that this relations cost is antitone in N. The probabilistic equidistribution of sums is a hypothesis.
novelty_note: Using Jacobian size versus rational-point count is classical (Gaudry, Enge-Gaudry). Not in my information: selecting covers by Niederreiter-Xing style N_q(g) tables rather than at random. The lab's hyperelliptic-cover tools make the test cheap; effect on prime-degree binary Koblitz fields depends on cover availability.

title: Strength-2 covering array screening of the autolab configuration space
handbook_section: 14.7.4 Covering arrays
mechanism: The IC autolab tournament has about 7 discrete factors (m, FB dimension class, symmetrisation on/off, solver F4/F5/XL, ordering, large-prime on/off, thread layout). A covering array CA(N;2,k,v) tests every pair of factor levels in N runs: binary k=7 needs 6 runs, against 128 for the full factorial. Combined with a main-effect plus pairwise model it identifies the best configuration with a small fraction of the runs.
claim: On toy curves, a 6-run (binary) or 9-run (ternary k=4) strength-2 covering array plus a pairwise model finds a configuration whose cost is within 10% of the exhaustive best on at least 80% of curves.
prediction: Within 10% of best in 80 to 95% of 50 toy curves, using under 5% of the 128 runs. Failures concentrate on curves with three-way interactions (solver x ordering x symmetrisation).
cheapest_test: Run the full 2^7 grid on 50 toy curves (n=17..23 binary, 20-bit prime) once; this is the ground truth. Replay the 6-row covering array and fit the pairwise model offline, preregistered with a fixed array and a fixed 10% threshold.
falsifier: Fewer than 60% of curves within 10%, or median regret above 25%.
lean_sketch: Definitions: arr : Fin 6 -> Fin 7 -> Bool. Provable by decide: for all column pairs (i,j) and all (u,v) : Bool x Bool, exists a row r with arr r i = u and arr r j = v (the covering property). The Cost record has phases factorBase/relations/linearAlgebra/descent, total := sum. Provable: if cost is additive over factors, total cost is determined by the pairwise tables, so the array identifies the argmin. Not provable: interaction order of the real system.
novelty_note: Covering arrays are standard in combinatorial interaction testing and not in the integrated list. This reduces tuning cost, which is a process cost, not a cost of an IC phase on a target; it is an efficiency tool for finding measured improvements.

title: Koblitz tau-adic Gray-code candidate enumeration with free Frobenius table and orbit-duplicate filter
handbook_section: 14.8.5 Digital (t,s)-sequences (Gray-code / Antonov-Saleev enumeration of digit strings) and 14.8.6
mechanism: On a Koblitz curve, enumerate candidate points R(a) = sum_j a_j phi^j(P) over tau-adic digit strings a in {0,1}^k in Gray-code order. Each step flips one digit j, so R changes by +/- phi^j(P), where phi^j(P) is a coordinate squaring (an ONB rotation), so no precomputed table is needed. log R = x_P * sum a_j lambda^j mod N is updated incrementally. Naive enumeration wastes half the candidates: a and a<<1 give R and phi(R), the same Frobenius orbit. Restricting to strings with a_0 = 1 (and top digit free) removes orbit duplicates, since rotations of such strings have a_0 = 0.
claim: Gray-code enumeration over a_0=1 strings gives one mixed addition per candidate, orbit-duplicate rate 0, and relation yield equal to i.i.d. sampling within 3%. Without the a_0=1 filter the orbit-duplicate rate is 50%.
prediction: Orbit-duplicate rate: 50% (+/-1%) unfiltered at k=20, 0% filtered. Yield per candidate ratio vs iid in [0.97,1.03]. Cost per candidate about 1 mixed addition (about 9 field mults, Lopez-Dahab) plus an amortised mean 1 squaring, against about 2*n/3 additions for two tau-NAF scalar multiplications.
cheapest_test: Koblitz curve a=1 over GF(2^n), n=17 and 19 with N prime times cofactor. Enumerate 2^20 strings of both kinds, count distinct orbits (canonical rotation of x), count m=2 relations over a Hamming-ball or random stable factor base, compare to iid tau-adic digits.
falsifier: Orbit-duplicate rate above 1% after the a_0=1 filter, or yield ratio outside [0.9,1.1]. Or relation-matrix rank growth per relation below iid by more than 1%, which would reveal digit-box structure.
lean_sketch: Definitions: digits a : Fin k -> Bool; lam : Fin N (Frobenius eigenvalue); Relation with Int coefficient lambda-sum; gray i := i xor (i/2). Provable: gray is injective on Fin (2^k), so the walk visits distinct strings, and consecutive strings differ in exactly one position (decide for k<=8, induction in general). Provable: with a_0=1 the map a -> rot a never lands in the filtered set for non-trivial rotation (within k<n). Provable: incremental log update equals the closed form. Yield equality is statistical.
novelty_note: Gray-code and tau-adic digit enumeration are known for scalar multiplication; applying them to IC relation generation with an orbit-duplicate filter is the concrete point. Cost saving is accounting unless the baseline pays full scalar multiplications per candidate; check the baseline.
