title: Longest-zero-run canonicalisation of Frobenius orbits
handbook_section: 14.9.2 Weights of multiples of polynomials (cyclic structure F_2[X]/(X^n-1)) and cyclic words/necklaces
mechanism: With a hashed orbit-quotient factor base, every candidate x must be mapped to its orbit representative before lookup. The naive canonical form is the minimum over n rotations. The lexicographically minimal rotation always starts at a start of a maximal run of zeros (preceded by a one). So find the longest zero run with clz/ctz on 64-bit words, collect the starts of runs of that maximal length (about 1.5 to 2 expected for random n=131 bit words, since the longest run is about log2 n), and compare only those rotations.
claim: The result is identical to naive minimum-rotation for all words, and costs about O(n/64) word operations plus about 2 comparisons.
prediction: Microbenchmark n=131: at least 10x fewer cycles than naive (e.g. about 60 versus 600 or more cycles). End-to-end per-candidate speedup at least 1.2x if canonicalisation was at least 20% of candidate cost, at most 1.05x otherwise. Mean number of tied longest runs in [1.3,2.2].
cheapest_test: C microbenchmark on random 131-bit words, 10^8 calls, verify equality with naive on 10^7 words plus all words for n<=24. Count ties. Use perf-ipc where a PMU exists; else report wall time with the repeat spread.
falsifier: Any word where the output differs from naive. Or speedup below 3x. Or mean number of candidate starts above 4.
lean_sketch: Definitions: Word n := List Bool, rot, canon w := minimum over rotations by lexicographic order, runStarts w. Provable by exhaustive decide for n<=12: canon w = min over rotations at runStarts w. General proof by an exchange argument: a rotation not starting at a longest zero run has a strictly larger prefix. Cost sketch: the number of candidates is at most the number of maximal runs of the maximal length. Expected count would need a measure and is not provable; the number of words of length n with exactly one longest zero run is computable by decide for small n.
novelty_note: Minimal-rotation tricks for necklaces are known (Booth, Duval); the reuse here is a hardware item on a phase component with a bit-parallel implementation. Likely already implicit in some Frobenius-orbit code; check. It is a speed-up of a component, not a new route.

title: Cyclotomic-coset factor base: table-free membership and free canonicalisation for any prime n
handbook_section: 14.7.1 Association schemes (cyclotomic scheme) and 14.6.5 Further families of difference sets (cyclotomic classes)
mechanism: Let s divide 2^n - 1, M = (2^n-1)/s, and C a Frobenius orbit (size n) in mu_M. Define F = {x in GF(2^n)* : x^s in C}. Squaring maps x^s to (x^s)^2, so F is Frobenius-stable for every n, avoiding the obstruction of idea 1. |F| = s*n, the orbit columns are s, and the canonical representative of x is Frob^{-j}(x) where x^s = c^{2^j}, found by an n-entry lookup. No |F|-sized table is needed. Membership is one exponentiation x^s followed by a lookup in C. The multiplicative structure (association scheme of cyclotomic classes) fixes the sizes exactly.
claim: For m=2, the relation yield per target equals that of a random Frobenius-stable set of size s*n within 10%, and no hash table of size |F| is stored.
prediction: Yield ratio in [0.9,1.1] (null). Per-candidate membership plus canonicalisation costs 1.0 to 1.5x a hashed lookup for |F| about 2^28 and is slower for small |F|. Real divisors near 2^(n/2) exist only for some n, for example n=29 with s=1103 (|F| = 31987).
cheapest_test: n=29: 2^29-1 = 233 * 1103 * 2089, so s=1103 gives |F|=1103*29 (about 2^15). Compare m=2 relation yield and column count against a random orbit union and a Hamming ball of equal size on a toy Koblitz curve, 10^6 candidates each. Separately list, for n in 53..131, divisors of 2^n-1 within 2^(+-3) of 2^(n/2) (factor tables).
falsifier: Yield ratio outside [0.8,1.25]. Or for most n in 53..131 no divisor within a factor 8 of 2^(n/2) (then the route is mostly unavailable; for n=131, 2^131-1 = 263 * a 123-bit cofactor makes it unusable).
lean_sketch: Definitions: modular exponent via Nat.pow mod over the field model is heavy; model GF(2^n)* as Fin (2^n-1) with log as the isomorphism: DLPInstance-style bijection. F := {i | (i*s) mod (2^n-1) in Corbit} where Corbit is the orbit of c under doubling of exponents. Provable: stability under i -> 2i mod (2^n-1), and |F| = s*n when ord of 2 mod M is n, by counting. Canonicalisation is a function of (i*s) mod (2^n-1) alone. Yield equality is statistical. Cost.factorBase counts s columns.
novelty_note: Cyclotomic and multiplicative-subgroup structures are classical, but I find no use as Frobenius-stable factor bases. The divisor availability is the real limit and is probably fatal at n=131; included mainly as the other route past idea 1 where factor tables allow.

title: 2-torsion translation as an extra x-line projectivity in the orbit quotient (subfield Weil restriction, binary curves)
handbook_section: 14.4.2 Collineations, correlations, and coordinate frames
mechanism: On y^2+xy=x^3+ax^2+b, T=(0,sqrt b) has order 2 and x(P+T)=sqrt(b)/x, a Moebius involution iota in PGL(2) of the x-line. For subfield factor base V=GF(2^d) inside GF(2^(dn)) with sqrt b in V, V\{0} is iota-closed. Since the cofactor h is even, the l-primary component of log(P+T) equals that of log(P), so P and P+T share one unknown. A relation sum(+-P_i)=R+eps*T holds mod l whatever eps is. If b is in GF(2), iota commutes with the subfield Frobenius, so the group acting on V has order 2d, not d, and unknown columns fall from about |V|/d to |V|/(2d). The solve per relation is unchanged. This differs from simply adding V union 1/V, which only doubles the targets and gains nothing.
claim: For even-order binary curves with an iota-closed subfield factor base, quotienting by <Frobenius, iota> instead of <Frobenius> halves the number of unknown classes and of relations needed, at the same cost per relation solve, with all relations still valid mod l.
prediction: Class count ratio (<pi,iota>)/(<pi>) = 0.50 +- 0.05. Relations to reach full rank ratio 0.50 +- 0.10. Relation-collection time x0.50-0.55. Dense linear algebra x0.25-0.5 (cost grows like B^2). Gap to matched rho shrinks by a constant of at most 2 in the relation phase and does not close.
cheapest_test: Curve y^2+xy=x^3+x^2+1 over GF(2^18), V=GF(2^6), m=3. Enumerate all V^3 decompositions, build relation matrices mod l (l the largest prime factor of N) with columns indexed by pi-classes, then by (pi,iota)-classes. Solve both, check every recovered log against a brute-force log table, and count relations needed for full rank in each.
falsifier: Class ratio above 0.6, or any relation failing the mod-l consistency check, or the recovered logs disagreeing with brute force. If the lab IC code already quotients by iota, the marginal gain is zero and the idea is rejected as not new.
lean_sketch: Define DLPInstance with G the quotient E/<T>, so log : G -> Fin l is bijective on classes. FactorBase B : Fin B -> G. Relation has Int coefficients c with a, b and the condition sum c_i*log(fb i) = a + b*logQ mod l. Hypothesis hT : the relation holds for P_i or P_i+T (stated via the quotient map). Provable: relation_transfer (a relation over representatives is a relation over classes), orbitRepresentatives N (2*d) <= orbitRepresentatives N d (Nat.div_le_div_left), and Cost.linearAlgebra monotone in B under the hypothesis linearAlgebra <= c*B^2. Not provable in core Lean: that x(P+T)=sqrt(b)/x; take it as a hypothesis on the group.
novelty_note: Torsion-translation symmetry is not on the lab's integrated list, but Faugere et al. 2012 and Karabina 2015 on binary-curve point decomposition may already use the 2-torsion action. Check the literature and lab code before claiming. Needs a composite extension degree, so it does not apply to ECC2K-130 (n=131 prime) with subfield V.

title: Determinantal (elliptic normal curve) decomposition system that keeps y
handbook_section: 14.4.5 k-Arcs (with 14.4.1 Projective and affine spaces)
mechanism: Embed E in PG(k-1,q) by |kO|. E(F_q) is then a (N,k)-arc: k distinct points are hyperplane-coplanar iff they sum to 0. The relation is det[phi_j(P_i)]=0 with phi_j a basis of L(kO) (1,x,y,x^2,xy,...). Keep (x_i,y_i) with the quadratic curve equations instead of eliminating y. The determinant has degree about k/2 per point, against 2^(k-2) per variable for Semaev S_k. Weil-restrict only x_i in V, so the variable count m(l+n) and equation count (m+1)n stay square when m*l=n.
claim: The y-retaining determinantal system has strictly lower F4/F5 degree of regularity and lower total solve time than the S_{m+1} Weil-restricted system for m=3 and m=4 at equal V.
prediction: d_reg lower by at least 1 at m=3. Solve-time ratio (det system)/(S_{m+1}) in 0.3-0.8 for n<=25. The advantage disappears once the extra n*m y-variables dominate, around n>=40. Direction: a constant-factor decomposition gain only.
cheapest_test: E over GF(2^21), V of dimension 7, m=3. Build both systems for 200 random targets x(R). Run the same F4 (msolve or Magma) on each. Record d_reg, matrix size, time, and that the solution sets match after projecting out y.
falsifier: d_reg not lower, or median time ratio >=1, or solution sets differing from the S_{m+1} systems.
lean_sketch: Model with DLPInstance and FactorBase. State hdet : forall P : Fin k -> G, (sum of log (P i) = 0 mod n) <-> detVanishes P, as a hypothesis, since geometry is not in core Lean. title: MDS-arc checksum protection for block Lanczos/Wiedemann on Spot
handbook_section: 14.4.6 k-Arcs and linear MDS codes
mechanism: Rows of a Vandermonde parity-check matrix on arc points c_i = alpha^i form an MDS code, so any r columns are independent. Precompute r checksum vectors w_j = c^(j) A over F_l. After each sparse matvec y=Ax, compare c^(j).y with w_j.x. Up to r faulty coordinates (bit flips, partial writes after preemption) are detected, and up to floor(r/2) are located and corrected from the syndrome by Vandermonde decoding. This replaces periodic full recompute-and-compare.
claim: With r=4 MDS checksum rows, every corruption of at most 4 coordinates per matvec is detected and at most 2 corrected, at under 2% extra cost, while a naive redundant-verification scheme costs about 100%.
prediction: Overhead r*(row weight)/(nnz) is about 0.01-0.1% extra multiplies at dimension 2^16 and weight 10-50. Detection 100% within the bound. Correction 100% for 1-2 faults. Time to solution on a simulated 5%-per-hour preemption schedule beats checkpoint-only by 1.2-2x. This reduces cost only, with no change to the exponent or the matched-rho gap.
cheapest_test: Block Lanczos mod a 31-bit prime l on a random sparse 2*10^4-dimension matrix with 20 nonzeros per row. Inject 1-5 coordinate faults per 1000 matvecs. Compare four arms (no protection, checkpoint-only, full duplicate, MDS checksum) for undetected-error rate, wall time, and final kernel validity.
falsifier: Any undetected corruption inside the bound, a miscorrection, or measured overhead above 2%.
lean_sketch: Use Int/Nat with modulus l and hypothesis hunit : forall i, Nat.Coprime (c i) l. Lemma single_fault_detect: if y' = y with coordinate i changed by e != 0 mod l, then dot c y' != dot c y mod l (provable with Int.emod and the unit hypothesis). MDS location needs hypothesis that the Vandermonde minors are units, which holds when the alpha^i are distinct mod l. Cost.linearAlgebra is scaled by (1 + r/B) as a stated bound.
novelty_note: Algorithm-based fault tolerance with Reed-Solomon checksums is classical (Huang-Abraham and successors). The new element is application to the IC kernel step on preemptible instances; this is an engineering saving, not an algorithmic one.

title: Sidon-defect (collision energy) of subspace sumsets across structured factor-base families
handbook_section: 14.5.3 Difference families and balanced incomplete block designs (with 14.4.4 Singer cycles, 13.5.5 Carlitz torsion)
mechanism: The fraction of targets decomposable as a sum of two V-points is |{x(P+Q)}|/q. A Sidon set (a Singer perfect difference set is the extreme case) has zero collisions, giving maximal coverage B(B+1)/2. The random model gives 1-exp(-lambda). Define the Sidon defect sigma(V)=C(|V|,2)-#distinct sums and measure it for four families of equal dimension: random subspaces, Frobenius-invariant subspaces, Carlitz/Drinfeld torsion subspaces ker(C_a) with C_T(x)=x^2+Tx (the A-module of 13.5.5, closed under a second linear operator), and Desarguesian spread elements mu*GF(q) (14.3.3).
claim: After quotienting by negation and Frobenius, the distinct-target coverage of all four families matches the Poisson model to within 1%, except possibly the Carlitz-torsion family, which is predicted to show a coverage deficit of more than 3% from structure-induced collisions.
prediction: Random and spread-element V: defect equals the Poisson prediction within 1%. Frobenius-invariant V: deficit only from orbit duplicates and zero after quotient. Carlitz-torsion V: 0 to 5% excess collisions, direction uncertain. If any family is more than 3% off, choosing V by measured coverage improves relation yield by that percentage (a constant, 1-5%).
cheapest_test: n=20-22 binary curve, dimension-7 subspaces, 50 subspaces per family, 5 curves. Exhaustively compute the pair-sum x-image size. Compare with the Poisson prediction using a negative-control population (random subsets of equal size) and a positive control (a planted arithmetic-progression-like V, which must show a large defect).
falsifier: All families within 1% of the Poisson model, which closes the door on structured-subspace coverage gains. Also falsified if the positive control does not show a defect.
lean_sketch: Define coverage (V : Fin B -> G) : Nat as the length of the deduplicated list of sums of pairs. Prove coverage V <= B*(B+1)/2, and equality iff the pair sums are injective on unordered pairs, using List.Nodup and injectivity (provable). The Poisson comparison needs a hypothesis that sums are uniform, which is not provable. smoothCount is the number of decomposable targets and expectedRelations = coverage*fraction, stated as an inequality.
novelty_note: The Poisson/birthday heuristic is standard, but exact multiplicity or collision statistics across structured subspace families are probably unmeasured in this lab. This is mostly a null-detecting instrument.

title: Latin-square XOR-skewed storage for conflict-free access to the pair-sum table

mechanism: Store table entry (i,j) of the F x F pair-sum or R-P_i table in bank beta(i,j)=i XOR j over GF(2^5) (the Cayley-table Latin square of the affine plane AG(2,32)). Rows, columns, and every line j=a*i+c with a != 1 hit all 32 banks once. This gives conflict-free access in the sort/hash stage and the R-P_i sweep.

prediction: Measured bank-conflict replays drop from about 2-4 per warp access to 0 for 32 banks. Kernel speedup 1.1-1.3x (memory-bound), none if compute-bound.

falsifier: Speedup under 5% or non-zero conflicts after skewing.

Correctness theorem: the multiset of computed sums is layout-independent. Cost unchanged except a constant factor, so no Cost inequality is claimed.

title: Inactivation-decoding order for relation filtering (erasure-decoding view of sparse relations)
handbook_section: 14.4.6 k-Arcs and linear MDS codes
mechanism: View unknown logs as erased symbols and relations as sparse parity checks. MDS parity checks reach rank B with zero overhead but are dense. Sparse relations are solved by peeling, which stalls at a stopping set. Inactivation decoding (RaptorQ-style) inactivates the maximum-residual-weight column when peeling stalls and solves the small dense core last. Use this order in place of greedy singleton/clique removal. Column weights in IC are heavy-tailed (orbit and small-index elements dominate), which favours max-weight inactivation.
claim: At equal oversampling, inactivation ordering leaves a smaller dense core than singleton-plus-clique filtering, and so lowers block Lanczos cost.
prediction: At oversampling 1.1 and row weight 4-6, dense core size falls 15-40% versus greedy SGE, so dense-phase cost (about core^2 to core^3) falls 30-60%. Sparse phase cost is unchanged. Whole-solve effect is small if sparse Lanczos dominates.
cheapest_test: Generate relation matrices from toy collections (n=20-24, subfield V, orbit-quotiented). Run singleton-clique filtering and max-weight inactivation on the same matrices. Compare final dense core dimension and total operations, with the same rank check mod l.
falsifier: Core size not at least 10% smaller than the baseline, or rank differing after filtering.
lean_sketch: Relation as in the vocabulary (Int coefficients over Fin B). Peeling lemma: if column j has a single nonzero coefficient c in the active set and c is a unit mod n, then the solution set of the remaining system plus the back-substitution equation is the solution set of the original (provable with Int.emod). Inactivation is a column permutation, so solution sets are invariant (provable). Cost: linearAlgebra = sparse part + core^3 is a stated model; a core-size inequality is empirical, not provable.

title: Walsh-bias audit of the decomposable-target indicator to pre-filter targets
handbook_section: 14.2.3 Directions and Redei polynomials (with 14.2.4 Sets of points determining few directions)
mechanism: Let D_V be the set of x(R) decomposable over V^m. Compute its Walsh-Hadamard spectrum on GF(2)^n for toy n. Redei/direction theory ties direction-determining sets to linear structure of the graph of a map. A large non-trivial Walsh coefficient means decomposability correlates with a linear functional Tr(alpha*x(R)), so targets with a favourable parity can be preferred. A flat spectrum shows that no linear pre-filter exists.

prediction: For random V, max |W|/|D| <= sqrt(2 ln(q)/|D|), about 0.01-0.02 at n=22. For inversion-closed V the bias at alpha=1 may reach 0.02-0.1. A useful pre-filter yields 1+delta yield per solve, at most 1.02-1.1x, and likely a null.

title: Displacement-rank solve of the Frobenius-twisted relation matrix
handbook_section: 13.4.5.2 Structured matrices and displacement rank (with 13.2.6 Hankel and Toeplitz)
mechanism: On a Koblitz curve, tau acts on the order-ell subgroup as a scalar lambda. If relations are stored un-quotiented, with one column per factor-base point and orbit shifts tau^j P_i placed at adjacent columns, the shift structure makes the block of M over F_ell satisfy M - Z M D = G H^T for a cyclic-shift operator Z and diagonal D = diag(lambda^j). Test whether the generator rank alpha of that displacement is small (a few units) instead of about B. If so, a Toeplitz-like or Cauchy-like solver (Gohberg-Semencul or Bitmead-Anderson style) applies, with cost O(alpha^2 B) per structured block instead of dense elimination or B^2 w Wiedemann on the core.
claim: After full orbit expansion, the dense core of the relation matrix over F_ell has displacement rank w.r.t. (Z, D) bounded by a constant independent of B (at most 8 on toy Koblitz curves). It is not close to B/2, as it would be for an unstructured random sparse matrix.
prediction: Median displacement rank <= 8 for n in {17,19,23} with B from 2^8 to 2^11. A random matrix control gives rank >= 0.45 B. If the claim holds, the solve cost of the dense core falls from about B^3 to about 64 B^2 or less, a 10x or larger gain at B = 2^11.
cheapest_test: Take existing toy Koblitz IC runs, un-quotient the orbit columns, reduce mod ell (a 20-30 bit toy ell), build the dense core and compute rank(M - Z M D) by Gaussian elimination over F_ell. Compare with a control that has the same row weights and random column positions. Runs in seconds for B <= 2048.
falsifier: Displacement rank grows linearly in B (slope >= 0.2) and is statistically indistinguishable from the shuffled control. Smooth-relation columns carry no shift structure because the relation support is chosen by smoothness, not by Frobenius.
lean_sketch: Definitions: Cost with phases factorBase, relations, linearAlgebra, descent : Nat; Relation as Fin B -> Int; shift Z : Fin B -> Fin B as k+1 mod B; a displacement-rank predicate on Int matrices defined by existence of G H with inner dimension alpha. Hypothesis: the relation set is closed under the twist, meaning r in R implies the cyclic rotation of r with weights lambda^j in R (mod ell). Provable without Mathlib: closure implies M - Z M D has row rank at most the number of orbit boundaries, a combinatorial count over Fin B, hence alpha <= number of orbit starts. It does not prove cost savings, only the rank bound, as Nat arithmetic with omega. Statement: linearAlgebra cost of the structured solver is <= c * alpha^2 * B, under an abstract cost axiom for the solver stated as a hypothesis.
novelty_note: Orbit quotienting is integrated; this keeps the expanded matrix and asks for a displacement structure, which none of the integrated linear-algebra items (block Wiedemann/Lanczos, quotienting) use. It may collapse to the quotient if the rank is only the number of orbits, so the test must separate those two.

Plain relation-collection cost scales with relation count, so the relations phase falls by the same fraction.

title: Frobenius-invariant subspaces from divisors of x^n-1 as a curve-selection filter
handbook_section: 13.2.3 Matrix representations of finite fields (with 13.2.4 Circulant matrices)
mechanism: In a normal basis, Frobenius is the cyclic shift, a circulant. F_2-subspaces of GF(2^n) invariant under Frobenius correspond to divisors g of x^n-1 over F_2 via V_g = ker g(sigma). Allowed dimensions are sums of degrees of irreducible factors of x^n-1, set by ord_d(2) for d | n. So the dimension menu for a Frobenius-invariant factor base is a pure function of n. For n = 23, factors are x+1 and two degree-11 factors, giving dimensions 1, 11, 12, 22. For n = 53, 59, 61 (2 primitive), only 0, 1, n-1, n. title: Waring-type coverage guarantee for descent steps
handbook_section: 13.1.6 The Waring problem over finite fields
mechanism: Waring over GF(2^n): every element is a sum of k d-th powers, with explicit g(d, 2^n) and Weil-bound existence thresholds. Apply it to the descent step where a target quantity (x-coordinate of a randomised target R or a large-prime cofactor) must be written as a sum of k terms drawn from the factor-base coordinate set {v^d : v in V}. Coverage theory predicts the exact k beyond which every target is representable and Gauss-sum bounds on representation counts N(t), giving a guarantee that the descent step never needs re-randomisation instead of the usual geometric retry heuristic.
claim: For subspace V of dimension m and d = 3 (the degree appearing in x1x2x3 and x^3 terms), the representation count N_k(t) of a target t as a sum of k elements of V^3 satisfies |N_k(t) - 2^{km-n}| <= (k-1 choose ...) 2^{km/2 + something} (Weil-type), so coverage is complete once km >= n + 2 log2(n) + O(1). Below that, a fraction exp(-2^{km-n}) of targets is uncovered.
prediction: On GF(2^17), 2^19, 2^23 with m = n/3 + 2: uncovered-target fraction matches exp(-mu) with mu = 2^{km-n} within 20% for km - n in [-2, 3], and drops to 0 exactly at km - n >= about 5. Descent retry count per target then has mean 1 + exp(-mu), not the geometric estimate currently assumed.
cheapest_test: For n = 17 and m = 8, k = 3, tabulate N_3(t) for all t in GF(2^17) by convolution (Walsh-Hadamard transform over F_2^17, 17 * 2^17 ops). Compare histogram to Poisson(mu) and find the smallest km - n with zero uncovered targets.
falsifier: Histogram variance exceeds Poisson variance by more than 1.5x (structure in cubes of a subspace breaks the heuristic) or full coverage requires km - n > 10.
lean_sketch: Definitions: Cost record with descent field; cover k V t := exists x : Fin k -> V, sum of cubes = t over a model of GF(2^n) as Fin n -> Bool with abstract add and cube. Hypothesis: card V = 2^m. Provable without Mathlib: pigeonhole lower bound, if 2^{km} < 2^n then cover cannot hold for all t (Fintype-free counting via Fin n functions, injectivity of image), hence km >= n is necessary. The Weil-based sufficiency is stated as a hypothesis (character-sum bound as an axiom) and conditionally yields coverage.
novelty_note: Descent randomisation is integrated; a coverage-completeness threshold derived from Waring number theory replacing retry heuristics is not, and it changes descent cost modelling from probabilistic to deterministic.

title: Rank-count law as null model to detect exploitable structure in S3 pair matrices
handbook_section: 13.2.1 Matrices of specified rank (with 13.3.5 Orthogonal groups, characteristic two)
mechanism: For Koblitz/binary curves, S3(x1,x2,x3) = (x1x2)^2+(x1x3)^2+(x2x3)^2 + x1x2x3 + b is, for fixed (x2,x3), F_2-linear-affine in the coordinates t of x1 in V: c2 x1^2 + c1 x1 + c0, c2 = x2^2+x3^2, c1 = x2x3. So it defines an n x m matrix M(x2,x3) over F_2 and the solvable pairs are those with consistent right-hand side. The number of n x m matrices of rank r over F_2 (13.2.1) gives the null distribution of kernel dimension, P(ker >= k) about 2^{-k(n-m+k)}. Pairs (x2,x3) whose M drops rank give 2^k solutions at once. The mechanism: select V (or x3-slices) maximising the measured excess of rank-deficient M over the null, using the Dickson/Arf classification of the associated quadratic forms (orthogonal group O^pm over char 2).
claim: There exist subspaces V (for example Frobenius-invariant or trace-orthogonal ones) for which the fraction of pairs (x2,x3) in V^2 with ker M(x2,x3) of dimension >= 1 exceeds the uniform-matrix rank-count prediction by a factor >= 2, which would raise relations per candidate pair above the 2^{3m-n} average.

falsifier: All structured V have excess within 10% of the null (95% bootstrap CI contains 1), meaning the matrix family is rank-generic and no V selection can raise relation density.

title: Reverse Cuthill-McKee column reordering of the relation matrix for block Wiedemann matvecs
handbook_section: 13.4.5.1 Reordering (with 13.4.4.1 Wiedemann)
mechanism: Block Wiedemann cost is dominated by sparse matrix times block-vector products whose throughput is limited by cache misses on column gathers. Smooth-relation matrices have heavy-tailed column weights (small factor-base elements appear in most relations). Reorder columns and rows by degree-sorted plus Cuthill-McKee ordering so heavy columns sit in L1/L2 and the light tail is accessed in near-sequential bands. The mathematical content is unchanged (a permutation, kernel preserved); the operation count is identical but cycles per nonzero fall.
claim: On relation matrices with B >= 2^20 and 130-bit ell (32-byte vector entries per column), RCM plus heavy-column grouping cuts L2 misses per nonzero by at least 30% and cycles per nonzero by at least 1.25x vs the discovery (insertion) ordering.
prediction: Cycles per nonzero 1.25x-1.8x lower; at B = 2^16 on toy data the gain is small (<1.1x) because the matrix fits in L2, growing with B. IPC rises from about 0.6 to about 0.9 on a Skylake-class x86 core.
cheapest_test: Synthetic matrices with B = 2^14..2^22, row weight 6, column weights Zipf(1) matching toy IC statistics. Time matvec with insertion order vs RCM vs degree sort using perf stat (cycles, L2 misses) on an isolab host. Paired runs, 20 repeats.
falsifier: Cycles per nonzero ratio < 1.1 at B = 2^22 with paired CI excluding 1.25, or hardware PMU unavailable and cachegrind-simulated miss reduction < 10%.
lean_sketch: Definitions: Relation := Fin B -> Int; permutation pi : Fin B -> Fin B as an Equiv; FactorBase reindexed as fb o pi. Hypothesis: relation r satisfies sum r_i * log(fb i) = 0 mod ell. Provable: reordered relation r o pi^{-1} satisfies the same equation for fb o pi (Finset sum reindexing; in core Lean via a fold lemma over List.finRange), so solution set and the Cost fields factorBase/relations/descent are unchanged and only an extra cycle-level constant changes. The theorem proves invariance, making clear this is a cycles-per-op improvement and not an op-count change; report it under hardware, not accounting.

title: Halving-trace character as a free linear equation in the Weil-restricted decomposition system
handbook_section: 12.2.6 torsion subgroup / 12.2.7 pairings (degenerate in char 2, so Artin-Schreier replaces the Tate pairing); 12.2.5 twists
mechanism: On y^2+xy=x^3+ax^2+b over F_{2^n}, P is in 2E(F_q) iff Tr(x_P)=Tr(a). So psi(P)=Tr(x_P)+Tr(a) is a homomorphism E(F_q)->Z/2, and negation does not change it. Any decomposition sum eps_i P_i = R therefore forces Tr(x_1+...+x_m+x_R)=(m+1)Tr(a). With x_i in an F_2-subspace V, this is one F_2-linear equation in the m*l coordinate bits. It is a degree-1 consequence of the system plus on-curve membership, but F4 only finds it late or never. Add it up front, eliminate one bit by substitution, and add the on-curve conditions Tr(x_i+a+b/x_i^2)=0 as well.
claim: Adding the linear trace equation (and removing one variable) to the Weil-restricted S_{m+1} system removes no true decomposition, and cuts F4 or hybrid-guess solve time at fixed (n,l,m).
prediction: Toy Koblitz curves a=0 (cofactor 4) and a=1 (cofactor 2), n=29..41, m=3. Zero true decompositions lost, over all runs. Hybrid solve time ratio (with/without) is about 0.5 to 0.7, with one fewer guessed bit. Degree of regularity changes by at most 1. Memberships and S_{m+1} are unchanged.
cheapest_test: For n=31, l=10, m=3, take 200 random x_R. Solve with and without the extra equation using msolve or Sage F4 over F_2 (or a hybrid guess loop). Compare the solution sets and the wall time. Brute-force 2^{3l} to confirm the equation holds on every true decomposition.
falsifier: Any true decomposition violating the equation (a derivation error). Or a time ratio above 0.9 over 200 instances. Or F4 already derives the equation at degree at most d_reg-1, so the ideal gains nothing.
lean_sketch: Definitions: DLPInstance with a log bijection to Fin n; psi : G -> Nat with hypothesis hpsi : psi (mul g h) = (psi g + psi h) % 2. A Relation is a list of (coeff:Int, idx:Fin B) plus a target. Provable: a relation implies sum a_i*psi(FB i) = psi R mod 2, by list induction using hpsi and psi(inv g)=psi g. Provable: the equation count mod 2 implies bits mL -> mL-1 in the Cost record's unknown count. Not provable in core Lean: that psi = Tr(x)+Tr(a), and the time speedup. Both are field-theory or empirical hypotheses.

title: Volcano ascent to the j=0 or 1728 crater for an Aut-6 or Aut-4 orbit quotient

The DLP transports by log' = d*log (mod n). The factor base can then be closed under the zeta-action (x -> w x), so unknown logs number B/6 instead of B/2 at the same B. Relations needed and linear-algebra dimension both drop, with a negligible isogeny cost.

title: Factor-base subspace selection by exponential-sum bias on the Semaev curve

The bound is vacuous for l <= 3n/4, so the real yield depends on which resonant (u,w) lie in V^perp. The choice of V is currently random or a polynomial basis. The idea is to treat the count of collinear factor-base triples T(V) as a random variable over V, and select V by offline search or by algebraic structure (trace-kernel of a code, Frobenius-invariant, Sidon-type).

title: Coordinate-optimised summation polynomials: x-shift/scale and Montgomery or Edwards forms for lower F4 matrix size

mechanism: In Montgomery form the S3 relation is (x1-x2)^2 x3^2 - 2((x1x2+1)(x1+x2)+2a x1x2) x3 + (x1x2-1)^2: a special, sparse biquadratic whose product and sum structure (x(P+Q)x(P-Q)=(x1x2-1)^2/(x1-x2)^2) has no linear term. The map to short Weierstrass is affine in x, so every x -> u(x-c) with c,u in the subfield F_p keeps the factor base F_p intact (E over F_{p^n}, x_i in F_p). The number of monomials in S_m and in the Weil-restricted equations depends on (c,u), and short Weierstrass is not the sparsity optimum. Choose (c,u), or a 2-isogenous Montgomery model, to minimise nnz of S_m.

title: Batch-affine versus projective candidate generation in relation collection, with a binary versus prime split
handbook_section: 12.3.3 coordinate systems, 12.3.4 explicit formulas, 12.3.6 char-2 short Weierstrass, 12.3.8 twisted Edwards
mechanism: Relation collection forms R_k = R_{k-1} + T_j (random walks) and needs the affine x for the factor-base lookup. A projective mixed add (López-Dahab 8M+5S) plus batch conversion of x=X/Z (3M) costs about 11M+5S. Batch-affine uses one Montgomery simultaneous inversion across k walks: an add is 1I+2M+1S, amortised to about 3M+2M+1S = 5M+1S. In binary fields with CLMUL, S is about 0.1 to 0.2 M, so the ratio is about 2x. For Curve25519-class (extended Edwards 7M mixed add) the ratio is near 1.
claim: Batch-affine candidate generation with k>=64 walks is at least 1.6x faster per candidate than projective plus batch conversion in GF(2^n), n=131, on CLMUL hardware, and at most 1.1x on 255-bit prime-field Edwards.
prediction: GF(2^131) with PCLMULQDQ: speedup 1.8 to 2.3x at k=64..256. GF(2^53): 1.3 to 1.6x (single word, cheaper M). Prime 2^255-19: 0.95 to 1.1x. Measured with perf-ipc cycles per candidate and a counted M/S/I ledger.
cheapest_test: A C microbenchmark of 1e7 candidate additions with both schemes at the same table and seeds, on the lab isolab-eks route, with the ops ledger matching the formulas. The A/A arm compares the same scheme to itself. Report cycles per candidate.
falsifier: Measured binary speedup under 1.15x at k=64, or a prime-field speedup above 1.3x. Either falsifies the cost model (I/M or S/M assumptions).
lean_sketch: Definitions: Cost record with phases factorBase/relations/linearAlgebra/descent; unit costs M,S,I : Nat. Provable: with weights, 5M+S <= 11M+5S for all M,S (omega). Provable: amortised batch inversion cost (3(k-1)M+I)/k <= 3M + I/k. Provable: Cost.relations(batchAffine) <= Cost.relations(projective) when 3M+I/k <= 6M+4S. Not provable: the measured cycle ratio, which is an empirical hypothesis about hardware.
novelty_note: Batch affine addition is standard in rho implementations (Bos-Kleinjung-Lenstra, Bernstein-Lange). The explicit binary versus prime split inside an IC relation-collection loop, with measured counts, is a bounded engineering improvement. Mark it low novelty and a constant factor only.

title: Z/4 torsion character from Artin-Schreier-Witt halving, used to prune relation sign patterns and reject corrupt rows
handbook_section: 12.2.6 torsion and Tate module, 12.2.7 Weil and Tate pairing (Tate pairing to F_q^*/4 is empty in char 2 since mu_4 is trivial)
mechanism: x-only decomposition systems return x_i but not the signs eps_i in sum eps_i P_i = R. Today signs are found by testing up to 2^m combinations with group additions. On cofactor-4 curves (a=0 Koblitz, ECC2K-130 has h=4) E(F_q) = Z/4 x Z/r. psi4 : E(F_q) -> Z/4, computed by two successive point halvings (half-trace and a square root, so O(n) squarings), is a homomorphism with psi4(-P) = -psi4(P). For every candidate relation the signs must satisfy sum eps_i psi4(P_i) = psi4(R) mod 4. For prime-field Montgomery or Edwards with h=8 (Curve25519), the Tate-Lichtenbaum pairing with a 4-torsion point gives psi4 via a power of (p-1)/4 and a 2-step Miller loop.
claim: Precomputing psi4 once per factor-base element and checking the congruence prunes about half the sign patterns on average and rejects corrupted or twist-contaminated rows with probability 3/4, before any group operation or linear algebra.
prediction: Over 1e5 toy relations at n=31, m=3: surviving sign patterns fraction 0.35 to 0.6 of 2^m on average (exactly 1/2 when all psi4 are odd). Mean group additions for sign resolution drop by 1.5 to 2x. Injected corrupted rows (random sign flips or replaced indices) are rejected with probability about 0.75. psi4 is a homomorphism on 1e6 random point pairs.
cheapest_test: On an a=0 toy Koblitz curve (n=31) compute psi4 via the halving ladder. Check homomorphism and psi4(-P) = -psi4(P) on random pairs. Then take 1e5 relations from brute-force m=3 decompositions with known signs, and count survivors and rejections for true and corrupted rows. Controls: a=1 (h=2) curve to show the character degrades to mod 2.
falsifier: psi4 fails the homomorphism check. Or survivors fraction above 0.6 on average. Or corrupted rows rejected under 60%. Or the psi4 cost per factor-base element exceeds the saved sign-resolution cost.
lean_sketch: Definitions: psi4 : G -> Nat with hypotheses psi4 (mul g h) = (psi4 g + psi4 h) % 4 and psi4 (inv g) = (4 - psi4 g) % 4. A Relation with integer coefficients a_i in {1,-1}. Provable: a valid relation implies sum a_i psi4(P_i) = psi4(R) mod 4 by list induction. Provable: if all psi4(P_i) are odd, exactly 2^{m-1} of the 2^m sign patterns satisfy any fixed target residue of the right parity (finite counting over Fin m -> Bool, decide for small m, induction in general). Not provable: that psi4 is the halving ladder, which is field arithmetic.
novelty_note: Halving and the cyclic cofactor character are known for rho and for scalar multiplication. Using psi4 as a cheap necessary check and sign-pruner on IC relations is not in the integrated list. The gain is a constant factor in relation filtering plus a validation aid.

title: Coppersmith-style small-x decomposition for prime-field curves
handbook_section: 12.3.5 short Weierstrass large characteristic, 12.3.7 Montgomery x-only (biquadratic S3 form), 12.2.2 group law
mechanism: For prime p with factor base F = {x in [0,B)} on-curve points, an m=2 decomposition of R means (x1,x2) with S3(x1,x2,x_R) = 0 mod p, where S3 is bidegree (2,2) in the small unknowns. The current baseline scans x1 in F and hashes x2: cost about B per target R. Treat it as a small-root problem for a bivariate modular polynomial mod the prime p, and use a Coppersmith or Jochemsz-May lattice (LLL on a lattice of dimension about 20 to 40) to find all solutions with x_i < B in polylog(p) time, valid for B up to p^theta (heuristically theta between 1/8 and 1/6). Then the per-relation cost no longer scales with B.
claim: For B <= p^theta, the lattice method finds at least 90% of existing small decompositions and beats the O(B) scan on wall time once B is large enough (p about 2^200 and up). Total IC cost stays above rho, so the gap to matched rho is reported as the remaining distance.
prediction: Toy p about 2^96 with planted P1+P2 = R, x_i < 2^12 (theta = 1/8). Recovery rate at least 0.9 for theta <= 0.12 to 0.15 and falling to under 0.3 above 0.2. Lattice time about 10^7 to 10^8 operations. Break-even versus scan near B about 2^22 to 2^25, i.e. p about 2^180 to 2^200. Projected total IC exponent for p 2^255 with B = p^{1/8}: about p^{7/8}, still above rho's p^{1/2}.
cheapest_test: Sage plus fpll or LLL: 500 planted instances at p about 2^96 and theta in {0.08, 0.12, 0.16, 0.2}, with a matched brute-force scan as positive control and the same lattice on random (unplanted) R as negative control, which should find nothing. Record the success rate and time per instance.
falsifier: Success rate below 50% at theta = 1/8, or lattice cost above the scan cost at every p up to 2^256 at B = p^theta. Or the relation yield for unplanted R is not B^2/(2p) times the scan completeness.
lean_sketch: Definitions: DLPInstance with log; FactorBase small x as Fin B -> G; a decomposition predicate dec x1 x2 R := FB x1 * FB x2 = R or its inverse variant. Provable: a brute-scan search is sound and complete for dec (Fin B x Fin B fold). Provable: with a hypothesis oracle LatticeComplete (it returns every dec solution when B <= p^theta), the lattice search equals the scan result. Provable: Cost.relations(lattice) <= Cost.relations(scan) iff c_L <= B (Nat inequality). Not provable in core Lean: the Coppersmith heuristic and its success rate.
novelty_note: Coppersmith small roots are used widely in RSA and in some Weil-descent or hidden-number contexts. I am not aware of it applied to the x-only point-decomposition problem for small-x factor bases. The success rate is purely empirical here and the bound theta is heuristic. A measured per-relation speedup is not a total beat of rho.

title: Frobenius-orbit canonical key by Booth or Duval minimal rotation in normal-basis words
handbook_section: 12.2.8 endomorphism ring and automorphism group (Frobenius tau on Koblitz), 12.3.6 char-2 arithmetic
mechanism: The Frobenius orbit quotient needs, for each candidate x in the factor base, a canonical representative of its orbit {x, x^2, ..., x^(2^(n-1))} to index the unknown. In polynomial basis this costs about n squarings (each n/64 words). In a normal basis, Frobenius is a bit rotation, so the canonical key is the lexicographically minimal rotation of an n-bit word, computed by Booth's algorithm in O(n) bit operations (word-parallel with a constant). Keep normal basis only for the key and the membership test (a linear map), converting from polynomial basis once per candidate by one n x n bit-matrix product.
claim: For n=131 candidate-orbit canonicalisation via one basis change plus Booth costs at least 1.5x fewer cycles than min-over-n-squarings in polynomial basis, with no change in the orbit partition.
prediction: Cycles per canonicalisation, n=131, AVX2: polynomial-basis squarings about 1.3e3 to 2e3 cycles, normal-basis Booth about 4e2 to 8e2, speedup 1.6 to 3x. At n=53 the gain is 1.0 to 1.3x (single word). Orbit partition identical on 1e6 random x (all sizes 1 or n for prime n).
cheapest_test: A C benchmark on 1e6 random x for n in {53, 83, 131}: arm A polynomial-basis min over squarings, arm B Booth on a normal-basis image. Check equal orbit ids via a hash map and compare perf-ipc cycles. A/A arm for the noise floor.
falsifier: Speedup under 1.15x at n=131, or any orbit partition mismatch, or the basis-change cost exceeds the saving.
lean_sketch: Definitions: orbitRepresentatives N k = N / k; a canonical-key function key : Nat -> Nat that is rotation-invariant over an n-bit word. Provable: key (rotate w) = key w, and key w <= w. Provable: the orbit count from keys over a free action of a group of prime order n on N elements equals N / n (Nat.div after free action, with hypothesis that no fixed points exist). Not provable in core Lean: the cycle ratio, and the basis-change correctness over F_{2^n}.
novelty_note: Canonical-form hashing for Frobenius equivalence is standard in rho on Koblitz curves (Wiener-Zuccherato, Gallant-Lambert-Vanstone). Its use in the IC orbit-quotient lookup, and the Booth step specifically, is only a bounded engineering gain. Mark it low novelty.

title: Coupon-collector relation count for full rank
handbook_section: 11.6.10 Sparse linear systems of equations
mechanism: Each relation is a sparse row with at most m nonzero +-1 entries over the factor-base columns. Full rank B-1 needs every column covered. If columns are hit roughly uniformly, the relation count needed is about (B/m)(ln B + c), not B(1+eps) as cost models usually assume. Intervention: when a column is under-covered, fix x_1 to that rare factor-base element and solve the remaining m-1 variables for the next relation.
claim: On toy Weil-restricted decomposition data, the number of relations needed to reach full rank mod the group order follows (B/m)(ln B + c) with c = O(1). A fixed-x1 steering rule for rare columns lowers the relations-to-full-rank count by a measurable factor. Steering has to be shown to cost no more per relation than unsteered collection.
prediction: n=24 to 30, m=3, B=2^8 to 2^10: relations to full rank are 3 to 5 times B, and the ratio grows with ln B. Steered runs reach full rank with about 1.3 to 2 times fewer total solver calls, or the steering overhead cancels the gain. This is an accounting-sensitive prediction, so total solver calls must be reported, not relation counts.
cheapest_test: Run the existing toy decomposition on 3 to 5 curves with GF(2^n), n in {22, 24, 26}. Log each relation's column set in arrival order and compute rank mod the prime group order incrementally. Plot rank against relation count and fit B/m*(ln B + c). Repeat with fixed-x1 steering and compare solver calls to full rank, using 20 seeds each.
falsifier: Rank reaches B-1 with at most 1.15 B relations on the unsteered arm, or steering needs at least as many total solver calls to reach full rank as the unsteered arm.
lean_sketch: Definitions: DLPInstance with log : G -> Fin n bijection, FactorBase B := Fin B -> G, Relation := Fin B -> Int with support size at most m, Cost with relations field. Hypothesis: every relation has at most m nonzero coefficients. Provable without Mathlib: if the relations cover fewer than B columns then the matrix has a zero column, so at least one factor-base log is undetermined (no relation determines it); and a covering family needs at least ceil(B/m) relations (pigeonhole on supports). Probabilistic ln B is stated as a hypothesis-free Nat inequality only, not proved.
novelty_note: Cost models in the lab count about B relations. This replaces that with a coverage-driven count and a steering rule. It is a count change, not relabelling, only if solver calls to full rank drop.

title: Orbit-quotient coverage law, relations scale with B/k
handbook_section: 11.6.10 Sparse linear systems of equations; 11.2.3.5 Relations to permutations and integers
mechanism: After the Frobenius orbit quotient the unknowns are orbit classes (about B/n of them). A relation touches at most m orbit columns. The coverage law then needs about (B/(n m)) ln(B/n) relations, so the saving from the quotient is a factor n times a log ratio, which is not the same as the 'multiply by n' that cost models assume. The orbit-size distribution (fixed points, short cycles, from the permutation-cycle view in 11.2.3.5) shifts the constant.
claim: The measured relation requirement after orbit quotient follows (B_orb/m) ln(B_orb) with B_orb = number of orbit classes, and the observed saving over the unquotiented count is n*ln(B)/ln(B/n)-like, not n.
prediction: n=25 to 31 Koblitz toy, m=3, V Frobenius-invariant: ratio (relations to full rank without quotient)/(with quotient) is within 15% of n*lnB/ln(B/n), and below n by a factor of 1.1 to 1.4.
cheapest_test: Reuse the idea-1 data. Fold columns by Frobenius orbit using the eigenvalue lambda mod N (log(sigma P) = lambda log P) and count relations to full rank on the folded matrix. Compare against the unfolded count for the same arrival order.
falsifier: Saving ratio equals n within 5%, or folded relation count to full rank is not within 25% of (B_orb/m)(ln B_orb + c) with the same c as the unfolded fit.
lean_sketch: Definitions: orbitRepresentatives N k = N / k as given; Relation over Fin B; a fold map Fin B -> Fin (B / k). Hypothesis: the fold is surjective and respects the orbit relation. Provable: surjective fold gives the column-count bound ceil((B/k)/m) <= relations, and a zero folded column implies a zero original orbit of columns. No probabilistic statement is proved.

title: GF(2)-defined Koblitz summation polynomials: support and polytope structure
handbook_section: 11.5.2.2 Irreducibility tests based on indecomposability of polytopes; 11.5.2.3 Sparse bivariate Hensel lifting driven by polytopes
mechanism: For a Koblitz curve (a in {0,1}, b=1) the Semaev polynomials S_m lie in GF(2)[x_1..x_m], so S_m(x^2) = S_m(x)^2 and the support is a union of Frobenius-closed exponent sets. Compute S_4 and S_5 once over GF(2) in elementary-symmetric coordinates. Study the Newton polytope, its lattice-point count against the weighted-dense count, and Minkowski indecomposability (Ostrowski-type test). A strictly smaller support gives sparse Macaulay rows. Indecomposability certifies that no factorization shortcut exists.
claim: The support of S_m (m=4,5) over GF(2) in e-coordinates fills at most 30% of the weighted-dense monomial set, and the Newton polytope is Minkowski-indecomposable, so S_m is absolutely irreducible. The density falls as m grows.
prediction: S_4: density 15 to 40%. S_5: density 5 to 25%, lower than S_4. The polytope is indecomposable at m=3,4,5.
cheapest_test: Compute S_3 by hand, then S_4, S_5 by resultant over GF(2) with a CAS. Count monomials in e-coordinates against the weighted-dense bound and test Minkowski indecomposability with a small enumeration of lattice summands. Then run F4 on S_4-based toy systems with sparse versus dense row storage and compare matrix nonzeros.
falsifier: Density at m=5 at least 60% of the weighted-dense set, or the polytope is decomposable at some m with a nontrivial factorization of S_m.
lean_sketch: Definitions: polynomial as Finsupp-like list of (exponent vector, coefficient in Bool), Frobenius as exponent doubling. Hypothesis: the support list is Frobenius-closed. Provable: the monomial count of a computed S_m equals the stated number by decide on the concrete list for small m. Indecomposability is a finite check on the support (enumerate subsets of lattice points) and is provable by decide for m=3,4.

title: Hamming-weight degree and mixed-volume predictor for F4 cost
handbook_section: 11.5.2.1 Ostrowski's theorem; 11.5.2.2 polytope indecomposability
mechanism: In Weil restriction over GF(2), x^(2^s) is linear in the bits, so the bit-degree of a monomial x^alpha is the binary weight of its exponents, not the exponent. Ostrowski's theorem says the Newton polytope of a product is the Minkowski sum of the polytopes. Compute the weight-degree profile of S_m and the BKK mixed volume of the Weil-restricted system's supports. Use these to predict the maximum Macaulay degree and matrix size of F4 more tightly than the semi-regular or Bezout bound.
claim: A predictor built from the weight-degree profile (plus mixed volume of supports) predicts the F4 maximum degree to within +-1 on at least 85% of toy instances. The semi-regular bound does so on at most 65%.
prediction: Over 100 toy systems (n=15 to 24, m=3, k=n/3): weight-degree predictor hits the observed max degree in 85 to 95% of cases, the semi-regular predictor in 50 to 65%.
cheapest_test: Generate 100 Weil-restricted S_3 and S_4 systems with random targets, run F4 (any open implementation) recording the max degree and matrix size, and compute both predictors. Compare hit rates.
falsifier: The weight-degree predictor is no better than semi-regular within 5 percentage points, or hit rate under 70%.
lean_sketch: Definitions: Cost record with phases, weightDeg : Nat -> Nat as popcount, a monomial as Fin m -> Nat. Hypothesis: bit-degree of x^alpha is sum of popcounts. Provable: popcount(a+b) <= popcount a + popcount b, and weightDeg is bounded by total degree; the predictor is a function computing max over support. The relation to F4 is empirical, not provable.
novelty_note: F4 is integrated. A weight-degree plus mixed-volume predictor of F4 cost, checked against measured max degree, is new. It is a cost-model tool, not a speed-up by itself.

title: Artin-Schreier splitting density of subspace factor bases
handbook_section: 12.1.3 Extensions of function fields
mechanism: The binary curve is the Artin-Schreier extension w^2+w = x + a + b/x^2 of F(x). A degree-one place x=v splits in F(E) iff Tr(v + a + b/v^2) = 0, so only about half of any subspace V lies on E and the rest are twist points whose solutions are wasted. The E-density of V is a character sum of the Kloosterman type, sum over v in V of (-1)^(Tr(v)+Tr(sqrt(b)/v)). Choose V (or a coset v0 + V) to maximise the split density.
claim: The best coset of a k-dimensional subspace has E-density 0.5 + O(sqrt(k(n-k)) 2^(-k/2)). The useful-solution fraction per Groebner call rises by (rho/0.5)^m. The gain is visible only for small k and vanishes at cryptographic sizes.
prediction: n=24, k=8, m=3: best of 10^4 random cosets has rho about 0.60 to 0.70, giving a 1.7x to 2.7x gain in useful solution fraction. At n=48, k=16 the best of 10^4 has rho within 0.51 of 0.5 (gain under 1.15x). That is a negative scaling result unless structured V (not random) beats it.
cheapest_test: For n=20 to 30, compute the E-density of 10^4 random k-subspaces and cosets by direct trace evaluation. Fit the best density against the Fourier/Chernoff prediction. Then run S_3 solves restricted to the best versus a median V and compare useful relations per call.
falsifier: Best-of-10^4 density within 0.02 of 0.5 at n=24, k=8; or density gain does not translate to at least 1.3x useful relations per call.
lean_sketch: Definitions: DLPInstance, FactorBase B := Fin B -> G, a predicate onCurve on x-coordinates given as a Bool-valued function. Hypothesis: onCurve x = (trace condition). Provable: counting lemma that the fraction of useful m-tuples is the m-th power of the per-element density (product of independent indicators, as a Nat identity on Finset-free lists). The density bound itself is a hypothesis, not proved.
novelty_note: The half-twist waste is known. Optimising V against the Kloosterman-type character sum is not in the integrated list and probably collapses at scale. The scaling test is the contribution.

title: Riemann-Roch counting bound on descent depth
handbook_section: 12.1.2 Divisors and Riemann-Roch theorem
mechanism: On an elliptic curve (g=1) the space L(kO) has dimension exactly k, so effective degree-k divisors with sum O correspond one-to-one to nonzero functions mod scalars. The number of ways to write a random point Q as a sum of m points from a factor set V' is about C(|V'|, m-1)/q. Requiring at least one solution gives |V'| >= ((m-1)! q)^(1/(m-1)), a sharp lower bound on the level size of any descent step that uses m-term sums.
claim: For a descent step using m-term sums, the success probability is 1 - exp(-C(|V'|,m-1)/q) with a sharp threshold at |V'|^(m-1) = (m-1)! q. For m=3 the first descent level needs |V'| about sqrt(2q), which is rho-scale. Descent is cheap only for m >= 4.
prediction: n=24, m=3: fraction of random Q with a decomposition from V' of dim d crosses 0.5 near d=12 or 13 (about sqrt(2q) = 2^12.5). For m=4 the crossing is at d about 8 or 9 (q^(1/3)*6^(1/3)).
cheapest_test: Enumerate all pairs/triples from V' of dimension d=8..14 on a toy n=24 curve with a hash table of x-sums and measure the fraction of 10^4 random targets decomposed. Compare to the Poisson curve.
falsifier: Measured threshold dimension differs from the formula by at least 1.5 in d at m=3, or at m=4.
lean_sketch: Definitions: DLPInstance with log bijection to Fin n, Relation over Fin B. Hypothesis: the sum map from m-subsets of V' to G is injective on pairs (no collisions). Provable: counting lower bound that if C(|V'|, m-1) < n/ (number of Q targets then fewer than half... ) precisely: a map from a set of size s to G of size n cannot be onto if s < n, so a descent step covering all targets needs C(|V'|,m-1) >= n. That inequality is a Nat theorem and is proved by Fintype-free pigeonhole.
novelty_note: A generic counting heuristic, so the claim is modest. The use is cost-model: it states the descent-depth floor against which randomized descent is measured. It is not a speed-up.

title: Fano factor of solution counts: Frobenius clumping
handbook_section: 11.2.3.2 Factorization patterns; 11.2.3.5 Relations to permutations and integers
mechanism: Solutions of the decomposition system on a Frobenius-invariant subspace come in Frobenius orbits of size dividing n (cycle structure as in the permutation view of 11.2.3.5). The number of solutions per target is therefore a compound Poisson variable with variance/mean (Fano factor) about the mean orbit size, not 1. Independent relations per solver call are orbits, not solutions. The yield accounting must divide by the orbit multiplicity.
claim: The Fano factor of solutions per target is about n for generic Frobenius-invariant V on a Koblitz curve and 1 for a non-invariant V. Counting solutions without orbit division overstates relations per call by about the same factor.
prediction: n=23, m=3: Fano factor 15 to 23 for invariant V, 0.9 to 1.2 for non-invariant V; the mean number of independent orbits per call equals the non-invariant mean times 2^k-ratio, within 20%.
cheapest_test: Solve S_3 for 2000 random targets with an invariant V (normal-basis span) and a random V of the same dimension. Record solution counts and orbit counts. Compute variance/mean and mean orbits per call.
falsifier: Fano factor for invariant V below 3, or the non-invariant arm shows Fano above 2.
lean_sketch: Definitions: orbitRepresentatives N k = N / k, a Frobenius action as an iterate of a function on Fin B. Hypothesis: each orbit has size dividing k. Provable: number of solutions = sum of orbit sizes, hence solutions <= k * orbits and orbits >= solutions / k, a Nat inequality by induction on a list of orbit sizes.
novelty_note: Orbit quotient is integrated. The Fano-factor accounting of yield per call is a cost-model correction, to be reported with matched rho gap, not claimed as a speed-up.

title: Linearized-polynomial divisibility test for subspace roots
handbook_section: 11.3.3 Rabin's irreducibility test; 11.4 Factorization of univariate polynomials
mechanism: Rabin's test uses gcd(x^(q^i) - x, f). For a subspace factor base V of dimension k the product of (X - v) over V is the subspace polynomial L_V(X), an F_2-linearized polynomial with k+1 terms. For a univariate completion polynomial N(X) of degree d (the last variable of S_m after fixing the others), the test 'all roots of N lie in V' is L_V mod N = 0, which costs k Frobenius powers mod N rather than the n of distinct-degree factorization or 2^k evaluations. Use it as an inner filter in hybrid solvers (guess m-2 variables, close with this test).
claim: For d <= 16, the L_V mod N test is at least 2x cheaper than distinct-degree plus equal-degree root finding for deciding 'N has a root in V', and gives the same decisions. The gain is about n/k = m over the distinct-degree stage.
prediction: n=48, k=16, d=8: field mult counts per test 16*d^2-ish vs 48*d^2-ish plus equal-degree stage, ratio 2.5 to 4 in counted multiplications.
cheapest_test: Implement both on GF(2^n) toy fields (n=24..48), run on 10^5 random N of degree 4 to 16 with planted V-roots at rate 1%, compare decisions and counted field multiplications.
falsifier: Decisions differ on any instance (bug or false theory), or counted multiplications are not lower by at least 1.5x.
lean_sketch: Definitions: polynomial over a finite field as a list, FactorBase as Fin B -> G with G = field. Hypothesis: L_V is the product over the factor base of (X - v). Provable: if N divides L_V then every root of N is a factor-base element (root of a product of linear factors), a core lemma by list induction. The cost count k vs n is an arithmetic statement on a Cost record.
novelty_note: Rabin/Cantor-Zassenhaus root finding is standard. Using the linearized structure of L_V as a filter is a known trick in the subspace method; the measured counted-multiplication comparison inside the hybrid solver is what is new here, and a negative result is likely at small d.

title: Canonical sign bit Tr(y/x) resolves x-only Semaev solutions without point additions
handbook_section: 11.1.9.2 Squares and square roots, even characteristic (half-trace); 11.1.6.2 Squaring in characteristic two
mechanism: For odd n on y^2+xy=x^3+ax^2+b, the two lifts of x are y and y+x, and Tr((y+x)/x)=Tr(y/x)+Tr(1)=Tr(y/x)+1. So s(P)=Tr(y/x) is a canonical negation-sign bit, and the half-trace gives y from x in one linear map. For a zero-sum triple the line y=lam*x+c gives x1x2x3=b+c^2 and e1=a+lam^2+lam. Then sum s(P_i)=Tr(lam)+Tr(c*sum 1/x_i) is a function of the x's alone, costing one sqrt, one trace and one inversion. This should select the valid sign pattern of an x-only solution algebraically, replacing the 2^(m-1) trial point additions.
claim: For odd n and m=3, the parity of sum Tr(y_i/x_i) over the true lifts of any x-only S3 solution equals a closed-form function of (x1,x2,x3) that distinguishes the valid sign class from the invalid ones in 100% of toy cases.
prediction: Closed form agrees with brute-force sign resolution in all tested triples (exact, not statistical). Sign-resolution field-op count falls from about 2 affine additions per candidate to about 1 inversion plus 1 half-trace. Total relation-phase time changes by less than 5%, because solving dominates.
cheapest_test: Enumerate all points of 5 toy curves over GF(2^n) with n in {11,13,15,17,19}. For all zero-sum triples compute sum Tr(y_i/x_i) and compare it with the closed form. Time sign resolution against brute-force addition for m=3,4.
falsifier: Any triple where the closed form disagrees with the true sign class, or a sign-resolution time share under 2% of the decomposition phase, which makes the gain irrelevant.
lean_sketch: Needs: structure BinCurve (field F with trace Tr : F -> Fin 2, points as (x,y) pairs, add operation), DLPInstance, Relation. Hypotheses: n odd (Tr 1 = 1), P not O. Provable in core Lean: lemma sign_flip: s(-P)=s(P)+1 from Tr additivity and Tr 1 = 1, so s is a section of the quotient by negation. Then orbitRepresentatives N 2 = N/2 gives the factor-base size. The closed-form triple identity needs field axioms assumed abstractly and is provable by ring-style rewriting. The statement says a Relation lifted via s has integer coefficients all +/-1 and verifies sum eps_i*P_i=R.
novelty_note: Negation quotient is integrated; the new element is the trace-based canonical sign as an algebraic oracle for the x-only sign ambiguity. Small expected gain (under 5%); an honest test of whether sign resolution matters at all.

title: Itoh-Tsujii inversion plus Montgomery batching as the measured affine-add primitive in the relation inner loop
handbook_section: 11.1.8.2 Inversion in extension fields; 11.1.5.2 Multiplication in extension fields
mechanism: Over GF(2^n), Itoh-Tsujii computes 1/x as (x^(2^(n-1)-1))^2 using an addition chain on n-1, costing about floor(log2(n-1))+hw(n-1)-1 multiplications plus n-2 squarings. For n=131, n-1=130=10000010b, so 8 multiplications. With Montgomery batching, k inversions cost 3(k-1) multiplications plus one Itoh-Tsujii inversion. Affine addition amortises to about 5 multiplications (lambda, lambda^2, x3, y3 plus batch overhead) with no projective Z coordinate, against about 8 to 11 multiplications for López-Dahab mixed addition. Relation collection computes huge numbers of R_ij = aP+bQ+F_k sums where only x is needed.
claim: A batched affine-add inner loop with Itoh-Tsujii and batch size at least 16 beats López-Dahab mixed addition per point-sum in wall time on GF(2^n), n in 53..131, with PCLMUL-class multiplication.
prediction: Throughput gain of 1.3x to 1.8x for batch size 16 to 64 at n=131. Break-even batch size is about 4 to 8 when squaring costs about 0.1 multiplication, and larger when squaring costs more. Gain shrinks for small n where the inversion-to-multiplication ratio is lower than the batching overhead.
cheapest_test: Microbenchmark on GF(2^n) for n in {53,83,131} with fixed-seed random affine points: affine+batch+Itoh-Tsujii against LD mixed add, interleaved arms, A/A arm included, batch sizes 1,4,16,64. Report ns per add and multiplications per add.
falsifier: LD mixed addition is at least as fast at batch size 16 for n=131, or the break-even batch size exceeds 64.
lean_sketch: Define Cost record {factorBase relations linearAlgebra descent : Nat} plus a PrimitiveCost {mul sqr inv : Nat}. Define itohTsujiiMuls (n : Nat) = log2floor (n-1) + popcount (n-1) - 1. Provable by decide for n=131 that it equals 8. Provable: batchInvMuls k = 3*(k-1) with one inv, and the amortised affine add count as an arithmetic bound as a function of k. No claim about wall time is provable. Only the operation-count identity is, and it is labelled an accounting fact, not a speedup.

title: Degree collapse of S_4 on the symmetrised diagonal as an iterate-degree-growth anomaly
handbook_section: 10.5.3 Degree growth
mechanism: For an iterated map, deg f^k = d^k unless the map is degenerate. Semaev S_{m+1} is built from S_m by resultant composition with S_3, so its degree in each variable grows as 2^(m-1), as an iterated-composition degree. On the diagonal x1=x2 the identity 2P+P3+P4=O means S_4(x,x,x3,x4) has a repeated-point structure. Claim: S_4(x,x,X3,X4) is divisible by an extraneous square factor corresponding to the degenerate P+P=O branch, so its effective degree is below the generic 2^(m-1)=4 per variable. Stripping it shrinks the Weil-restricted system.
claim: The diagonal specialisation S_4(x,x,y,z) over GF(2^n) has an extraneous factor, so its squarefree part has total degree strictly lower than the substituted generic S_4. Removing it lowers the F4 degree of regularity of the restricted system by at least 1 for at least one tested (m,l) setting.
prediction: The squarefree part has degree about 25% lower in X (3 instead of 4 on some variables). F4 time on the diagonal subsystem falls by 20% to 50% at fixed toy sizes. No effect on non-diagonal systems.
cheapest_test: With sympy or Singular over GF(2^k), k=7..13, build S_3 and S_4 for 3 curves. Substitute x1=x2, factor, and record degrees. Run F4 on the Weil-restricted diagonal system with and without the extraneous factor (matched seeds, order randomised).
falsifier: The substituted polynomial is squarefree of full generic degree, or F4 time and degree of regularity are unchanged within the A/A band.
lean_sketch: Needs: Poly over an abstract commutative ring, degree function, a SemaevPoly spec as a predicate (S x1 x2 x3 = 0 iff exists points summing to O). Provable: for S_3 explicit formula, degree in each variable is 2 (decide on coefficients). The general-m divisibility claim would be a hypothesis, as statement 'diagonalFactor | S_4(x,x,y,z)' assumed as an explicit hypothesis, with a conditional corollary that factorBase-cost bound on degree reduces. The factor-degree lemma is an unconditional polynomial identity only for fixed small curve coefficients.

title: Character-sum bias selection of affine factor-base cosets
handbook_section: 10.4.4.3 Legendre sequence and related bit sequences
mechanism: A subspace or interval factor base V keeps only x with a lift, that is the Legendre symbol chi(x^3+ax+b)=+1 (odd p) or Tr(x+a+b/x^2)=0 (binary). The fraction kept is 1/2+(1/(2|V|))*sum_{x in V} chi(f(x)). Weil bounds control complete sums, but sums over a coset v+V of a structured V fluctuate with standard deviation about 1/sqrt(|V|). Searching T random cosets and keeping the best gives bias about sqrt(2 ln T/|V|), so the same enumeration effort yields more usable points. This uses the Legendre-sequence bit pattern of the sums rather than random coset choice.
claim: Best-of-T coset selection by lift fraction raises the fraction of factor-base x-values that lift from 1/2 to 1/2+sqrt(2 ln T/(4|V|)) (about 1/2+0.35*sqrt(ln T/|V|)), at one-time cost T*|V| trace or Legendre evaluations.
prediction: At |V|=2^10, T=2^10, gain in B per enumerated x of about 2.6 to 3 percent; shrinks like 1/sqrt|V| for the sizes that matter (|V|>=2^20 gives under 0.1 percent). Relations per sweep scale as B^m so m=3 gets about 3x that percentage.
cheapest_test: On GF(2^17) and GF(p), p about 2^20, evaluate lift fraction over 2000 cosets of a dimension-10 subspace and compare the max with the Gaussian prediction and with a random-coset null. Include A/A of repeated random draws.
falsifier: Max over T cosets exceeds the iid-binomial null prediction by less than one standard error, or realised gain is below 0.5 percent at |V|=2^10.
lean_sketch: Needs: FactorBase as Fin B -> G, liftFraction (V : Finset F) (chi : F -> Int) : Rat, hypothesis |chi|<=1. Provable: liftFraction = 1/2 + (1/(2|V|)) * sum chi (algebraic identity for chi in {+1,-1}). Provable: best-of-T cannot decrease the fraction (monotone max). The sqrt(ln T/|V|) size is a probabilistic claim, stated as an explicit hypothesis not proved. Statement: orbitRepresentatives N 2 = N/2 sizes unchanged, factor-base size scales by (1+2*bias).
novelty_note: Small honest effect; selection of cosets by character-sum bias is not the integrated 'subspace FB' but a tuning layer. Likely below the noise gate at real sizes, useful as a toy negative control.

title: Low-discrepancy (a,b) lattice sweeps to cut duplicate relations at saturation
handbook_section: 10.4.5.5 Discrepancy; 10.4.5.2 Lattice test
mechanism: Random pairs (a,b) in Z_N^2 for R=aP+bQ produce duplicate decompositions at rate about N_samples^2/(2*search_space_effective), which matters when the number of needed relations is a significant fraction of the distinct decomposable pairs (small toy and symmetrised, orbit-quotiented spaces). Replacing independent draws by a Korobov rank-1 lattice or Sobol set in (a,b) with low discrepancy covers the (a,b) plane uniformly, and the lattice test guards against LCG-style planar structure that would correlate relations in a sublattice. This is a sampling-design change, distinct from the walk and sieve variants.
claim: At relation counts at least 10 percent of the effective space size, a rank-1 lattice sweep over (a,b) has fewer duplicate relations and faster rank growth of the relation matrix mod N than iid uniform sampling; below 1 percent saturation it makes no difference.
prediction: At saturation 20 percent, duplicate fraction falls from about 10 percent (birthday) to under 3 percent; relations needed for full rank fall by 5 to 8 percent. At 1 percent saturation, difference under 0.5 percent (null).
cheapest_test: Toy curve of order about 2^16 with B=64 factor base: collect relations by iid uniform vs Korobov lattice vs Sobol (3 arms, interleaved seeds, A/A), record relations to full rank over 100 repetitions, paired bootstrap.
falsifier: Relations-to-full-rank intervals of lattice and iid arms overlap at 20 percent saturation, or the lattice arm shows lower rank due to planar correlation.
lean_sketch: Needs: Relation with Int coefficients, relationMatrix : List Relation -> Matrix, rank as a predicate (no Mathlib, so state as existence of a nonzero minor or use Fin-indexed Gaussian elimination spec). Provable: duplicate count of a list is non-negative and a Finset-valued sweep (injective map Fin M -> pairs) has zero duplicates, so lattice sweep duplicates = 0 by injectivity of a -> (a, k*a mod N) for gcd(k,N)=1... only if distinct (a,b) imply distinct relations, which is a hypothesis about decomposition determinism. Not provable: rank gain, empirical.

title: Defining-polynomial choice for Weil-restriction coordinate sparsity (trinomial vs dense over the subfield)
handbook_section: 11.1.3.2 Modular reduction in extension fields; 11.1.1.2 Extension field generation
mechanism: Weil restriction of S_m over GF(2^l) expresses each x_i in a basis of GF(2^n)/GF(2^l), and multiplication by x^m reduces modulo the defining polynomial. The number of monomials in the restricted equations equals the number of nonzero coefficients generated by reducing x^(2m-2). A sparse trinomial or pentanomial over GF(2^l) produces sparser polynomial systems than a dense irreducible polynomial. The fields are isomorphic via a linear map, so dreg is invariant, but the matrix density and the F4 constant change.
claim: On composite n=l*m (for example 55, 57, 91, 93, 95), choosing a sparse relative defining polynomial lowers F4 time by a constant factor but leaves the degree of regularity identical to a dense choice.
prediction: Dreg identical across choices (exact). F4 runtime ratio dense/sparse of 1.2x to 2x at n=57 with l=19, m=3. Memory ratio similar. No exponent change.
cheapest_test: For n=55 (l=5,m=11) and n=57 (l=19,m=3), generate the restricted S_3 system with 5 random irreducibles and the best sparse one, record monomial count, dreg and F4 time with randomised order, A/A repeated.
falsifier: Runtime ratio within A/A noise, or dreg differing across choices, which would contradict the linear-isomorphism argument and indicate a bug.
lean_sketch: Needs: a ring hom spec between two representations, F K -> F K', and a degree function for polynomial systems. Provable: the isomorphism preserves degree (linear change of variables does not raise degree), so dreg(system) = dreg(system') as a statement over an abstract degree-of-regularity function with the hypothesis that dreg is invariant under invertible linear substitution. Cost record unchanged in the exponent; only a constant scale hypothesis is stated. This is an invariance lemma, not a speedup proof.
novelty_note: Mostly an engineering constant; the lab's composite-n rows are where it applies. Prime n (53, 59, 61, 67, 131) cannot use it, so applicability is limited.

title: Exact smooth-polynomial counts as the smoothCount model for polynomial-basis x-coordinate decomposition

mechanism: Panario's saddle-point or generating-function counts give the exact number of monic degree-n polynomials over F_2 with all irreducible factors of degree at most m: coefficient of z^n in prod_{d<=m}(1-z^d)^(-I_d), I_d=number of irreducibles of degree d. For a factor base F={P: x(P) as a polynomial in the polynomial basis has all factors of degree at most m}, density is exactly this count over 2^n, not the Dickman estimate rho(n/m). This gives an exact smoothCount for the factor-base size and the lift-adjusted yield, replacing the asymptotic u^-u estimate, which is wrong by factors of 2 to 10 at n=53..131.

title: Primitive-polynomial LFSR enumeration of factor-base x-coordinates by shift-and-reduce
handbook_section: 11.1.1.3 Primitive elements; 11.1.1.4 Order of an irreducible and primitive polynomials; 11.1.3.2 Modular reduction in extension fields
mechanism: With a primitive trinomial f of GF(2^n), the powers t^i (i=0..B-1) form a geometric progression whose successor needs one shift and at most hw(f)-1 XORs, not a field multiplication. A factor base whose x-coordinates are {t^i} costs about 1/50 of the multiplications of a random-x base to enumerate, then needs the half-trace lift (a linear map, cheaper than a general exponentiation). The order of t equals 2^n-1, so the x-coordinates are distinct for B up to 2^n-1. A related variant is a factor base closed under multiplication by t^k for chosen k, so Semaev S_3 queries with x1=t^i, x2=t^j reduce to a function of i-j and i+j-type invariants when the curve has b=1.
claim: Enumeration of an LFSR-power factor base is at least 10x cheaper in field operations than random-x sampling per base element, and the factor base so generated gives relation yield statistically indistinguishable from a random-x base of the same size.
prediction: Enumeration cost: about 1 shift plus 2 to 4 XOR per element against about 1 multiplication-equivalent for random sampling with lift test, so 5x to 15x cheaper in bit operations. Relation yield per factor base element within +/-5 percent of random-x base (null). Factor-base time is already a tiny share of total, so end-to-end gain under 2 percent.
cheapest_test: On 3 toy curves over GF(2^n), n=19,23,29, build both bases at B=2^10, count decomposable S_3 pairs for 10^5 random targets each, matched seeds and interleaved, A/A arm, then count bit operations.
falsifier: Relation yield differs by more than 10 percent (structure hurts), or enumeration saving under 3x in measured cycles.
lean_sketch: Needs: FactorBase as Fin B -> G, a Monoid-like field spec with element t and hypothesis 'order of t = 2^n-1' (primitive). Provable: t^i = t^j -> i = j mod (2^n-1), so the map Fin B -> F is injective for B <= 2^n-1; hence FactorBase entries have distinct x. Cost.factorBase bounded by B*(1+hw f). No claim on relations. Injectivity is the only provable statement; yield is empirical.
novelty_note: Choosing a factor base for cheap enumeration is not the same as subspace or Frobenius-invariant bases; the effect on total cost is expected tiny (factor base phase is minor), so this is mostly a constant and a negative control for 'structured bases hurt yield'.

title: Characteristic-function factor base inside the prime-order subgroup (cofactor filter)
handbook_section: 10.1.4.3 Characteristic functions (with 10.1.3 DFT, 10.1.4.4 Gauss sums)
mechanism: For cofactor h, the image subgroup H = hE(F_q) has a character-sum indicator. Binary curve, cofactor 2: x is the x-coordinate of a point of 2E iff Tr(x) = Tr(a), which is an additive character of GF(2^n). Cofactor 4 adds one half-trace test. Draw the factor base only from x whose point lies in H, by rejection sampling at h tries per element. Then every sum of factor-base points lands in H, and so do the targets aG+bQ, since G and Q lie in the prime-order subgroup. Every candidate x3 = x(R - P1 - P2) is then an x-coordinate of a point of H. It lands in F with probability |F|/|H| instead of |F|/|E|. Relevant to ECC2K-130 (cofactor 4) and Curve25519-class curves (cofactor 8, though a mod-8 test needs higher residue symbols).
claim: At fixed |F| and fixed m=3 enumeration cost, the decomposition success per (x1,x2) tuple is h times higher for the H-filtered factor base than for an unfiltered one. Linear-algebra dimension is unchanged. The relation phase therefore drops by about h.
prediction: Relation yield ratio (filtered / unfiltered, equal |F|, equal tuples) is 2.0 +/- 0.15 for cofactor 2 (Koblitz a=1) and 4.0 +/- 0.4 for cofactor 4 (a=0), on GF(2^17..21) toys. Matched rho in H is cheaper by sqrt(h), so the net gap to rho closes by at most sqrt(h) (about 2 for h=4). Report both.
cheapest_test: GF(2^19), one a=0 and one a=1 Koblitz curve. Build F (|F|=2^6) filtered and unfiltered. Run exhaustive m=3 decomposition of 2000 random targets in H. Count relations per 10^6 tuples with a paired bootstrap, and check the halving criterion against brute-force 2E membership first.
falsifier: Yield ratio with 95% CI upper bound below 1.2 for h=4, or the halving test disagreeing with brute-force membership on more than 0 points.
lean_sketch: Definitions: DLPInstance over an additive group G with log : G -> Fin N bijective, a predicate H : G -> Prop closed under add, a FactorBase F : Fin B -> G, and h with card H = orbitRepresentatives N h = N/h. Hypotheses: (forall i, H (F i)) and H closed under add. Provable: every F i + F j is in H, so the pair-sum map Fin B x Fin B -> H has an average fibre of at least B^2/(N/h) = h B^2/N (pigeonhole). That is a rigorous statement that the representation count is h times the unfiltered average. smoothCount is then defined as the number of (i,j) with target - F i - F j in range F, and its sum over targets in H equals B^3 up to multiplicity. The probabilistic yield claim stays empirical.
novelty_note: Cofactor clearing is standard in rho and in DLP reductions. The new part is restricting the factor base itself to H by a character test, which raises per-tuple yield by h. It could be called relabelling if the atlas already runs IC in H. Check the atlas, and report the matched rho in H.
