title: Multiplier-closed factor base through commuting x-only maps (Dickson analogue)
handbook_section: 9.6.1 Basics and 9.6.2.2 The maps Phi_a, Psi_a (composition D_m o D_n = D_mn)
mechanism: Dickson polynomials commute, D_m(D_n(x)) = D_mn(x), because they are the x-only multiplication on the norm-1 torus. The Lattes maps R_k with x([k]P) = R_k(x(P)) commute the same way, so a table T = { x(k F_j) : k in K } for a smooth multiplier set K = {2^a 3^b <= K0} is built by composing the cheap maps R_2 and R_3, with Montgomery batch inversion. A lookup of x3 in T gives a relation with coefficient +/- k on F_j. The unknowns stay at B, while the hit probability per tuple rises by about |K| and the table costs |K| B. The relation phase becomes about N/K + K B tuples, against about N for K=1. The minimum is 2 sqrt(N B) at K = sqrt(N/B).
claim: A dependent multiplier table raises relations per tuple by a factor of about |K| without enlarging the matrix. Relation-phase cost follows K B + N/K up to the sqrt(NB) optimum, and the resulting matrix keeps full rank B - O(1).
prediction: On GF(2^20) with B=2^7 and |K|=16, relations per 10^6 tuples rise by 16 +/- 3 (negation-orbit halving is already counted). Matrix rank is at least B - 2. Total group-operation cost at the optimum K is about 2 sqrt(NB) = 2^14.5, against 2^20 for K=1. This still exceeds rho (2^10), so the gap narrows but does not close.
cheapest_test: Toy GF(2^20) binary curve with m=3, B=128. Run K = 1, 4, 16, 64. Record relations per tuple, table-build cost, and GF(2) / mod-ell rank of the relation matrix. Compare against a plain factor base of size K B with the same enumeration budget.
falsifier: Yield gain below |K|/2, or rank deficiency above 3 from multiplier-induced dependencies, or total cost at optimal K not below the K=1 cost by at least 4x.
lean_sketch: Definitions: Relation with Int coefficients over Fin B, FactorBase F : Fin B -> G, an extended table t : Fin B -> Fin K -> G with t j k = k . F j. Hypothesis: log is a homomorphism, log(k.g) = k*log g mod N. Provable: relation_scale, i.e. a relation among table entries with coefficients c_(j,k) yields a Relation over F with coefficients sum of k*c_(j,k), preserving the log identity. Provable: the Cost bound factorBase + relations >= 2 sqrt(N B) from (K B + N/K)^2 >= 4 N B in Nat. Not provable without a distribution model: the |K| yield gain. State it as a hypothesis about smoothCount.

title: Dembowski-Ostrom rank spectrum of the fixed-s S_3 system (MinRank structure)
handbook_section: 9.5.5 Planar DO polynomials, with 10.1.4.2 Nonlinearity
mechanism: Binary curve, m=3. Put x2 = x1 + s with s in V fixed. Then S_3 = x1^4 + (s^2 + x3) x1^2 + s x3 x1 + s^2 x3^2 + beta. This is a Dembowski-Ostrom type quadratic map over F_2 in the bits of (x1, x3) in V x V: bilinear terms plus Frobenius-linear terms. Each of the n component functions Tr(mu * Q_s) has a bilinear-form rank r(mu) on 2d bits, which is the nonlinearity / Walsh-spectrum view. Components with low r(mu) are MinRank / Kipnis-Shamir leverage that generic F4/XL on the system does not exploit. Fixing s costs 2^d guesses, and each remaining bilinear system is solved by a rank-aware elimination.
claim: For structured subspaces V (subfield-adjacent or Frobenius-stable), the minimum rank over mu of the component forms is at least 2 below the random-quadratic-map expectation. Such V give cheaper per-s solves than generic F4 hybrid.
prediction: n=21, d=7: for 200 random V, the min-rank distribution matches the random-map null (KS p>0.05). For structured V (containing a subfield or stable under x -> x^2 in a normal basis), min rank is lower by 2 or more in at least 30% of cases. If so, an elimination exploiting rank-r components reduces unknowns by about (2d - r) / 2 bits.
cheapest_test: For n=21 and d=7, enumerate all 2^21 values of mu. For each, build the 14x14 bilinear form matrix over F_2 and compute its rank by bit-parallel elimination. Compare the min-rank histogram for random V, structured V, and 200 random quadratic maps of the same shape.
falsifier: No V family differs from the random-map null in min rank at the 5% level, or rank deficiency exists but F4 degree of regularity is unchanged when the low-rank components are added.
lean_sketch: Definitions: a local GF2n type as a char-2 commutative ring class (no Mathlib), a Frobenius-linear map, a bilinear form as Fin d -> Fin d -> Bool, a rank function by explicit elimination. Provable: the expansion identity S3 x1 (x1+s) x3 = x1^4 + (s^2 + x3) x1^2 + s x3 x1 + s^2 x3^2 + beta, by calc from the char-2 axiom. Provable: rank <= 2d. Not provable: any claim about the rank distribution (empirical). The Cost record would charge phase descent 2^d * rankSolveCost, with rankSolveCost taken as a hypothesis from measurement.
novelty_note: F4/XL and symmetrisation are integrated, but explicit MinRank / component-rank screening of the Weil-restricted S_3 system by subspace is not on the integrated list. It may reproduce a Gröbner degree-of-regularity effect already folded into F4, hence the paired comparison with F4 degree.

title: Additive-energy audit of factor bases in log space
handbook_section: 10.1.4.5 Uncertainty principle (with 10.1.3 DFT)
mechanism: Over Z/ell the uncertainty principle (Donoho-Stark; Tao for prime ell: |supp f| + |supp f^| >= ell + 1) and Cauchy-Davenport force |F+F+F| >= min(ell, 3(B-1)+1), with Cauchy-Schwarz giving |2F| >= B^4 / E(F), where E is the additive energy. Relation yield is the covering rate of the m-fold sumset in log space, so factor-base construction rules (subspace, random, Frobenius-orbit-closed, x-sorted, multiplier-closed) at equal B differ in yield through E(F), which is computable on toys where logs are known. This turns 'which factor base is best' into a measurable one-number predictor.
claim: At equal |F|, the m=2 and m=3 distinct-sum coverage of different factor-base rules is predicted by additive energy of their logs to within 3%, and standard rules (subspace, Frobenius-orbit-closed, random) have energy within 5% of random. Only AP-like (multiplier-closed) bases deviate strongly.
prediction: Across at least 8 factor-base rules on 3 toy curves (n=15..19), the correlation between measured coverage and B^4/E(F) is at least 0.9. Subspace and orbit-closed bases show E/E_random in [0.95, 1.05]. Multiplier-closed bases show E/E_random above 3, with matching coverage loss in distinct sums, which quantifies the cost side of idea 2.
cheapest_test: Brute-force the group on n=17 (about 1.3e5 points), computing all logs. For each rule, build F, compute r(s) = #{(i,j): log F_i + log F_j = s} and E = sum r^2. Measure the fraction of group elements covered by F+F. Regress coverage on B^4/E.
falsifier: Correlation below 0.5, or any standard rule with E/E_random outside [0.8, 1.25], which would then imply a hidden bias worth exploiting.
lean_sketch: Definitions: Fin N as Z/N, FactorBase F : Fin B -> Fin N via log, repr r s = card {(i,j) | F i + F j = s}, energy = sum r^2, support size. Provable without Mathlib by a Finset/list sum argument: (sum r)^2 <= card(support) * sum r^2 (Cauchy-Schwarz), and sum r = B^2, hence B^4 <= card(2F) * energy. That bounds smoothCount from below by B^4 / energy. Cauchy-Davenport for prime N is provable but longer (induction on Davenport transform). Distribution claims are empirical.
novelty_note: Diagnostic and selection tool, not a new attack. It is useful because it prices the multiplier-closed structure in idea 2 and could reject factor bases silently losing yield. No integrated technique uses energy as a selector.

title: Exact Gauss/Kloosterman-sum descent yield for codimension-c targets
handbook_section: 10.1.4.4 Gauss sums (with 10.1.3 DFT)
mechanism: In descent from a large subspace V1 to a smaller V', the target condition x3 in V' (codimension c) is an average of 2^c additive characters (-1)^{Tr(c' x3)} over the annihilator. For binary S_3, x3 is the Artin-Schreier root of s^2 x3^2 + p x3 + p^2 + beta, so sum over (x1,x2) of psi(x3) is a Kloosterman-type exponential sum. The Weil bound gives yield = |V1|^2 2^{-c} (1 + eps) with |eps| <= C 2^c sqrt(q) / |V1|^2. It supplies exact yield and the sign of the deviation per (V1, V', beta), replacing the heuristic cost model's constant 1.
claim: The deviation of descent decomposition counts from the 2^{-c}|V1|^2 heuristic obeys the Weil-type bound with C <= 4. At |V1| = q^{1/3} it decays like q^{-1/6}, so any exploitable bias exists only at toy and moderate sizes.
prediction: For n=19..23, d=6..8, c=1..3, random V1 and V', relative deviation |eps| stays below 4 * 2^c * 2^{n/2} / 2^{2d}, and it exceeds 10% only when that bound exceeds 10%. At d >= n/3 the median |eps| is below 3%. Net prediction: no exploitable bias at cryptographic sizes (a null).
cheapest_test: Exhaustively count solutions (x1,x2) in V1^2 with x3 in V' for 300 random (V1, V', beta) triples at n=19..23 in C; compare with the character-sum bound. About 2^16 pairs per triple.
falsifier: Any observed |eps| above the bound with C=4, or a persistent positive bias above 10% at d >= n/3 across structured V1 families, which would be exploitable.
lean_sketch: Definitions: BitVec-style vectors Fin n -> Bool, Subspace as an annihilator list of masks, dot-product character chi c x = (-1)^(c . x), Relation count N = number of pairs with root in V'. Provable: orthogonality, indicator (x in V') = 2^-c * sum_{c' in annihilator} chi c' x, hence the count identity N = 2^-c * sum over characters of the pair sums. title: Lattice of Frobenius-invariant subspaces from the factorization of X^n - 1 over F_2
handbook_section: 10.2.1 General properties of LFSR sequences and 10.2.3 Maximal period sequences
mechanism: In a normal basis, GF(2^n) is isomorphic to F_2[X]/(X^n - 1) with Frobenius acting as multiplication by X. Its F_2[Frobenius]-submodules (Frobenius-stable subspaces) correspond to divisors g of X^n - 1, with dimension deg g. These are the LFSR sequences of period dividing n, and a primitive (maximal-period) characteristic polynomial means no proper invariant subspace. A factor base that is both subspace-structured and Frobenius-closed exists only if X^n - 1 has a divisor of degree d near n/3 (m=3) or n/2. For n with ord_n(2) small there are many such divisors. For n where 2 is a primitive root mod n and X^n - 1 = (X - 1) * (irreducible of degree n - 1), none exist. That would make the combined subspace-and-orbit factor base impossible for that field degree.
claim: For prime n in 53..131 the existence of a Frobenius-stable subspace of dimension d in [n/3 - 2, n/3 + 1] is decided by ord_n(2) and the divisor degrees of X^n - 1. Primes with 2 primitive modulo n have none, so combined subspace-and-orbit IC is blocked there. Primes with small order (73, 89, 127, ...) have several.
prediction: Among prime n in 53..131, at most 25% admit an invariant subspace of dimension within 1 of n/3. For n=131 (ECC2K-130) the answer depends on ord_131(2), a computation I did not run here. If it is 130 or 65, the combined structure does not exist for n=131. Where it exists, the yield gain over subspace-only is predicted to be about n (orbit size) with the same factor-base size.
cheapest_test: Factor X^n - 1 over F_2 for n = 53..131 with a CAS or a short Cantor-Zassenhaus script. Tabulate subset-sum-achievable divisor degrees near n/3 and n/2. Then, for one n with a hit (for example n=73, d=24 or 25), compare measured relation yield of the invariant subspace factor base against a generic subspace of the same dimension on a toy curve.
falsifier: A prime n with 2 primitive modulo n that nonetheless admits a Frobenius-stable subspace of dimension near n/3, which would mean the theory is misapplied. Or, where a stable subspace exists, no yield gain over a generic subspace of equal dimension.
lean_sketch: Definitions: Frob as a cyclic shift on Fin n -> Bool, an invariant FactorBase F : Fin B -> (Fin n -> Bool) with F closed under Frob. orbitRepresentatives N k = N/k used for the orbit count. Provable: if Frob has no fixed point on the set and order exactly n, then n divides the cardinality, so representatives = B/n. Provable: submodule dimensions are the degrees of divisors of X^n - 1, if polynomials over Bool are defined by hand with a divisibility predicate, and a decision procedure for a specific small n by `decide`. The factorization of a specific n=73 or 131 polynomial can be checked by `native_decide` or a certificate. Yield gain is empirical.
novelty_note: Frobenius-invariant subspace factor bases are integrated as a technique. The new content is the number-theoretic existence condition (divisor lattice of X^n - 1) and using it to rank field degrees n. It may already be implicit in the n selection for ECC2K.

title: Run-structure canonicalization of normal-basis orbit representatives
handbook_section: 10.2.4 Distribution properties of LFSR sequences (run property) and 10.3.2 Autocorrelation of sequences
mechanism: Orbit quotienting by Frobenius requires a canonical representative of each necklace (cyclic rotation class) of the n-bit normal-basis vector. The naive route tries n rotations or runs Booth/Duval in O(n) bit steps. For random bit strings the longest run of equal bits has length about log2 n with a geometric (2^-k) tail, the run property, so only the rotations starting at a maximal run can be minimal. Expected candidates are 1 to 2. Canonicalizing means locating maximal runs with a few word-level clz/ctz operations, then comparing 1 to 2 rotations by word ops. For n=131 this replaces about 131 rotate-compare steps with about 10 word ops per canonicalization. It matters in relation filtering, where every x_i of every relation is canonicalized, and in factor-base lookup.
claim: Maximal-run canonicalization of 131-bit necklaces is at least 10x faster than naive minimum-rotation and 3x faster than Booth in cycles per canonicalization, with identical outputs. Expected candidate rotations are below 2.5 for random vectors.
prediction: Measured on random 131-bit inputs: mean candidate rotations 1.6 +/- 0.4; speedup over naive 15-40x and over Booth 3-8x on x86-64. Inputs from real relations are indistinguishable from random (checked by the same run-length histogram).
cheapest_test: C microbenchmark with 10^7 random 131-bit vectors, three implementations (naive, Booth, run-based), assert identical outputs, report cycles per call and the histogram of candidate counts. Repeat on x-coordinates of toy-curve relations at n=131 field arithmetic.
falsifier: Outputs differ from naive on any input, mean candidates above 4, or speedup over Booth below 1.5x.
lean_sketch: Definitions: necklace as Fin n -> Bool with rotate, canonical v = lexicographic minimum over rotations. Provable (structural, no probabilities): canonical v is among the rotations that begin at the start of a maximal run (a lemma about lexicographic minima: the minimum rotation starts at a maximal run of the minimal symbol, 0). So the run-based algorithm returns canonical v. Cost: per-call op count is at most (number of runs of maximal length) * n/64. Not provable without a distribution model: the expectation of 1.6. Link to the Cost record: relations phase is multiplied by per-relation canonicalization cost, an input to orbitRepresentatives.
novelty_note: The minimum-rotation-by-longest-run trick is classical string-algorithm folklore. Applied to Frobenius orbit canonicalization in the IC filtering step it is an implementation speedup (measured wall-clock only, not counted group ops), not a change in operation counts. Counts as an improvement only if reported as measured phase time.

title: Berlekamp-Massey linear-complexity screen of the trace-bit sequence of x(kG)
handbook_section: 10.4.2 Analysis of the linear complexity and 10.4.4.1 Explicit sequences
mechanism: For a smooth ordinary curve of large prime order the bit sequence s_k = Tr(x(kG)) (k = 1..N) is expected to have the linear complexity profile of a random sequence, L_N = N/2 + O(1) with deviation d having probability about 2^(-2|d|). Results of Hess-Shparlinski type give large linear complexity for elliptic-curve generator sequences. A sequence with abnormally low linear complexity signals algebraic structure: a singular (nodal) fibre, where x(kG) is a rational function of g^k and so s_k obeys a linear recurrence of order at most 3n, or hidden torus/subfield structure. Cost: N point additions plus O(N^2) BM, for N=2048 negligible.
claim: Across all curves in the ecdb with GF(2^n) base field (n <= 40 for exact addition) the BM linear complexity of N=2048 terms lies within N/2 +/- 8. The screen has a positive control: a nodal cubic gives linear complexity at most 3n.
prediction: All smooth curves tested (at least 1000) fall in [1016, 1032] (false-alarm probability about 2^-16 each). Positive control (nodal b=0 cubic over GF(2^21)) gives L at most 63. Negative expected result: no weak-curve detection. Value is a validated, almost free screen, and a surprise in the ecdb would be a lead.
cheapest_test: Python or C: for each curve and each of 5 random generators, compute 2048 consecutive multiples, take the trace bit of x, run BM over GF(2), record L. Include the nodal and one supersingular curve as controls, and shuffle the sequence order as the negative-control null for the LC profile.
falsifier: Positive control not detected (L above 3n), or smooth ecdb curves outside the band at a rate above the 2^-16 prediction, which would cause a revisit of the null, or any deviation reproducible across generators.
lean_sketch: Definitions: DLPInstance with generator and sequence s : Nat -> Bool, linear complexity by an explicit BM function returning L over Bool lists. Provable: for a sequence defined by a recurrence of order r, BM returns L <= r (soundness of the recurrence implies LC upper bound, by induction); the nodal-curve case is provable as: if x(kG) = rational function of g^k then s_k satisfies an order <= 3n linear recurrence over F_2 (needs a trace-linearity lemma). The null claim (L = N/2 + O(1)) is a probabilistic statement and stays empirical.
novelty_note: BM tests of EC generator sequences are known as pseudorandomness checks. Using them as a cheap curve-selection screen with positive and negative controls inside the IC lab is the new angle. Expected outcome is a null, which still has value as a documented screen.

title: Point-halving parity: an implied F2-linear trace equation for every binary-curve relation
handbook_section: 9.1.1.2 Trace representation (with 9.1.2 Walsh transform)
mechanism: On y^2+xy=x^3+a x^2+b over GF(2^n), chi(P)=Tr(x(P))+Tr(a) is the point-halving homomorphism E(F_q)->E/2E=Z/2 (the 2-part of E[2] is cyclic for ordinary curves), and chi(-P)=chi(P). Every relation sum eps_i P_i = R therefore obeys sum_i (Tr(x_i)+Tr a) = Tr(x_R)+Tr a, which is linear over F2 in the bits of the x_i. Choose the factor-base subspace V inside ker Tr. Then the left side is the constant m*Tr(a), so Tr(x_R) = (m-1)Tr(a) is necessary for R to decompose. Half of all random targets are certainly undecomposable, and Gröbner/hybrid solvers currently spend a full solve proving that. The same equation can also be appended to the Weil-restricted Semaev system when V is not inside ker Tr, which removes one unknown bit and spurious twist-type solutions.
claim: With V contained in ker Tr, no target R with Tr(x_R) != (m-1)Tr(a) has any decomposition over V. Targets in the allowed class decompose at exactly twice the unconditioned rate. Skipping the forbidden class (one trace evaluation per target) halves solves per relation.
prediction: Toy Koblitz a=1 or a=0 curves with n in {23,29,31}, m=3, dim V about n/3+2: 0 decompositions in the forbidden class over >=10^4 targets. Allowed-class rate is 2.0x the pooled rate (95% CI containing 2). Wall time per relation drops 1.7-2.0x when the solver's time on infeasible instances is at least 80% of its time on feasible ones. If V is not in ker Tr and the linear equation is appended, F4 degree of regularity is unchanged or 1 lower and time falls 1.2-2x.
cheapest_test: n=23 Koblitz curve (cofactor 2 or 4), brute-force all (x1,x2,x3) in V^3 against 5000 random targets R=aG+bQ with V in ker Tr and V a generic subspace. Tabulate decomposition counts by class Tr(x_R). Then time Sage/msolve on 200 feasible and 200 infeasible instances with and without the appended linear equation.
falsifier: Any decomposition found in the forbidden class (the homomorphism claim or the code is wrong). Or solver time on infeasible instances is under 20% of feasible time (nothing to save). Or the allowed-class rate is below 1.5x the pooled rate.
lean_sketch: Definitions: a group G with an additive Z/2 target (chi : G -> Fin 2) and hChi : forall g h, chi (g*h) = chi g + chi h; chi (g^-1) = chi g; Relation as a List (Int x Fin B); DLPInstance with a log bijection onto Fin n. Provable without Mathlib: if sum c_i . FB i = target then sum (c_i mod 2)*chi(FB i) = chi target in Fin 2 (induction on the list; sign invariance from chi inverse). Corollary on counts: if V has chi=0 on all FB entries, smoothCount over the N/2 wrong-class targets is 0 and the right-class density is exactly 2x the pooled density (Nat arithmetic with N/2). Cost lemma: relations-cost with the filter <= relations-cost without. Not provable in Lean: that chi(P)=Tr(x)+Tr(a) on curves (stays an hypothesis field of the curve structure).
novelty_note: Point halving is known for scalar multiplication. It is not in the listed integrated techniques, and I know of no use of chi as a necessary parity condition or target filter in Semaev/Weil-restriction relation search. Check the lead atlas for cofactor-class filtering before claiming. Not a relabelling: it removes real solver calls. For cofactor-4 curves the 4-torsion homomorphism is nonlinear and is not covered.

title: Kloosterman-Walsh selection of Frobenius-invariant factor-base subspaces by point-existence density
handbook_section: 9.1.2 The Walsh transform; 9.1.1.2 Trace representation
mechanism: An abscissa x is a point iff f(x)=Tr(x)+Tr(a)+Tr(b/x^2)=0, so only a fraction ~1/2 of x in a subspace V are factor-base points, and a relation needs all m abscissae valid. The valid count in V is (|V|+S(V))/2 with S(V)=sum over V of (-1)^f. Expanded over V-perp it is a sum of Kloosterman sums over a coset (Walsh transform of x -> (-1)^{Tr(b/x)}). For Frobenius-invariant V, f is constant on orbits, so the coins are orbit-level: about |V|/n of them, and the spread of the valid fraction is about 0.5*sqrt(n/|V|), far wider than for generic subspaces. Selecting V with valid fraction 0.5+eps multiplies relation yield by (1+2 eps)^m at no per-relation cost.
claim: Among Frobenius-invariant subspaces of fixed dimension d, valid-point fraction varies with orbit-level binomial spread. The best of K candidates exceeds 0.5 by about sqrt(2 ln K)*0.5*sqrt(n/2^d), and the relation yield ratio best/median is about (1+2 eps)^m, measurable at toy scale.
prediction: n=23, d=8..9, m=3: orbit-level spread of the fraction is 0.12-0.16. Best of 2000 invariant subspaces has fraction >=0.75. Relation yield per target is >=2.5x the median subspace, and the effect persists on fresh targets. For generic (non-invariant) subspaces the best/median ratio is <=1.5x.
cheapest_test: Enumerate 2000 random Frobenius-invariant subspaces (sums of random orbits) of n=23, d~8. Compute the valid fraction by direct evaluation of f, and the relation count by brute force on 500 fixed targets. Regress yield on (fraction)^3.
falsifier: Fraction spread over invariant subspaces equals the iid-coin spread 0.5/sqrt(|V|) (orbit-level correlation absent), or yield ratio best/median <1.3x, or the yield does not track fraction^m (R^2<0.5).
lean_sketch: Definitions: isPoint : Fin N -> Bool (the Boolean function f), V : Finset or Fin B -> Fin N, validCount V = card of the filter, orbitRepresentatives N k = N/k for columns. Hypotheses: isPoint constant on k-orbits and V orbit-closed. Provable: validCount = sum over orbit reps of orbit size * indicator (a counting identity), and the yield bound relations <= validCount^m. Cost record: factorBase phase unchanged; relations phase scaled by (valid/|V|)^-m. The Weil/Kloosterman bound itself is not provable here and is stated as a hypothesis |S(V)| <= C.

title: Exact-count hill-climbing over subspaces using the F2-trilinear form of S_3
handbook_section: 9.1.3 Parameters of Boolean functions; 9.1.1.1 Algebraic normal form
mechanism: In char 2, x -> x^2 is F2-linear, so S_3(x1,x2,x3)=x1^2x2^2+x1^2x3^2+x2^2x3^2+x1x2x3+const is bilinear plus one trilinear term in the bits and is F2-affine in each variable separately (cubic over F2 in 3d bits). Each Walsh component Tr(u S_3) is thus linear in x3 once x1,x2 are fixed. The yield N(V)=|{(x1,x2,x3) in V^3: S_3=0, all valid}| equals (|V|/2^n) times a sum over u of partial sums with linear-form constraints, so a single swap of one basis vector changes N(V) through cheap rank-one updates. Local search on V maximizes N(V), which is a property of (curve, V), not of the target.

title: Heavy Walsh coefficient of the decomposability indicator as a free target prefilter
handbook_section: 9.1.2 The Walsh transform; 9.3.2 Basic properties of bent functions
mechanism: Let D(r)=1 iff x=r decomposes over V into m factor-base abscissae. Bent functions are exactly those with a flat Walsh spectrum, so max|D^(u)|/2^n measures distance from the bent (unbiased) regime. If D has a heavy coefficient at some u, the parity Tr(u r) predicts decomposability and selecting targets by that bit raises the success rate by about 1+|D^(u)|/(rate*2^n). Heavy coefficients can be found by Goldreich-Levin/Kushilevitz-Mansour with oracle access, without the full 2^n transform. For subspace V, u in V-perp makes Tr(u x_i) constant on the factor-base side, which is the natural place a bias would sit.

Provable: Parseval-type identity sum_u (walsh D u)^2 = N * sum D (needs orthogonality hypothesis, then Nat/Int algebra), hence max|walsh|^2 >= N*smoothCount/N... precisely a lower bound max|walsh| >= sqrt(sum D)/... using pigeonhole over u. Cost lemma: a prefilter with success gain g reduces relations cost by factor g (needs a proportional-cost hypothesis). The bias existence is empirical.

title: Low-degree annihilators (algebraic immunity) of the decomposability indicator
handbook_section: 9.1.6.3 Highly nonlinear functions with optimal algebraic immunity
mechanism: Algebraic immunity AI(D)=min degree of a nonzero g with g*D=0 or g*(D+1)=0. A random Boolean function on n bits has AI near ceil(n/2). If D (the decomposable-target set for a structured V) has an annihilator g of degree e << n/2 in the bits of x_R, then g(x_R)!=0 certifies undecomposable at cost C(n,e) bit-ops, much less than a Gröbner solve. The same degree e plausibly tracks the F4 degree of regularity on the Weil-restricted system, since both measure the lowest degree at which a polynomial identity separates the instances.

prediction: n=14..18, m=3, d=n/3+1: AI(D) <= ceil(n/2)-2 for >=80% of (curve,V); annihilator rejects >=20% of undecomposable targets. Random sets of equal density have AI = ceil(n/2) or ceil(n/2)-1.

title: Bilinear structure of the 2-point descent system: exploit multi-affine form in F2 bits
handbook_section: 9.1.1.1 Algebraic normal form; 9.2.7 Quadratic APN functions
mechanism: With the target abscissa r fixed, S_3(x1,x2,r) is, in the F2 bits of x1 and x2, bilinear plus linear plus constant: x1^2x2^2+r x1x2 is a bilinear map and r^2(x1^2+x2^2) is linear. A 2-descent step (R = P1 +/- P2, x_i in V, dim V = d>=n/2) is a system of n bilinear equations in two blocks of d unknowns. Bilinear Gröbner theory gives degree of regularity at most min(n_x,n_y)+1 and a Kipnis-Shamir style kernel-vector form (M(x2) (x1,1)^T=0 with M affine in x2, n x (d+1)). Generic quadratic F4 bounds for the same shape are weaker. Specializing 2delta+1 bits (delta=d-n/2) leaves a zero-dimensional bilinear system.
claim: F4 on the descent system has degree of regularity <= d+1, strictly below the generic-quadratic prediction for the same (n,2d). Wall time to the first decomposition scales with a base smaller than the 2^d per-x1 linear-algebra enumeration.
prediction: n=17..29, d=ceil(n/2)+2: observed dreg <= d+1 and at least 1 below the Fröberg/semi-regular quadratic prediction at n>=21. Log2 of time per decomposition grows with slope about 0.35n versus about 0.5n for enumerate-over-x1. Low confidence on the slope: bilinear Macaulay matrices have size about C(d+D,D)^2.
cheapest_test: msolve/F4 on Weil-restricted descent systems for n=17..27 (50 random targets each), recording dreg and time. Compare with (a) random bilinear systems of the same shape and (b) generic random quadratic systems, and with enumerate-over-x1 plus F2 linear algebra.
falsifier: dreg matches the generic quadratic/semi-regular prediction (bilinear structure unused), or time slope per bit >= enumeration slope at n>=25.
lean_sketch: Definitions: bits as Fin d -> Fin 2, BilinearSystem with coefficient array A : Fin n -> Fin d -> Fin d -> Fin 2 plus linear and constant parts; hypothesis that S3 restricted to V^2 equals such a system (stated as hypothesis hBil, derived from x -> x^2 additive). Provable without Mathlib: fixing x1 gives an affine system in x2 (linear algebra over Fin 2), so decomposition per x1 costs O(n d^2) bit-ops and the descent cost record descent <= 2^d * n*d^2 + ... is an arithmetic bound. title: Descent chain designed by Kloosterman point-existence at each level
handbook_section: 9.1.2 The Walsh transform; 9.1.3 Parameters of Boolean functions
mechanism: A descent from a large subspace V_k down to V_0 decomposes each current point into two or three points of the next, smaller subspace. Success probability at each level carries the same (valid fraction)^m factor as the factor-base idea, now for the intermediate subspaces. Choose the nested chain V_0 < V_1 < ... < V_k of Frobenius-invariant subspaces so that each level's Walsh-expanded valid fraction is high, not the chain by dimension alone. The total descent cost is a product of per-level expected trials, so even modest per-level gains of 1.3-1.5x compound over k=4..6 levels.

cheapest_test: Enumerate 500 random nested invariant chains at n=23. Measure per-level success on 2000 random points via exhaustive 2-decomposition, with the full-descent count as the endpoint. Compare with the product of valid fractions as predictor.
falsifier: Spread of per-level success across chains within binomial noise, or best/median expected-trials ratio >0.8.

title: Kloosterman-character-sum cost model replacing the uniform 1/2^m validity heuristic

mechanism: Relation-yield predictions normally use |V|^m/(m! 2^n) with an extra 2^-m validity factor, treating validity as independent fair coins. The exact validity count in V is (|V|+S(V))/2 and S(V) is a coset sum of Kloosterman sums over V-perp. A model using S(V), computed in 2^d operations by FWHT on V, should predict measured per-subspace yields far better than the uniform heuristic. The residual of the heuristic is itself a diagnostic: it quantifies how much of the observed yield variance is a free selection resource (feeds the two selection ideas) and how much is noise.
claim: Across (curve, invariant V) pairs at toy scale, a cost model using the computed valid fraction explains most of the log-yield variance, while the uniform heuristic explains almost none.
prediction: 200 (curve,V) pairs, n=21..25: R^2 of log yield on m*log(valid fraction) >=0.8 (slope 1+-0.15). R^2 of the uniform heuristic is <0.1 because it is constant for fixed d. Predicted-vs-measured relation count within 25% on 80% of pairs versus within 25% on <30% for the uniform model.

falsifier: R^2 <0.5, or slope outside 1+-0.4 (validity does not act multiplicatively as modelled), in which case the selection ideas lose their mechanism.

title: Kloosterman-biased subspace translate/scale for the binary factor base
handbook_section: 7.1.4 Artin-Schreier hypersurfaces; 6.3.4.3 Nonlinearity of Boolean functions; 6.3.5 Incomplete character sums
mechanism: On y^2+xy=x^3+ax^2+b, x lifts iff h(x)=Tr(x)+Tr(a)+Tr(sqrt(b)/x)=0 (Artin-Schreier). Any S3 solution over F_q with x_R liftable has every x_i liftable (pi acts as eps_i on P_i; sum constraint forces all eps equal except 2-torsion degeneracies), so relation yield from V^m scales as (2*liftFrac(V))^m, not as |V|^m/q average. liftFrac(V)-1/2 = (1/2|V|) sum_{v in V} (-1)^{h(v)} is an incomplete Kloosterman-type sum over a subspace. Parseval for the Walsh transform of the inversion indicator gives mean-square bias 1/|V|, so best of T random scalings/translates lambda*V+c has bias about sqrt(2 ln T/|V|)/2. Choose the best V instead of a random one. Cost T*|V| inversions, once.

title: Affine-hull dimension of S3(V^3) as a factor-base selection criterion (sum-product extremal subspaces)
handbook_section: 6.4.2 The sum-product estimate and its variants
mechanism: In char 2, with x3=x_R fixed, S3 = Phi(s*t) + x_R^2 (s+t) + c0 with s=x1+x_R, t=x2+x_R and Phi(z)=z^2+x_R z F2-linear. So the n coordinates of S3 over V1 x V2 are bilinear forms in the unknown bits through the product set V1*V2. Let w = dim of the affine hull of S3(V1 x V2 x {x_R}). Then Pr[S3=0] is 2^{-w} (when c0 lies in the hull) rather than 2^{-n}, and the n-w annihilating trace coordinates become purely linear equations in (s,t) that remove unknowns. Sum-product says V+V small forces V*V large; w measures the opposite regime: K-subspaces (K=GF(2^k), k|n, V=K+K*theta) have small products so w<n.
claim: For subspaces V of equal F2-dimension d, S3-solution count over V^2 (x_R fixed) is approximately |V|^2 * 2^{-w(V)} * [c0 in hull], with w = dim span(V*V) roughly. K-structured V reaches w well below n, giving yield above the generic |V|^2/q by a factor 2^{n-w}, but the linear-algebra rank may collapse: all factor-base logs can lie in E(K).
prediction: n=24, k=8, V=K+K*theta (d=16): w about 3k=24? Use k=6: V=K+K*theta, w <= 3k=18 vs n=24, so yield about 2^{6}=64x generic when c0 is in hull and 0 otherwise. Fraction of x_R with c0 in hull about 2^{w-n}=1/64, so average yield unchanged unless x_R is chosen (via a,b scalar choice). Net: success per candidate varies, so the gain appears only if hull-membership is cheap to test (a linear test) and the sampler can steer x_R into the hull.
cheapest_test: n=24, k=6. Enumerate V random vs K-structured, same d. Compute w by Gaussian elimination on S3 values over all (x1,x2) pairs for random x_R. Count solutions by brute force. Correlate log2(count) with n-w over 200 (V, x_R) draws.
falsifier: Corr(log2 count, n-w) below 0.8, or the average yield over x_R for K-structured V equals the generic value within 5 percent while hull-membership is not steerable (then no gain). Also falsified if rank of the resulting relation matrix (mod ell) of K-structured V is below 90 percent of columns.

Needs as hypothesis: the equidistribution of S3 over its affine hull. Not provable core-only: the hull computation itself.

title: Trace-form isotropic block pairs: free linear equations from V1 subset (mu V2)^perp

mechanism: Using the same identity S3 = Phi(s t)+x_R^2(s+t)+c0, coordinate Tr(lambda*S3) = Tr(mu(lambda) s t) + Tr(lambda x_R^2 (s+t)) + const with mu = sqrt(lambda)+x_R*lambda, i.e. trace bilinear forms B_mu(s,t)=Tr(mu s t) on V1 x V2. If V1 lies in (mu V2)^perp for a subspace M of mu values, the bilinear part vanishes identically on those coordinates, leaving dim M affine-linear equations in the bits of (s,t). Choose asymmetric blocks (V1,V2), e.g. V2 K-stable and V1 inside V2^perp with respect to the trace form, to maximize dim M. The pencil rank profile (min rank over mu) also sets the cost of a MinRank/bilinear Groebner solve.

title: Short-interval scalar sampling with incomplete character sums and correlation measures
handbook_section: 6.3.5.2 Measures of pseudorandomness; 6.3.5 Incomplete character sums
mechanism: Relation candidates are R_k = k*P (plus b*Q) for random k, each costing a scalar multiplication. If k runs over an interval [k0,k0+L), R_{k+1}=R_k+P costs one point addition (with Montgomery batch inversion, about 3-4 field mults). Validity needs the sequence s_k = [x(kP) in V] to behave as Bernoulli(|V|/q) with correlation measure C_2 small. Incomplete character sums bound the discrepancy of {x(kP)} over intervals of length L by roughly sqrt(q)*log q (Hasse-type) for the group Z/ell, so L above about sqrt(q)*log(q)/|V| intervals suffice for the frequency to be right, and the Mauduit-Sarkozy correlation measure of the 0/1 sequence controls pairs. Within a subspace V the sequence is linear-structured, but x(kP) is not.
claim: Scanning consecutive scalars from random starting offsets gives the same hit rate [x(kP) in V] as independent random scalars (hit-rate ratio within 1+-3 percent) and no excess correlation between hits at distance 1, 2, ..., 8, while costing about 1 addition per candidate instead of about 1.5 log2(ell) field-mult-equivalents.
prediction: Toy n=30 Koblitz-like, |V|=2^12: hit-rate ratio interval vs random = 1.00+-0.03; lag-1 correlation of hits |C| < 4/sqrt(number of hits). Candidate-generation cost drop about 20x (n=30 ladder with tau-NAF about 8 additions vs 1), end-to-end collection speedup about 5x to 10x since the S3 solve dominates only when |V| is small.
cheapest_test: Compute 2^24 consecutive points kP, count hits in V, compare with 2^24 independent random kP; compute autocorrelation up to lag 16 and the Mauduit-Sarkozy C_2 statistic for window lengths 2^6..2^12. Exact, one core.
falsifier: Hit-rate ratio outside 0.95 to 1.05, or lag-j correlation |z-score| above 4 at any lag below 16, or pair-collision rate of x-values within an interval differs from random by more than 5 percent.

title: Legendre-biased coset selection for prime-field factor bases (small-FB regime)
handbook_section: 7.1.5 Kummer hypersurfaces; 6.3.6.4 Character sums over arbitrary sets; 7.3.2 Solutions of diagonal equations (Jacobi sums)
mechanism: For y^2=x^3+ax+b mod p, S3 as a quadratic in x3 has discriminant 16 f(x1) f(x2), so x3 in F_p iff chi(f(x1))=chi(f(x2)); a solution with x_R liftable has all x_i liftable. Hence yield from x in a multiplicative coset g*H (index d, |H|=B) scales as (2*liftFrac)^m, liftFrac=(1/2)(1+(1/B) sum_{h in H} chi(f(gh))). This is a Kummer/mixed character sum over a coset. Scanning d_scan cosets g gives best-of-T bias about sqrt(2 ln T/B)/2 (Weil/Jacobi bounds control the worst case).

title: Multi-homogeneous Bezout / toric mixed volume as the F4 cost predictor for split Weil-restricted systems
handbook_section: 7.1.3 Toric hypersurfaces
mechanism: The restricted S3 system has block structure: bits of x1, x2, x3 and an intermediate point z, with the equation S3(x1,x2,z), S3(z,x3,x_R) bilinear in block pairs. The count of solutions and the Groebner complexity in toric settings is governed by the Newton polytope (Adolphson-Sperber, Bernstein-Kushnirenko), i.e. by multihomogeneous Bezout number B_mh = coefficient extraction in prod (sum ...) rather than the total-degree Bezout bound that cost models use. Use B_mh (or the mixed volume with field equations) as the predictor of F4 matrix size and time.
claim: log(F4 time) over random splitting systems correlates with log(B_mh) at Spearman at least 0.9, versus at most 0.6 for the total-degree Bezout bound; thus a cost model driven by B_mh predicts which (d,m,split) minimizes decomposition cost better than the current one.
prediction: n in 18..26, d in n/3..n/2, m in {2,3}: Spearman(B_mh, time)=0.9+-0.05; Spearman(Bezout, time)=0.55+-0.15; the argmin of predicted cost by B_mh matches the measured argmin in at least 70 percent of 20 n values while Bezout matches in 40 percent or fewer.
cheapest_test: Generate 200 systems, run msolve/F4 with timeouts, record max degree and time; compute the two predictors by symbolic extraction. Report Spearman with bootstrap CI.
falsifier: Spearman(B_mh) minus Spearman(Bezout) below 0.1 or CI overlapping zero difference; or argmin agreement not better than Bezout's.
lean_sketch: Cost record with phases factorBase/relations/linearAlgebra/descent; define costModel : (Fin k -> Nat) -> Nat (monomial counts per block) giving relations phase. Statement: costModel is monotone in each block-degree (provable by Nat.mul_le_mul induction). The correlation claim is empirical and cannot be a theorem; Lean checks only that the model's prediction is a well-defined monotone cost and that Cost.total = sum of fields.
novelty_note: Groebner solving is integrated, but selecting splitting and d by a toric/multihomogeneous predictor instead of Bezout or first-fall estimates is not listed. It is a cost-model improvement, not a speedup claim; accounting changes alone do not count as improvements under the owner rule, so a win requires that the chosen parameters measurably reduce time.

title: Fourier spectrum of the factor base in the log domain as a pseudorandomness audit of the yield and rank models

Structured factor bases (subspaces, Frobenius-closed sets) may have a spectral peak from additive structure of logs. The test is exact on toy curves where all logs are known.

If instead a peak exists the m-fold coverage and relation yield deviate from Poisson; the deviation is measurable as excess variance of the number of decompositions per target.

lean_sketch: DLPInstance with logBij onto Fin n; FactorBase B := Fin B -> G; define logs : Fin B -> Fin n via logBij; define coverage m := number of Fin n elements expressible as sums of m logs (finite, decidable). Provable: coverage monotone in m and bounded by n; counting identity decomposeCount summed over targets = B^m (Finset-free via Nat induction on m). Spectrum bounds need complex exponentials and cannot be stated in core Lean; state only the combinatorial coverage claim with a hypothesis on pair counts.

title: Descent-level Kloosterman bias: choose each descent level's smoothness set by liftable fraction

The inversive map x -> sqrt(b)/x (translation by the 2-torsion point) is the only nonlinearity in h, and the distribution results for inversive congruential sequences give the discrepancy of {1/x : x in V}. Per-level scaling/translate selection by best-of-T bias reduces expected attempts per node. Descent total cost is sum over nodes of attempts times solve cost.

title: Frobenius-invariant subspace census from x^n-1 over F_2 as a curve-size selector
handbook_section: 5.4.3 Cyclotomic modules and complete generators (with 5.2.1 Basics on normal bases)
mechanism: In a normal basis F_{2^n} is the cyclic module F_2[x]/(x^n-1) under Frobenius. Frobenius-invariant F_2-subspaces correspond one-to-one to monic divisors g of x^n-1 (cyclic codes of length n), and the dimension is n - deg g. For n prime, x^n-1=(x-1)Phi_n and Phi_n splits into (n-1)/ord_n(2) irreducible factors of degree ord_n(2). So the number and dimensions of invariant factor-base subspaces are fixed by ord_n(2). If 2 is a primitive root mod n, the only invariant subspaces are 0, F_2, a hyperplane and everything.
claim: Among primes n in [53,131], those with 2 a primitive root mod n (predicted: 53, 59, 61, 67, 83, 101, 107, 131) have no Frobenius-invariant subspace of dimension in [n/4, 3n/4]. This includes ECC2K-130 (n=131, ord=130). Primes with ord_n(2) <= n/4 (e.g. 73, 89, 113, 127) have dozens to thousands of such subspaces.
prediction: Direct factorisation of x^n-1 confirms the list above. The count of invariant subspaces with dim in [n/3, 2n/3] is 0 for the primitive-root primes and 2^((n-1)/ord)-scale for the others: about 2^18 for n=127, 2^8 for n=89, 2^4 for n=113.
cheapest_test: Factor x^n-1 over F_2 for all n in 53..131 with a short script (seconds). Tabulate ord_n(2), factor degrees, and the count of divisors with the target dimension. Cross-check the n=131 and n=127 rows against ecdb.
falsifier: Any prime in the predicted primitive-root list that has a divisor of x^n-1 with degree in [n/4, 3n/4], or an invariant-subspace count that differs from 2^(number of Phi_n factors) times the trivial cases.

The general census needs hypotheses ord_n(2)=n-1 and n prime as explicit Nat facts.

title: Rotation-closed low-weight factor base for n where no invariant subspace exists

mechanism: When no useful Frobenius-invariant subspace exists (n=131), use the rotation-closed, non-subspace set W_w = {x : Hamming weight of x in a normal basis <= w}. It is closed under Frobenius, which is a cyclic shift in a normal basis. Store necklace representatives only: |W_w|/n entries, no tables. Membership of a candidate x3 is a popcount against w. Relation probability should match that of a random set of equal density, since weight has no relation to the group law.

Storage and membership cost are 1/n and O(n/64) word operations. A subspace of the same size has no such cost advantage when it does not exist for that n.

title: Exact Fourier yield of S3 over cyclic-code factor bases, ranked by character sums
handbook_section: 6.2.2 Additive character sums / 6.2.4 Generic estimates (with 6.3.3.3 dual BCH distance)
mechanism: For V a Frobenius-invariant subspace (cyclic code with check polynomial h), the number N(V) of (x1,x2,x3) in V^3 with S3=0 equals (1/q) * sum over additive characters psi of sum over V^3 of psi(S3), i.e. a sum of exponential sums restricted to V. Poisson summation over V and V-perp turns it into |V-perp|-many unrestricted sums, and the dual distance of the cyclic code (BCH-type bound) makes low-order trace statistics exactly independent. The Weil/Deligne bound says N(V) = |V|^3/q up to O(q^{3/2}-ish) error, which is vacuous when |V| < q^{1/2}. So the deviation for |V| ~ q^{1/3} is determined by arithmetic of V, not by the bound, and can be measured.
claim: Different invariant subspaces V of the same dimension m ~ n/3 on the same Koblitz curve give relation yields N(V) that differ by more than binomial noise: the coefficient of variation of N(V)/E[N] over all V of dimension m is at least 3 sigma_binomial, and the top 10 percent of V yields at least 1.2x the median.

title: Sparse Gauss-period normal basis for the Weil-restricted Semaev system
handbook_section: 5.3.2 Gauss periods / 5.3.1 Optimal and low complexity normal bases
mechanism: In a type-T Gauss-period normal basis of F_{q^d} over F_q, the multiplication table has at most about (T+1)d nonzero entries, so each coordinate of a product of two elements is a bilinear form with O(d) monomials instead of O(d^2). Weil restriction of S3 (and of S4) to the subfield writes each F_q-coordinate equation as polynomials in the 3d coordinates; in a sparse normal basis the quadratic part (x1x2+x1x3+x2x3)^2 expands into far fewer monomials. Frobenius powers in the basis are index shifts, so the squaring in S3 costs nothing.
claim: On toy composite sizes n=d*m, the Weil-restricted S3 system written in a type-II optimal normal basis has at most 0.5x the monomial count and lower F4 degree of regularity (or equal) than the same system in a polynomial basis, and F4 time falls accordingly.

title: Cubic and sextic Jacobi sums for a mu_3 or mu_6 orbit quotient on j=0 prime-field toys
handbook_section: 6.1.2 Evaluations of Jacobi and Gauss sums of small orders
mechanism: For y^2=x^3+b over F_p with p = 1 mod 3, the order of the group is given by an explicit combination of the cubic Jacobi sum J(chi3,chi3) (with the sextic character picking the twist). The six twists b -> b*u^k have orders p+1-t_k with t_k determined by the Jacobi sum. Separately, x -> zeta3*x is an automorphism of the curve and S3 is invariant under it when a=0 (weighted homogeneity x:2, b:6). Take the factor base modulo mu_6 (negation and mu_3), so the base shrinks by a further 3 and each S3 solution gives 3 equivalent relations. The Jacobi sum is used to pick twists with prime order for the test panel.
claim: On j=0 toy curves, quotienting the factor base and relations by mu_3 (on top of negation) reduces relations needed by 3x and S3 search cost per relation by 3x, with the linear-algebra size dropping by 3x as well, provided the lifted log relation uses the eigenvalue of zeta3 acting on the log (lambda with lambda^2+lambda+1 = 0 mod N).
prediction: Measured relation-collection time to full rank drops by 2.5-3.2x versus negation-only on p about 2^28..2^36 toys. Rank deficiency stays under 2 columns. Final DLP answer matches the baseline on 100 of 100 instances.
cheapest_test: p ~ 2^30, p = 1 mod 3, b chosen by the cubic Jacobi sum so that #E is prime. Run existing IC baseline with orbit key (x up to negation) versus orbit key (x up to mu_3, applying lambda in the matrix). 10 seeds each, interleaved, same S3 solver. Validate logs against rho.
falsifier: Relation count to full rank falls by under 2x, or any wrong log (lambda mismatch). Or the baseline already uses the mu_3 action (then it is not new).

title: Frobenius-power membership test g(sigma)x=0 with sparse generator polynomial
handbook_section: 5.3.5 Fast arithmetic using normal bases / 5.2.1 Basics
mechanism: For V = ker g(sigma), x in V iff XOR over the support of g of sigma^j(x) is zero. In a normal basis sigma^j is a rotation of the bit vector (free), so the test costs wt(g) word-XORs of n/64 words. For V a subfield F_{2^d}, g = x^d+1 has weight 2. In a polynomial basis each Frobenius power is a squaring chain or a precomputed n x n bit matrix. Pair this with choosing, among the invariant V of the right dimension, one whose g has minimum weight.
claim: In a bitsliced relation-collection loop at n=127, x3 in V membership via rotation costs at most 0.1x the cycles of the polynomial-basis matrix version. Total relation-collection time improves by under 5 percent because the quadratic root and inversion dominate (a Cost-level statement), though the membership test itself improves by 10x.
prediction: Membership test: 8-15x fewer cycles. Whole loop: 1-5 percent faster. The type-II ONB multiplication is slower than carry-less polynomial multiplication by 1.5-3x at n=127, so converting only for the membership test would lose. Net effect under 1.05x or negative if the loop must multiply in the normal basis.
cheapest_test: n=127 with V of dimension 63 or 7*9 (g chosen from the 18 degree-7 factors). Microbenchmark membership only (1e8 candidates) in both bases, then the full S3 pair loop at n=31 toy in both bases. Use perf-ipc for cycles on a host with a PMU, otherwise report time only.
falsifier: Full-loop speed-up above 1.2x (then membership is not negligible and the idea matters), or membership speed-up under 3x (then the premise that rotations are free fails in the implementation).
lean_sketch: Definitions: rot : (Fin n -> Bool) -> (Fin n -> Bool), applyPoly g x := fold xor over support. Provable without Mathlib: rot^n = id, applyPoly commutes with rot, applyPoly g x = 0 is xor-closed (a subspace). Cost record: wt(g) * ceil(n/64) in the relations field per test. Hypothesis: g divides x^n-1 as a Bool-polynomial identity, checked by decide for fixed n. The performance claim is a measured Cost inequality, not a theorem.

title: Gray-code incremental products over a subspace factor base
handbook_section: 5.3.5 Fast arithmetic using normal bases
mechanism: Multiplication by a fixed x2 is an F_2-linear map on F_{2^n}. For x1 ranging over a subspace V with basis b_1..b_m, enumerate V in Gray-code order. Then p = x1*x2 changes by XOR with a precomputed b_j*x2 (m mults per x2, amortised over 2^m values of x1) and s = x1+x2 changes by XOR with b_j. In the char-2 S3 solve p x3 + s^2 x3^2 = p^2 + b, the product costs drop to XORs. Remaining per pair cost: one batch inversion (about 3 mults per element), one half-trace table lookup, one mult for x3 = (p/s^2) z.
claim: Inner-loop field multiplications per (x1,x2) pair fall from about 5 to about 4 (20 percent) and measured time per pair falls by 10-20 percent at m>=16.
prediction: Counted mults per pair 4.0 vs 5.0, measured throughput gain 1.1-1.25x, independent of n in [53,131]. No change in relation count. If the batch inversion is replaced by a table of inverses over V (when |V| <= 2^24) the gain could reach 2x for the inversion-bound regime.
cheapest_test: n=53, m=16, Koblitz toy. Implement the pair loop with and without Gray enumeration (same solver otherwise), count field mults with an instrumented field type, and time with 20 interleaved repeats. Check that the relation lists are identical.
falsifier: Counted-mult reduction under 10 percent, or relation list not identical (bug). Or wall-clock gain under 1.05x (memory traffic of the b_j x2 tables dominates).
lean_sketch: Definitions: Gray enumeration as List (Fin m) (the index of the flipped bit at step k is the count of trailing zeros of k+1). Provable without Mathlib: for linear f, f (x xor b_j) = f x xor f b_j, so the incremental update equals the direct product (by funext over Fin n -> Bool and xor algebra), and the Gray sequence visits every element of V exactly once (induction on m). Cost: relations field = pairs * (mults-per-pair) with 4 vs 5 as concrete Nat constants. Hypothesis: multiplication by x2 is Bool-linear, provable from distributivity given as a field axiom.
novelty_note: This is an engineering constant factor on top of the integrated F4/subspace method (it replaces the naive sieve inner loop). A counted-op reduction is an accounting change unless wall-clock is measured. Report both. Not a change in exponent.

title: Completely normal element giving nested compatible Weil-restriction bases for composite n
handbook_section: 5.4.1 The complete normal basis theorem / 5.4.3 Cyclotomic modules and complete generators
mechanism: A completely normal element beta of F_{2^n} over F_2 is normal over every intermediate field F_{2^d}, d | n, at once. Then the trace images Tr_{n/d}(beta) are normal in each subfield and coordinates in different subfields are related by trace-shift maps, so coordinate maps for the whole tower share one basis. For a descent that steps through several subfields (n = 6, 12, 18, 36 with restriction to degrees n/2, n/3, n/6), no basis conversion is needed between steps, and invariant subspaces for each level are nested kernels ker g_d(sigma) with g_d | g_{d'} where d | d'.
claim: For composite n with at least three proper divisors, a descent that restricts successively to subfields using a completely normal basis performs zero basis-conversion linear maps between levels, versus about one n x n bit-matrix multiplication per switch in an unrelated-basis implementation, and nested invariant subspaces V_d subset V_d' make every factor base of level d' contain the base of level d.
prediction: Conversion cost per descent step falls from about n^2/64 word ops to 0. Total descent cost at n=36 is reduced by under 3 percent (conversions are small versus Groebner solving). The nested factor-base property gives no change in relation yield. Existence: a completely normal element exists for every n over F_2 (theorem), so the claim holds for all composite n tested.
cheapest_test: n=12 and n=36 over F_2: compute a completely normal element by search (check normal at every divisor via the rank of the circulant of Tr_{n/d}(beta)), build bases, and count conversion operations in a three-level descent script versus independently drawn normal elements per level. Compare time of the whole script.
falsifier: Search fails to find a completely normal element within the first 1000 random trials at n=36 (the theorem guarantees existence, so a failure points to a bug), or descent time differs from baseline by more than 5 percent in either direction (then the conversion cost matters more than predicted).
lean_sketch: Definitions: IsNormalAt d beta := the d conjugates of Tr_{n/d} beta are F_2-linearly independent (as Fin d -> Fin d -> Bool with Gaussian elimination rank = d, decidable for fixed small n). IsCompletelyNormal beta := forall d, d ∣ n -> IsNormalAt d beta. Provable: by decide for n=6 (an explicit beta). Hypotheses: field arithmetic given as a Fin n -> Bool structure with an explicit multiplication table; existence in general (Blessenohl-Johnsen theorem) is not provable here and is taken as a hypothesis. Cost: descent field gets Cost.descent <= levels * (conversion cost) with conversion cost = 0 under the hypothesis.
novelty_note: Weil restriction descent is integrated, but the basis-compatibility across the subfield tower is not discussed. Expect a small effect. It is mainly relevant to composite n (e.g. 84, 90, 120) and not to prime n such as 131.
